Sports.title: England cannot afford trip to amputee World Cup – and the FA will not help
Sports.content:
Every time Scott Rogers walks into St George’s Park there is a sign on the wall that catches his eye. It boasts that the 330-acre site is the proud home of all England’s football teams. “I look at it every time and go, ‘Well, not all of them’” Rogers says.

As head coach, Rogers guided the England men’s amputee team to the Nations League trophy in 2023. But while the Football Association funds six para national teams, amputee football is not among them.

Now one of the world’s leading amputee nations is struggling to raise enough money to compete at the men’s World Cup in Mexico in November. England earned £21.5m in prize money for finishing third in the World Cup and got £1.1m in preparation funds. The amputee side are trying to scrape together £50,000 to cover their tournament costs.

“The FA say they’re funded for a certain amount of para teams and at the moment there isn’t the funding to bring amputee football into the fold,” Rogers says. “We’re Nations League champions, and there’s a chance we won’t go to this World Cup. For an England team at the top of the game to miss a World Cup due to funding, it doesn’t sit right.”

The amputee programme was under the FA umbrella until 2006, when the governing body cut funding. “That left a lot of bad feeling at the time,” Rogers says.

They set up as a charity and have built a thriving structure. The women’s team reached the quarter-finals of the inaugural World Cup in 2024. The junior system has more than 70 players aged four to 17. They have doctors, strength and conditioning coaches, analysts, technical coaches. It is run by volunteers and funded by donations.

Rogers, a former youth coach at Wigan and Blackburn, became involved in 2000. “Whatever I’d do with an under-18 elite able-bodied team, I’d do with these lads because they were incredible,” he says.

View image in fullscreen Scott Rogers (fourth from left) coached England’s men’s amputee team for a year and helped them win the Nations League. Photograph: Jake Kirkman/EAFA

“When people think about amputee football, they probably imagine it’s slow and laborious. It’s the opposite: fast-paced, brutal at times. They snap crutches almost every game. I fell in love with it.”

FA representatives shadowed the team at the 2022 World Cup and were impressed. But though they made a funding offer, it fell short of what was in place. “All the signs were good,” Rogers says. But the offer would have reduced training frequency and cut the number of coaches and specialists. It was declined. Coming back under the FA umbrella while continuing to take money from other sources was not an option, Rogers says.

When Owen Coyle Jr – son of the former Burnley manager – stepped down as head coach in 2023, Rogers took over. Previously, players each had to raise £1,500 to secure their place for tournaments, but Rogers scrapped the requirement.

An appearance on ITV’s Good Morning Britain provided the funding boost to play at Euro 2024, their pot rising from £4,000 of their £40,000 target to more than £50,000 within hours. For the World Cup this year, they are not even halfway to the £50,000 needed.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“These people don’t get paid for playing, they have jobs,” Rogers says. “If the programme isn’t of a certain level, what’s the incentive to continue to play? They sacrifice holidays with their families.”

View image in fullscreen Rhyce Ramsden (right) flies into an attempted tackle on fellow England amputee player Nathan Fisher (left) during a training session. Photograph: LAJ Photography

Rogers, who stepped down as head coach in 2024 but remains heavily involved, says even £50,000 a year from the FA would go a long way. “When you look at the funding within the FA and the money involved in football, what we’re asking for to make an amazing programme is a drop in the ocean.”

The amputee players are paying for their own flights for a game in Ireland next month. “It’s there, it’s ready to go,” Rogers says. “But the danger is if we don’t secure long-term funding soon – because we can’t keep going on telly, it’s a model that won’t continue to work – I feel that we’re going to start to fall away.”

Rogers says there are “brilliant” people at the FA who run the para programme and want amputee football included, but cannot secure the funding from above. “There are always ongoing conversations with the FA and it’s not a bad relationship. But unless something changes and somebody stands up and goes: ‘Listen, this can’t happen any more,’ I think it’ll be ground into the ground when we’re on the verge of something incredibly special.”

An FA spokesperson said: “We continue to work closely with the England Amputee Football Association to support, identify and help deliver their key priorities over the coming season, and the continued development of amputee football in England.”

Sports.title: Dejan Kulusevski and Mohammed Kudus left OUT of Tottenham's 35-man squad for pre-season tour as fears grow over stars' long-term injuries
Sports.content:
Both Dejan Kulusevski and Mohammed Kudus have been left out of Tottenham's squad for their pre-season tour of New Zealand and Australia, as the duo's recovery continues to falter.

Spurs are continuing their pre-season with three fixtures taking place across Auckland and Sydney, following a slender 1-0 win over League One side MK Dons at Hotspur Way on Wednesday.

But Kulusevski and Kudus have both been omitted from Roberto De Zerbi's 35-man squad, as both struggle to recover from long-term injuries.

There had been hope that Kudus was closing in on a comeback, having not featured for Tottenham since significantly injuring his quad against Sunderland in January, as he had been pictured back at the gym at the Spurs training base.

However, Kulusevski has not been pictured back in Enfield, with fears over his knee issues continuing to grow.

The Swede has not played for Tottenham in 14 months, having had surgery on his right patella after injuring it ahead of Spurs' Europa League triumph in May 2025.

Mohammed Kudus has returned to training but will not travel with Spurs' squad to New Zealand and Australia

Kulusevski has been absent for 14 months and is no closer to recovering from his knee injury

Two more wide players have also been left at home, with Wilson Odobert and Xavi Simons said to remain in London 'to continue their rehabilitation'.

Both Odobert and Simons are still months away from fitness after cruciate knee ligament surgeries.

Tottenham have also confirmed that Guglielmo Vicario will be absent from the pre-season tour after picking up a 'minor knock' in training.

£185million duo Sandro Tonali and Mateus Fernandes, fresh from his stunner against MK Dons, will travel with the squad to the southern hemisphere.

Fellow new signings Andy Robertson, Jan Paul van Hecke, and Martin Dubravka will also enjoy their first tour with Spurs, but Marcos Senesi is on an extended break after making the World Cup final with Argentina.

Robertson appears to have already made friends at the club, with James Maddison already making jokey jibes toward the Scottish left-back.

The midfielder posted a picture of the former Liverpool man looking moody on his Instagram story, followed by the caption: ‘He better liven up if he’s my company for this 26-hour flight.’

Sports.title: Inside Jeff Bezos' bid to buy into Liverpool: The role the Amazon billionaire could play, what 'super smart' £1.35bn investment means for transfer business, how it affects FSG - and what happens next
Sports.content:
As soon as the news emerged that Jeff Bezos was interested in forming part of a consortium to buy a stake in Liverpool FC, the jokes began.

Anfield was to become the Amazon Arena, a nod to the company where Bezos made his fortune. New signings would arrive on next-day delivery. Liverpool would not just be competing to be champions of Europe but the galaxy, referring to Bezos's part in the 21st-century space race.

Whatever your opinion on the fourth-richest man in the world, it is hard for Reds fans not to dream of the endless possibilities under a man worth £190billion according to Forbes.

But will Liverpool actually see any of the proposed £1.35bn investment? What role, if any, will Bezos play? And is it time for those supporters to get excited?

Daily Mail Sport has spoken to sources on both sides of the Atlantic to help tackle some of the big questions…

Jeff Bezos has discussed the possibility of joining a consortium which is pushing to buy a stake in Liverpool

Liverpool are in a period of transition with Andoni Iraola taking over as head coach in June

What is going on?

Liverpool's owners Fenway Sports Group are in talks to sell a stake in the club to a consortium backed by Amit Bhatia and funded in part by the family of steel tycoon Lakshmi Mittal.

Bezos is interested in being part of the consortium and other names are also keen to get involved.

Bhatia will be in charge of the bid. He stepped down as co-owner and director of Championship side Queens Park Rangers on Tuesday after nearly two decades at Loftus Road, where he has a stand named after him.

The 46-year-old is the son-in-law of Mittal, the 73rd richest man in the world with £23.4bn to his name per Forbes, and the consortium is keen to buy around £1.3bn in the club.

A spokesperson for Liverpool's owners FSG told Daily Mail Sport earlier this week: 'An investment consortium led, managed, and represented by Amit Bhatia has expressed interest in making a strategic minority investment in Liverpool Football Club.'

It is thought that FSG welcome the potential opportunity and this is another way the conglomerate, who also own the baseball behemoth Boston Red Sox, are looking to further position the club for success.

It would be a similar move, though on a larger scale, to when FSG sold 4 per cent to Dynasty Equity in September 2023. Principal chair John W Henry has always been eager for additional investment while still being keen to hold the majority stake.

FSG sources stress that no deal is signed just yet, with the parties in early discussions at this stage, though the fact the consortium has been put together is a significant development. And there are signals that everyone involved is keen for a deal to be done.

Businessman Amit Bhatia is part of the consortium in talks to buy a stake in the Reds

Would it be a wise move for FSG?

Football finance expert Kieran Maguire certainly thinks so.

He tells Daily Mail Sport: 'As far as the potential Liverpool investment is concerned, it looks like it's going to be up to 30 per cent or £1.3bn. That values the club at just over £4bn, which is broadly in line with expectations.

'From FSG's point of view, it's a super smart piece of business. Yes, they have sold part of the club before but this will ensure they still own a controlling stake of around 60 per cent.

'So in terms of the long-term strategy of the club and the individual transfer windows and recruitment issues, it is still FSG's decisions that are being made. If they are selling 30 per cent, that money goes to FSG not Liverpool, so there is no physical impact upon the club's coffers.

'If the club is looking to borrow money at a future date for whatever circumstances and you are owned by Mittal's son-in-law and Bezos, they will be in a position to lend money on an interest-free basis which can only help in terms of cash flow.

'Also, having a potential partner of the magnitude of Bezos does mean there is the opportunity for synergies. If Amazon Prime want to increase their global influence, then one way could be to do a partnership with Liverpool, whether in terms of content or sponsorship.

'Liverpool goes out to the world and Amazon goes out to the world as well. As well out of the world, maybe! He is flying people into space after all.'

Finance experts believe it would be 'a super smart piece of business' from FSG to sell a stake in the club

What is Bezos's involvement?

Bezos, who made his massive wealth by founding Amazon out of his Seattle garage in 1994 and has since launched ventures such as (the unfortunately-named, for Liverpool fans) space company Blue Origin and the Washington Post news group, is interested.

Sky News reported that Bezos was invited to join the syndicate led by Bhatia. His exit from QPR on Tuesday, the same day the news broke about his interest to invest in Liverpool, came at a telling time.

The intentions of the consortium are clear, though Bezos has historically been cautious when it comes to major sports deals. He was interested in buying the current Super Bowl winners Seattle Seahawks and fellow NFL team Washington Commanders but pulled out.

There has been an influx in similar deals in recent years, notably Ineos' investment in Manchester United and Todd Boehly with Clearlake at Chelsea.

While Boehly is still seen as the figurehead of that move, Behdad Eghbali and Clearlake run the show. Eghbali loves football and has been pleasantly surprised at the English sporting culture when attending games at Stamford Bridge.

Perhaps we will see Bezos in the posh seats at Anfield before too long, too.

It is believed that Bezos was invited to join the syndicate led by Bhatia

What happens next?

The news of FSG being open to selling a stake came as a surprise to many, including some personnel at the club.

It is not said to be an indication that Liverpool's Boston-based owners, who bought the club in 2010, are looking to sell up. If anything, it is part of their strategic plan to position the club to prosper.

Some fans point the finger at FSG for various shortcomings.

They are no saints, for sure – some of their ticketing policies and price hikes have irked many – but they have done far more good than bad during their time as custodians of the club, including regenerating Anfield and financially backing the club into a successful era on the pitch.

As for the consortium, sources believe they are serious.

The day-to-day running of the club would be unlikely to change if it goes through, but being backed by such mega-rich investors can never be a bad thing.

Sports.title: How Sandro Tonali and Mateus Fernandes proved in just 45 minutes that this is a whole new Tottenham this season - and why £185m duo's new team-mates could barely believe their eyes
Sports.content:
If first impressions are anything to go by, then Tottenham Hotspur should get used to controlling midfield.

Their new-look £185million pivot dictated play in their opening pre-season friendly - a 1-0 win against MK Dons on Wednesday - providing a 45-minute glimpse of what to expect from club record-breaking transfers Sandro Tonali (£100m from Newcastle) and Mateus Fernandes (£85m from West Ham).

Let’s get the balancing act out of the way. Yes, it was only a pre-season match. Yes, it was only one half of football. And yes, it was against inferior League One opposition, MK Dons.

But their desire to impose themselves immediately was encouraging. Fernandes took just three minutes to exhibit his natural ability. MK Dons goalkeeper Craig MacGillivray punched Mathys Tel’s corner clear, but Fernandes lurked outside the area and wrapped his right foot around the ball on the volley and hammered it into the top corner.

Pre-season or not, it was a top-quality finish - a sneak peek at his talent. Seeing the first manifestation of his £85m transfer fee, his new team-mates laughed in disbelief when the ball hit the back of the net. Spurs chiefs would have celebrated with a sigh of relief as he demonstrated the first sign of being a hit.

What a hit, Mateus Fernandes 💥



Watch our pre-season games live on SPURSPLAY! — Tottenham Hotspur (@SpursOfficial) July 22, 2026

Mateus Fernandes finds the top corner inside five minutes of his Tottenham debut

Sandro Tonali, whose fee could rise to £100million, also impressed in the pre-season friendly

Spurs changed their entire XI at half-time - as is customary at the start of pre-season - making the sample size small. Regardless, it was an extremely active debut. Everything went through Fernandes. 81 touches in the first half; no player had more.

Playing as a No 8, he was supported by fellow new arrival Tonali in a more deep-lying role. And for a pair playing together for the first time, they showed a surprising level of synchronisation. They both picked up on each other’s movement, finding space or covering when the other was on the ball.

If that can be developed in a week, then Spurs are on the right footing with this pair as they attempt to return to the top half after finishing 17th in consecutive seasons - avoiding relegation last term by just two points. Much like Fernandes, Tonali was busy - registering 70 touches; only his midfield partner had more.

Tonali was given the license to run forward into the channels from his holding midfield role as Spurs tried to break down MK Dons’ disciplined, low block. The Italian is versatile; not only is he a ball-winner, but he has a big engine and an array of line-breaking passes at his disposal. It enables him to play as a six or an eight. Partnering Fernandes, however, it seems that can be relatively fluid.

Perhaps the biggest boost is that Spurs’ lavish midfield is well-rested after Italy failed to qualify for the World Cup while Portugal overlooked Fernandes. It offers Roberto De Zerbi a full pre-season to get his ideas across to the heartbeat of the team, the anchors between defence and attack - a luxury that most managers do not have this summer.

What remains to be seen, though, is how they will handle teams that pose a greater threat. There was little to handle from the MK Dons attack, and they did not have bundles of the ball, which limited the occasions Spurs could press with intensity - a hallmark of De Zerbi’s teams.

The pair will need to step up to the increased workload, and that process should begin to take shape as the quality of opposition increases.

Tottenham will now jet off Down Under, facing Auckland FC, Sydney FC and Chelsea, before returning to north London to play Getafe and Hoffenheim, with little under a month to go until the Premier League opener at Brentford on August 22.

Fernandes and Tonali are among £240m worth of reinforcements given to Roberto De Zerbi this summer

There were a couple of mistakes. Both gave the ball away in dangerous areas as MK Dons embarked on encouraging counter-attacks. Tonali was bailed out by the offside flag, Fernandes by a lung-busting run from a recovering defender. A couple of misplaced passes deserve the pre-season benefit of the doubt, though.

That said, it was an exhibition of intelligent passes in the main - particularly from Tonali, who played a pivotal role in transition as he shifted the ball into wide areas.

His highlight came as he carried the ball from deep towards the halfway line before disguising a bending pass with his right foot into the feet of Tel, who cut inside and squared to Conor Gallagher inside the penalty area. An incisive move from back to front - crafted by Tonali - Gallagher couldn’t quite connect to top it off.

On the basis of this showing, the Englishman will need to step it up to keep up with Spurs' new dynamic duo.

Sports.title: Argentina assistant coach explains reason behind Dani Olmo 'punch' in ugly post-World Cup final scenes - as he insists 'it was more of a push'
Sports.content:
Argentina assistant coach explains reason behind Dani Olmo 'punch' in ugly post-World Cup final scenes - as he insists 'it was more of a push'

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Argentina assistant coach Roberto Ayala has attempted to downplay his post-match clashes with Spain's players after the World Cup final.

Lionel Scaloni's side were so close to retaining their title on Sunday after lifting the trophy in 2022, but were beaten 1-0 by Spain following a tense and scrappy affair.

They were aggressive throughout the match, as they had been during their semi-final victory over England, yet things escalated at the end of the game.

Having already had Enzo Fernandez sent off for a wild late challenge on Pau Cubarsi towards the end of normal time, Paredes grabbed Eric Garcia by the throat and pushed Gavi to the ground by putting his hand in the Spaniard's face.

Nahuel Molina also thumped Rodri in the torso as he was running by to celebrate Spain's triumph, while Thiago Almada was involved, too.

Paredes even appeared to throw punches during the altercations and Ayala, who is Scaloni's assistant, held Garcia around the throat before he was caught on camera striking Dani Olmo.

Argentina coach Roberto Ayala has tried to downplay his clashes with Spain's players

Ayala clashed with Eric Garcia before he appeared to strike Dani Olmo after Sunday's final

Then, as the Spanish squad lifted the trophy, Argentina's players faced away from their opponents in what was viewed by many as a poor show of sportsmanship.

FIFA have since launched an investigation into their behaviour, which could have serious consequences for those involved.

However, Ayala has attempted to defend what happened, insisting his clash was 'more of a push than anything else'.

Addressing the incident for the first time, he told Esports Migdia on Valencia Capital Radio: 'Obviously I’m sorry. Because of my position, I can’t allow a feeling, or what I might receive from the other party, to change my mood and my actions.

'I’m sorry, but for me, these are things that stay there and that’s it. For me, things need to be put behind us and left there.

'It was more of a push than anything else, it wasn’t a punch like they’re saying, and that’s it. It was a reaction to something he said, but that’s it. If I see him, I’ll obviously apologise to him in person.'

Ayala then tried to add further context to the general ugly scenes on the pitch at the MetLife Stadium as he added: 'It’s a shame, and you have to accept the facts and the things you’ve done on the field.

'When the game ends, what I see is a fight in the middle of the pitch, and we rush to go after our players, and it ends up like that because that’s not who we are.

'I take responsibility for what I did. My intention was to go and separate them, that was my intention, but sometimes things happen and emotions run high, but that’s no excuse.

'And given my position, my behaviour has to be different, regardless of what I receive.'

Ayala (right), a former Argentine international, serves as assistant to boss Lionel Scaloni

Announcing their probe into what had gone on in the aftermath of Sunday's game, FIFA said: 'Following an assessment of the relevant match reports for the FIFA World Cup final between Spain and Argentina, and in line with article 36 of the FIFA disciplinary code (FDC), the FIFA disciplinary committee has appointed a disciplinary and ethics prosecutor to investigate potential breaches of the FDC with regard to the post-match incidents.

'Further details will be communicated by the FIFA disciplinary committee once the prosecutor’s report has been completed.'

Despite the nasty scenes, Spain midfielder Gavi, who was pushed to the ground by Paredes amid the chaos, surprisingly defended his Argentine counterparts.

During Spain's celebrations back home, Gavi was asked for his take on what had gone on and said: 'No, to tell you the truth, I don't think he (Leandro Paredes) should be suspended.

'I understand it's not a good image for children, but I think there's also that side to football, which is a bit more physical, more aggressive.

'The most logical thing would have been to send him off during the match, and that's it. In the end, I think it's all football, and it has to be that way.'

'Every time I was in the middle, I saw my average drop... it was disheartening': JAMIE SMITH on his horror Ashes, repaying England's faith and the 'fantastic' coach changing his game

Unlock more of the best of our cricket coverage with a DailyMail+ subscription - brilliant exclusives, in-depth insight and the writers you love every day

Jamie Smith wants to use the Hundred to reignite his England white-ball career – and plans to ensure his Test average heads back in the right direction after a difficult few months in which both his batting and his wicketkeeping have been under scrutiny.

Smith has not played any limited-overs international cricket since struggling in New Zealand before the Ashes, while he has averaged just 21 in Tests since his stunning double of 184 not out and 88 against India at Edgbaston in July 2025.

But he regards his move to Southern Brave, his third Hundred franchise in three years, as a chance both for a fresh start and to impress England white-ball coach Brendon McCullum, sacked as Test coach but in the pink after T20 and ODI series wins over India.

‘My goals have always been to play three formats for England,’ Smith tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘I’ve had a little taste of it, and the Hundred is always a great opportunity to go out and do well against some of the best players in the world and use it as a springboard.’

Smith has played only five T20s, mainly because England have a settled and destructive opening pair in Phil Salt and Jos Buttler. But his 19 ODIs have produced just three fifties and an average of 21.

‘It just wasn’t consistent enough,’ he says. ‘I had a couple of decent enough innings, but didn’t make them count. I can’t complain with the opportunity I was given. It’s trying to learn from that.’

Jamie Smith endured a difficult Ashes Down Under last winter, in a series he admits was 'disheartening'

But the wicketkeeper is intent on repaying England's faith in him, and rediscovering his best form

But his main goal, ahead of next month’s three-match series against Pakistan, is to repay the selectors’ faith after they moved him above Ben Stokes up to No 6 in the Test side against New Zealand.

He describes his series as ‘disjointed’, having made a crucial 39 in a low-scoring first Test at Lord’s before missing the second at the Oval because of paternity leave. In the decider at Trent Bridge, his well-paced second-innings 60 came too late to save England as the Bazball era ended in smoke and flames. But he appreciated his promotion.

‘It was a confidence-booster, especially after a disappointing Ashes,’ he says. ‘I felt like every time I was walking out to the middle, I was seeing my average drop. When you’re not playing well, it’s quite disheartening.

‘That’s something I’d be looking to improve on, trying to push that up as much as possible. There’s no reason why I can’t go to No 6 and have success. I know it’d be a good effort to go back to the standards I set at the start. But if I can go a little bit further towards pushing it back in the right direction, that’d be nice.’

Smith, whose average has slipped from 58 after that Edgbaston Test to just under 40, faced criticism during the Ashes for his demeanour behind the stumps, especially from former England wicketkeeper Matt Prior, who felt he was too quiet.

‘I understand people’s opinions,’ says Smith. ‘You want to do the best you can, but I think the thing for me is trying to put my own stamp on it. I don’t think I’d be changing too much.’

It’s why he has parked the captaincy ambitions he once harboured at Surrey. ‘I wouldn’t say it necessarily is for me – not with my personality. I’m very relaxed and enjoy the way things are going now, and playing off other people. I’m happy to play the supporting role.’

Smith says he will miss McCullum’s Test coaching after feeling supported by him on his entry to the team two years ago, but has enjoyed working closely with the former England wicketkeeper Sarah Taylor at a time when every mistake behind the stumps is accompanied by social-media cries of ‘Ben Foakes wouldn’t have dropped that’.

‘Sarah’s been fantastic,’ he says. ‘She brings a lot of energy to the group, not just for me, and she’s always willing to work at things and chat them through.

‘It’s disappointing when you drop a couple of catches and the same sort of things crop up about your keeping.

'But I felt like overall I was keeping a lot better. It’s frustrating that they’re the things that get brought up.’

‘She's been fantastic,’ says Smith of Sarah Taylor (pictured). ‘She brings a lot of energy to the group, not just for me, and she’s always willing to work at things and chat them through'

Smith showed immense promise in the early stages of his international career - now it's time to build on it

The pressure grew against New Zealand, whose own wicketkeeper, Tom Blundell, provided a masterclass in standing up to the stumps, keeping Harry Brook and Joe Root tethered to the crease.

Once England had left out Ollie Robinson after Lord’s, their bowlers were generally too quick for Smith to mirror the tactics. He says it felt ‘out of my comfort zone’, but adds: ‘It’s definitely something we’ll be working on.’

Smith has just turned 26, but has already established himself as one of the cleanest strikers in the English game. His international strike-rates are all formidable: 73 in Tests, 112 in ODIs and 194 in T20s. If he can get his other numbers heading in the right direction, there may be no stopping him.

Sports.title: 'I can't wear high heels too often... my feet are my money-makers!': Britain's 'sexy and aggressive' sprinter AMY HUNT reveals how 'radical confidence' helped her gatecrash world's elite - and her love of 14th-century Italian poetry
Sports.content:
Amy Hunt is waiting for her mum, Claire, to arrive on the train from Newark to London.

‘We always enjoy a leisurely ladies' lunch when we’re here,’ she explains, putting down her Gucci handbag and sipping on a double espresso in the Daily Mail Sport offices in Kensington.

‘Sometimes it needs to be a quick Wagamama but if it’s Mum then I like to treat her. I’m now in a position where I’m lucky enough to be able to spoil my parents and really take care of them. I like fine dining. I like to give her a boujie experience and make her feel all lovely.

‘It wasn’t easy raising two incredibly sporty, high-achieving daughters. My mum would be at cricket practice at Trent Bridge with my sister (who was in Nottinghamshire's academy) and my dad would be with me at track practice. My legs run really fast and because of that I can now give my parents the life I want them to have.’

Winning a silver medal in the 200metres at last year’s World Athletics Championships has opened plenty of doors for England’s latest track star.

The 24-year-old will compete in the 100m and 4x100m relay at the Commonwealth Games in Scotland over the next fortnight, the latest chapter in her blossoming career which was turbo-boosted when she described herself as 'sexy and aggressive' after that runners-up finish in Tokyo.

Hunt's confidence, her glamorous look and her choice of words – she also said you can be 'an academic badass and a track goddess at the same time' – propelled her from the back pages to the front.

British sprint star Amy Hunt, photographed in the Daily Mail Sport studios

Hunt graduated from the University of Cambridge with an English literature degree in 2023 but student halls are a thing of the past. Here in London, the Hunts are booked into the suite at the luxury hotel Kimpton Fitzroy – one of model David Gandy’s favourites – and a spot of shopping is on the cards, too.

‘We went to the Saatchi gallery last time we were here,' Hunt adds. 'They had an exhibition on flowers, with some William Morris prints. I’ve lived abroad in Padova (Italy) for three years now so I don’t get to see her as often as I would like. Spending time together in the UK is a joyful rarity.

'Mum manages antiques fairs. We have the same enjoyment for beautiful, material things. If there’s time, then we might go to Liberty's (department store) and have a wander around.

‘Winning a world individual medal definitely puts you in new rooms and new conversations. We don’t get the same financial support as other sports but we’re in the lucky position where we get paid more than niche Olympic sports like pentathlon.

‘Every sport is chasing the PR jump that F1 had (through the Netlflix documentary Drive to Survive) and there are always new initiatives coming in to try and make track big. We train in Italy so I have to say no to a lot of things. Vogue parties, movie premieres, opportunities to fly to Goodwood in a helicopter...

‘Spending an entire day in tiny stiletto heels isn’t ideal for training. I don’t wear heels as often as most women so my feet aren’t used to it. We work in such fine margins. My feet and my ankles and my legs are my money-makers, essentially.

'They’re quite susceptible to minor changes. Even when I get a new pair of spikes, sometimes I get blisters. That can have a big knock-on effect on one week of training.

‘This is so gross but my two big toenails had to be removed in Tokyo and then I got blisters on the end of both toes. Before every single race, my coach was having to tape up my toes so they weren’t bleeding everywhere. We were in a very hot, muggy climate and if they get infected, then that can have a big knock-on effect. It’s not all glamorous parties and holidays.’

Hunt's confidence, her glamorous look and her eloquence have propelled her from the back pages to the front

She won silver in the 200m at last year’s World Championships and will compete in the 100m and the 4x100m relay at the Commonwealth Games in Scotland over the next fortnight

Hunt oozes self-confidence. She is as comfortable discussing Italian opera as Charli xcx. Her apartment overlooks a basilica and one of her goals is to learn enough Italian to be able to read Giovanni Boccaccio’s 14th-century poetry in its native tongue.

‘I live the coolest life,' she says. 'One thing I really love about myself is I go out of my way to create my dream life. I moved to Italy at 21 and live in a gorgeous renaissance city surrounded by artwork. The world’s first botanical garden is 200 metres from my house.

‘It’s a place where I can really enjoy being Amy and where I can build my life outside of track. It’s also so good for training because it’s just us in our little bubble. We go to this track in the mountains which has church towers and the bells start ringing. You just think, “Wow”. If I’m having a bad day, I just go and buy a gelato, walk around and read my book. I really love it.

‘I’m now in a place where I can wake up and say to myself, “I am one of the fastest women in the world”. That’s really cool, it’s something I’ve always dreamed of doing. I’ve been gaining confidence week on week for the last two years. I have to stand on that start-line thinking, “I’m the fastest person here, I’m going to win this race”. Otherwise, why would I be standing on that start line? It’s all a game of confidence.

‘I’ve realised the better way to approach things is with that somewhat reckless optimism. My coach (Marco Airale) prepares us for everything and has his massive spreadsheets with figures crawling everywhere, but once I step on that start-line there’s absolutely nothing he can do.

'Especially with the 100m, there are no tactics involved, no gameplan… it’s all on me. I have to have a radical confidence.’

Posing for photographs in our Daily Mail studio, Hunt needs no instructions on how to work the camera. She explains her OUAI haircare routine to the photographer and discusses her upcoming nail appointment with one of London’s top manicurists.

‘I’ve fallen more and more in love with racing so now that confidence comes easily,' she says. 'I have a lot of love for (American sprinter) Sha'Carri Richardson on the track because she knows exactly who she is.

'Spending an entire day in tiny stiletto heels isn’t ideal for training. I don’t wear heels as often as most women so my feet aren’t used to it'

'You only get one shot at it all, so why would you not live every day with reckless abandonment and reckless confidence?'

'She doesn’t care if you or I disagree with her. The best sprinters in the world have such a strong sense of self that they’re unshakable. It’s the same with Noah Lyles. I aspire to be like that, too.

‘I love people like Dua Lipa in the same sort of way. She knows exactly who she is and she lives a very cool life. She’s just got married to her gorgeous fiancee, she’s a popstar and she has that sense that life is supposed to be fun.

'You only get one shot at it all, so why would you not live every day with reckless abandonment and reckless confidence? I would like a wedding like hers. I would love to get married in Italy because I have such strong roots there, but I don’t have anyone to get married to right now… so!’

Hunt’s immediate focus is on the finish line at Scotstoun. She became just the fourth British woman to break the 11-second barrier for the 100m last month and successfully defended her British title. Her star is rising and, as a self-confessed material girl, her eyes are only for gold.

‘The Commonwealth Games is overlaid with all these different memories of watching it,' Hunt says. 'There’s a picture of me freshly-born on the changing mat watching Darren Campbell, who is now my mentor. It’s a bit of a full circle moment.

‘Our No 1 priority this year is the Europeans but the Commonwealths will be super exciting because I’ve never done it. People I train with say Birmingham 2022 was one of the most fun champs they’ve ever done, so I’m looking forward to it.

‘I have really big dreams and goals... I want to win multiple Olympic golds, I want to win world titles and I don’t feel like I should be ashamed to say that'

'A gold medal at the Commonwealths would be unbelievably cool. As a sprinter, we always get asked what matters most: times or medals. It’s medals, without any shadow of a doubt.

‘I have really big dreams and goals. When we’re in relay meetings, we know we can challenge the best in the world from this tiny little country. Collectively, we’ve never been stronger.

'I want to win multiple Olympic golds, I want to win world titles and I don’t feel like I should be ashamed to say that. I don’t want to sit here and say, “Now I’ve won a medal, I just want to make the final”.

'I’ve won a silver medal so now I have to back myself towards gold. I have to wake up every morning thinking, “I want to win that Olympic gold”. If I don’t believe in myself, then why should you? I have to be my biggest cheerleader and it excites me. I love the journey I’m on towards that Olympic gold.’

Sports.title: MLS launches bombshell investigation into David Beckham's Inter Miami for alleged tampering over Casemiro signing
Sports.content:
MLS launches bombshell investigation into David Beckham's Inter Miami for alleged tampering over Casemiro signing

Follow all of today's transfer developments with Window Watch HERE

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Former Manchester United midfielder Casemiro’s move to Inter Miami is under investigation by Major League Soccer over allegations of tampering by Sir David Beckham’s club.

Miami announced Casemiro’s signing on Wednesday in a deal to run until the end of next season with the option to extend it until 2029. However, almost immediately MLS revealed that they are looking into an allegation relating to how Miami acquired the discovery rights from LA Galaxy to sign the 34-year-old Brazil international.

The discovery list gives MLS clubs first refusal over prospective signings and prevents them from competing against one another for a player. The Galaxy had the discovery rights to Casemiro but Miami said they acquired them in an agreement believed to be worth around £750,000.

‘Major League Soccer is reviewing a tampering allegation against Inter Miami CF,’ the statement read. ‘The league is gathering all relevant information and will refrain from further comment until the review is complete.

‘While Inter Miami CF and the LA Galaxy have reached a settlement for the discovery priority to sign Casemiro, the terms will be released upon conclusion of the tampering investigation.’

Inter Miami confirmed the signing of former Manchester United midfielder Casemiro

MLS immediately confirmed an investigation has been launched into David Beckham's into an allegation relating to how Miami acquired the discovery rights from LA Galaxy

Miami have fallen foul of MLS’s financial regulations in the past. In 2021, they were fined £1.5m for falsely reporting Blaise Matuidi’s salary, which also resulted in chief operating officer Paul McDonough being suspended for a year and managing owner Jorge Mas being fined £187,000.

The club were also hit with penalties of £1.7m relating to similar breaches involving Andres Reyes, Leandro Gonzalez Pirez, Nicolas Figal and Julian Carranza.

Casemiro is joining Miami as a free agent following four years at Old Trafford after United decided not to extend his contract. The former Real Madrid star helped Brazil reach the quarter-finals of the World Cup earlier this month where they were knocked out by Norway.

Sports.title: Only ONE England player makes FIFA's 2026 World Cup team of the tournament as fans choose Man United star in defence - and cult hero gets the nod
Sports.content:
FIFA have only selected one England player in their World Cup team of the tournament.

After six weeks of action in the United States, Canada, and Mexico, in which Spain ended up adding a second star to their crest after beating Argentina at MetLife Stadium on Sunday, the football governing body has announced their ‘Dream XI’.

The team of the tournament is selected based on votes from the fans, and only Jude Bellingham managed to sneak into the side from the Three Lions squad.

The 23-year-old midfielder netted seven goals, the most-ever by an England player in a single World Cup, as the Three Lions secured their best placing at the tournament since the triumph in 1966 by beating France 6-4 in the third-place play-off.

The majority of the team was completed by the fellow semi-finalists as three spots in the team were filled by Spain players, with three more from France, and two from the former champions Argentina.

Bellingham is joined by Rodri, who lifted the World Cup trophy aloft as Spain captain, and Michael Olise.

Jude Bellingham was the only England player voted to be in the World Cup 'Dream XI'

40-year-old Vozinha was selected in goal after earning cult hero status for his role in Cape Verde's run to the round of 32

The Spanish midfielder was back to his best at this tournament, and his performances in the spine of the champions' side earned him the Golden Ball. Meanwhile, Olise secured the record for the most assists at a single World Cup with seven.

In front of them, the new all-time World Cup record goalscorer Kylian Mbappe, who won the Golden Boot, occupies the right wing, while the man he overtook in his final game of the tournament, Lionel Messi, is on the left.

Messi was the first to break the scoring record, netting five goals in his first two games of the tournament to surpass Miroslav Klose's previous record of 16 goals.

However, the goals dried up after the round of 16 stage, and he has likely finished his World Cup career with an astonishing 20 goals.

In between them is Norway's Erling Haaland, who spearheaded his country to a first-ever quarter-final by scoring seven goals in his first appearance at the competition.

The back four contained Spanish full-backs Marc Cucurella and Pedro Porro, while France's Dayot Upamecano and Argentina's Lisandro Martinez were selected in the heart of defence.

And at the base of the team, in between the sticks, was none other than Cape Verde goalkeeper Vozinha.

The 40-year-old was one of the heroes of his country's remarkable run to the last-32 stage before they were beaten 3-2 by Argentina after extra-time.

As well as keeping a clean sheet against Spain and Saudi Arabia, Vozinha made 18 saves across the tournament and outperformed his xG against by 0.9.

The shot-stopper also hit the headlines for gaining an outrageous amount of Instagram followers throughout the World Cup.

At the start of Cape Verde's World Cup opener with Spain, he only had 50,000 followers on Instagram. But after making a memorable seven saves, that number dramatically increased, with Vozinha now having 29.5million followers.

Sports.title: Tyson Fury pulls rabbit out of the hat to justify Mariusz Wach fight
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury pulls rabbit out of the hat to justify Mariusz Wach fight

Tyson Fury takes on Mariusz Wach on Friday night in a warm-up fight nobody asked for - but the giant heavyweight has a trick up his sleeve

View Image Tyson Fury and Mariusz Wach face off

Tyson Fury has turned the fight nobody wanted to see into the hottest ticket in town - by competing for free.

‌



Fury had insisted he would only return to the ring to face bitter rival Anthony Joshua. But he is now putting that mega-fight at risk by taking on veteran heavyweight Mariusz Wach in Thailand tomorrow night. Fury has been criticised for his choice of opponent - but claims he won't take a penny from the clash.

‌



Instead the £250,000 banked from the 1,500 fans in attendance will be donated to a local children's charity. And Fury said: "This is a beautiful place with beautiful people and great training facilities. "I feel at peace with everything here whereas before I had a lot of pressure on me and I felt a little bit s****y all the time.

‌



"The rain at home wasn't good. I thrive in warmer climates and I feel rejuvenated. I found the Father Ray Foundation and arranged to visit. They've helped thousands and thousands of sick and deprived children all over the country. Most of their donations come from people gift-giving, rather than government funding so it means a lot to me to be able to give back.

‌



"Being a father of seven children myself, it was heartbreaking to see those little kids and to do something good for them and give back is an unbelievable opportunity for me. Which other world champion or high-level athlete on earth would do a performance in a 1,500-seater in Pattaya?

"Do you think David Beckham would play a professional football match here, or someone famous like that? They're just not going to do it, because a lot of celebrities and big sports stars think they're bigger than they actually are whereas I just think I'm the same I've always been, a big fat f***er in the shower."

Fury, who laboured to a points victory over Arslanbek Makhmudov in April, should swat Wach aside with ease. The 46-year-old has lost seven of his last 10 fights and recently switched to MMA. Earlier this year he took on three social media influencers in a ridiculous three-on-one circus fight.

Article continues below

Victory for Fury coupled with the same result for Joshua will leave the rivals free to finally face each other later this year. But Fury insists he is not looking past Wach. "Everyone comes to try and beat me up and they very rarely do," he added. "Mariusz had had a lot of professional fights and he's a big, dangerous guy.

"I've got to be on my A-game, and I've picked him because I want some good rounds out of him. He is the same size as me, the same weight as me and he's had the same amount of fights as me. He's been in there with the elite-level champions of two generations.

"I'm not interested in what's going on with Joshua. “This is about me and Mariusz, not about anybody else. I've never been one to fall into that trap, I've always taken my opponents seriously."

Sports.title: Making Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury should have been easy... instead it's in turmoil
Sports.content:
Making Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury should have been easy... instead it's in turmoil

Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury signed to fight each other three months ago but there is still no date or venue for the all-British showdown

View Image Tyson Fury challenges Anthony Joshua (Image: Getty)

How hard could it be, really? Two of the best British heavyweight boxers of all time. The prospect of at least two money-spinning fights each held in front of 90,000 fans at Wembley. The settling of a decade-long debate. Pretty tricky, as it turns out.

Three months ago, Anthony Joshua put pen to paper on a contract to fight Tyson Fury. His rival had agreed his own separate terms earlier in the year. Both men could earn up to £100million each for a maximum of 36 minutes of work. And yet the fight billed as the biggest in this country's history still has no date and no venue. It might not even be staged in the UK.

We have, regrettably, been here before. Both men signed a two-fight deal in 2021 only for the agreement to collapse when Fury was ordered to instead fight Deontay Wilder for a third time. Both Brits ultimately lost their world titles to Oleksandr Usyk meaning a clash which would once have crowned the best heavyweight on the planet now has little more to offer than domestic bragging rights.

Learn more £19.99 or £0 DAZN Order the fight here Product Description Anthony Joshua returns to the ring to face Kristian Prenga on Saturday, July 25, in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia. Fans can order the fight on DAZN PPV for £19.99 or watch it at no extra cost with DAZN Ultimate.

But there is at least hope on the horizon; for by Saturday night Joshua will have returned to the ring for the first time since he escaped death in a car crash last Christmas. The smash which killed two of his closest friends left the former world champion's future in doubt. So it is understandable he would insist on a warm-up fight before taking on Fury. And in Kristian Prenga he has found a willing patsy.

For behind the headline stats of 20 knockouts from 21 fights lies a record with plenty of holes. Joshua will have no business sharing a ring with Fury if he cannot stop the Albanian. At which point we will be served up a dose of deja vu, only this time the roles will be reversed.

In April, Fury called on Joshua to join him in the Wembley ring following his comeback win over Arslanbek Makhmudov. Joshua refused, leaving Fury incensed and threatening to retire if his fellow countryman continued to play hardball. At the time Fury insisted he would not set foot in a ring again if Joshua wasn't in the opposite corner.

Tyson Fury lashes out at current world champions in blistering rant READ MORE :

And yet on Friday night he will do exactly that against battle-worn Mariusz Wach in Thailand. Fury has sugarcoated what is a glorified sparring session by donating the ticket proceeds to local charities and by claiming he won't bank a penny. Only the 1,500 fans in attendance will be able to watch the fight with no TV deal in place.

Instead, any highlights will be shown on the next series of Fury's Netflix show. The giant Traveller will have a private jet on standby to whisk him the 4,000 miles to Jeddah to watch Joshua from the front row. And if Fury complies where Joshua resisted, we will finally witness the first face-off between two of our most iconic sportsmen. We might even, by the end of the year, see them fight.

Sports.title: Scottie Scheffler 'not a fan' of what Rory McIlroy said at The Open as he speaks out
Sports.content:
Scottie Scheffler 'not a fan' of what Rory McIlroy said at The Open as he speaks out

Scottie Scheffler has weighed in on the ongoing row between Rory McIlroy and Bryson DeChambeau

View 2 Images Scottie Scheffler suggested he's "not a fan" of Rory McIlroy's chosen response to the latest Bryson DeCheambeau controversy (Image: Richard Heathcote, Getty Images)

World No. 1 Scottie Scheffler has suggested he's not in favour of Rory McIlroy's response to the latest Bryson DeChambeau controversy. McIlroy spurred things on after DeChambeau was served a two-stroke penalty at The Open for interfering too much with the grass around his ball in the second round.

‌



While others gave DeChambeau the benefit of the doubt, McIlroy was more gung-ho in saying he felt the whole ordeal felt "performative." However, PGA Tour superstar Scheffler made no secret of his distaste for such conduct.

‌



Scheffler was quizzed at the 3M Open about McIlroy's remarks following DeChambeau's two-shot penalty at Royal Birkdale. The World No. 1 rejected the notion that golf requires personal feuds away from the action to generate compelling storylines.

‌



"I've never been a big fan of personal jabs," he said. "I don't think that rivalry is a big thing in golf just because, like I said, my biggest rivalry week in and week out is the golf course."

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! All the best sports news and much more on our dedicated Facebook page

Scheffler outlined how golf differs fundamentally from basketball and other contact sports, as NBA players go head-to-head directly. In golf, competitors must also contend with the demands of an entire layout meticulously designed by masters of the sport.

‌



Scottie Scheffler breaks silence on Bryson DeChambeau penalty controversy at The Open READ MORE :

Scottie Scheffler rages at The Open as tempers flare in dramatic scenes READ MORE :

"I felt like when I played basketball there would always be rivalries in basketball," he added. "Because you're going to play defence against a person and that is much more personal in a sense like because I'm actively trying to stop [them]."

DeChambeau's controversy erupted on the par-four fifth hole ahead of making the cut on Friday. His ball came to rest in dense rough and television replays appeared to show him trampling near the ball in a manner that officials determined had enhanced his backswing.

The furore dominated the broadcast and compelled USA Network to remain on air. Meanwhile, Golf Channel's Live From The Open coverage shifted into a prolonged rules discussion.

‌



View 2 Images Scheffler sought to defend DeChambeau in light of his latest scandal after saying his fellow American is "not a cheater" (Image: Oisin Keniry/R&A, R&A via Getty Images)

Golf Channel pundit Brandel Chamblee accused DeChambeau of "weed wacking" the surrounding area and backed the penalty decision. Viewers subsequently witnessed DeChambeau practising on the range in darkness as the controversy raged on.

DeChambeau initially threatened to pull out of the tournament after agent Brett Falkhoff claimed he had been treated unjustly. McIlroy maintained the two-shot penalty was justified and acknowledged he isn't "particularly fond" of DeChambeau.

‌



The LIV Golf star's conduct pushed back some players' tee times until 6pm BST due to his heated protests. PGA players, including Justin Thomas and Marco Penge, voiced their frustrations about the hold-ups on social media.

McIlroy accused the LIV Golf star of holding The Open hostage and remarked on his behaviour towards officials: "I think a lot of it's performative. I think a lot of it's for attention."

Article continues below

DeChambeau had previously discussed McIlroy's attitude towards him during The Masters at Augusta National. There, he revealed McIlroy hadn't said a single word to him as he went on to claim his second Green Jacket.

Sports.title: Cameron Menzies gives update on condition after worrying World Matchplay incident
Sports.content:
Cameron Menzies gives update on condition after worrying World Matchplay incident

World No.27 Cameron Menzies was leading Ross Smith 2-1 in his second-round match at the World Matchplay in Blackpool when he fell ill and had to forfeit the match

View 2 Images Cameron Menzies had to be helped off the stage (Image: Ben Roberts Photo/Getty Images)

Cameron Menzies has reassured his fans that he is feeling better after being forced from the stage at the World Matchplay.

‌



Menzies had to be helped off the stage in Blackpool on Wednesday night during his second-round match against Ross Smith. The Scot needed medical attention after feeling faint and swaying at the oche.

‌



The 37-year-old was unsteady on his feet and there was real concern shown by the referee and opponent Smith. After being assessed by medical professionals, the incident was put down to high blood pressure.

‌



Writing on Facebook, Menzies has now given an update. “Thanks to everyone who’s checked in and sent messages. I’m okay," he said.

Smith wrote on X: "So glad my good friend Cameron Menzies is ok. Health comes before anything. You will come back stronger than ever. Love ya mate."

Cameron Menzies urgently treated by medics and out of World Matchplay after scary incident READ MORE :

A PDC statement on Wednesday night read: "Cameron Menzies was taken ill during his round two match against Ross Smith at the Betfred World Matchplay on Wednesday evening.

‌



"Cameron experienced high blood pressure, which caused him to feel dizzy and subsequently faint. Following an assessment by the on-site medical team, Cameron was deemed well enough to return to his accommodation.

"We wish Cameron all the best and look forward to seeing him back in action soon."

Menzies is the world No.27 and has been in great form. He lead Smith 2-1 when dizziness struck, prompting Glen Durrant to say on Sky Sports: "He's in tip top form at the moment. It's a real tough one to take."

‌



View 2 Images Cameron Menzies had been in great form before falling ill (Image: Ben Roberts Photo/Getty Images)

With Menzies unable to continue, Smith advanced to the quarter finals of the competition alongside Gian van Veen, James Wade and Gerwyn Price.

Having trailed 3-2, Price won six legs in succession to knock out Rob Cross by a 11-5 scoreline. The Welshman will face Smith in the last eight at Winter Gardens.

‌



Van Veen booked his quarter-final spot by overcoming fellow Dutchman Wessel Nijman 14-12 in a tie-break.

Wade, meanwhile, beat 11th seed Ryan Searle 11-8 to set up a quarter-final against Van Veen. The sixth seed won the competition in 2007.

The other quarter-finals are Luke Littler vs Josh Rock and Gary Anderson vs Dirk van Duijvenbode. World number one Littler hit a nine-darter in his 11-8 win over Nathan Aspinall in the previous round and will be the huge favourite to win the competition.

Article continues below

"That's two unbelievable performances from myself here," he said after the win. "Hopefully I can pick up the title again, but I just have to focus on who I play next."

Sports.title: The World Cup hidden gems Arsenal, Man Utd and Premier League rivals should sign
Sports.content:
The English transfer market appears out of control with a premium on any player with a sniff of Premier League experience - £117m for Morgan Rogers, £116m for Elliot Anderson, £100m for Sandro Tonali and £85m for Mateus Fernandes.

So plenty of clubs will have been on the lookout for a bargain deal from the hundreds of players who were on show at this summer's World Cup.

Now, we'll freely admit signing players based on a strong World Cup doesn't always work out - see case studies Karel Poborsky, Kleberson, Marcos Rojo (all Manchester United).

That's why, when compiling a list of the best value players from every position at the tournament who could make a difference in the Premier League, we've also looked at their numbers at club level to reveal a clearer picture of what these players can do.

‌



Using Machine Football's model, we can uncover the World Cup's hidden gems and identify the clubs where they could make the biggest impact.

World Cup awards in full as Golden Boot, Player of the Tournament and Young Player decided READ MORE :

Goalkeeper: Raul Rangel, 26 (Guadalajara, Mexico; True Value: £10.2m)

View 15 Images Raul Rangel of Mexico (Image: Getty Images)

The goalkeeping ranks produced fewer stand-out bargains, but this shot-stopper's performances over the summer have elevated him into that category.

Rangel actually entered the World Cup off the back of a steady but unspectacular Liga MX campaign with Club Deportivo Guadalajara, starting all 32 matches and playing 2,880 minutes.

‌



He faced 116 shots across the season, saving 66.4% of them, while conceding 39 goals at 1.22 per 90. Guadalajara's third-place finish reflected a strong team campaign, but Rangel's individual numbers did not suggest a goalkeeper ready to make a major impact on the international stage.

The World Cup, however, told a very different story. Rangel started all five of Mexico's matches, playing 437 of a possible 450 minutes, and produced numbers far beyond his domestic baseline.

Per Machine Football's tournament tracking, he faced 2.01 shots on target per 90 and made 1.46 saves, conceding just 0.55 goals per 90. His expected-goals-saved figure of 0.85 across the tournament shows he prevented almost a goal more than he should have done, given the quality of chances faced.

Your World Cup glossary of football tactics, data and stats buzzwords READ MORE :

He was also composed in possession, completing 91% of his passes and 80% of his goal kicks, while coming off his line 0.91 times per 90 to deal with danger.

‌



Four of Mexico's five matches ended in clean sheets, an 80% rate that more than doubled his best full-season domestic return.

The numbers were backed up by moments of individual quality. Against South Korea, Rangel produced one of the saves of the group stage, using his foot to deny a close-range header before recovering instantly to claw away the rebound and preserve Mexico's second consecutive clean sheet.

That contrast is exactly what makes Rangel an intriguing profile. His club numbers have yet to reflect the level he reached on the international stage, suggesting a goalkeeper whose ceiling may be higher than his domestic record indicates.

Verdict: For clubs searching for a high-upside option, the World Cup offered evidence that there could be more to unlock. Hull City and Newcastle United are on the hunt for a keeper.

‌



Right-back: Alex Freeman, 21 (Villarreal, USA; True Value: £7.25m)

View 15 Images Alex Freeman of the USA (Image: Getty Images)

USA defender Alex Freeman's father, Antonio, won a Super Bowl with the Green Bay Packers. The younger Freeman, though, has forged his own path - breaking through with Orlando City before earning a January move to Villarreal, where he is yet to nail down a spot or register a domestic goal involvement.

The World Cup told a different story entirely. He started all five of the USA's matches, playing 100 minutes against Belgium, 110 against Bosnia-Herzegovina, 105 against Australia - where he scored - and 103 against Paraguay, where he assisted.

Across those 441 minutes he won 5.7 duels and completed 6.9 progressive passes per 90. A goal, an assist and elite ball-winning numbers from right-back all inside the same tournament – this was a genuine breakout for a 21-year-old still finding his feet at club level.

‌



Freeman's numbers from MLS last year suggest he won't have to wait too long to make that next step. From 27 starts at Orlando City in the regular season 2025, Freeman bagged six goals from right-back while laying on three assists for his teammates, also making more touches in the opposition box (132) than any other full-back in the division.

Verdict: So which Premier League side actually needs him? David Moyes's Everton ranked in the 36th percentile for offensive duels won and 29th for defensive duels last season, a side losing individual battles at both ends of the pitch. Freeman's all-round game, not simply his ability to overlap, looks like a direct answer to that problem.

Every Premier League summer transfer as Man Utd, Arsenal and Liverpool splash the cash READ MORE :

Right centre-back: Jhon Lucumi, 27 (Bologna, Colombia; True Value: £21.2m)

View 15 Images Colombia's Jhon Lucumi facing Portugal (Image: Alex Gottschalk/DeFodi Images/Shutterstock)

Classed as an 'Enforcing 4' by the Machine Football model, Lucumi is an old-school defender focused on winning duels rather than dictating games in possession.

‌



The World Cup provided the perfect test of that profile. Colombia started him in all five matches, including the full 127 minutes of their penalty-shootout defeat to Switzerland.

Across 538 minutes he completed 91.7% of his passes and won 1.7 aerial duels per 90 at a rate of 72.7%, combining composure with remarkable durability. With Lucumi at the heart of their defence, Colombia conceded one goal over the course of their five-game run to the round of 16, managing a four-game streak of clean sheets.

Lucumi was a regular starter in Serie A for Bologna last season and demonstrated a knack for sweeping up effectively, with his 5.23 recoveries per 90 higher than 95% of other centre-backs in the division.

Verdict: Where does that profile find a home? Xabi Alonso has only just arrived at Chelsea, but the Blues' lack of physical prowess was there for all to see last season, and it didn't improve as the managers changed.

‌



Under Enzo Maresca, the manager that oversaw most of the minutes, they ranked in the 27th percentile for aerial duels and 14th for defensive duels. Under Liam Rosenior, who took over next, both numbers got worse. Caretaker Calum McFarlane's brief spell saw aerial duels fall further still.

Three managers, one problem which none of them managed to improve. Lucumi's profile targets it directly.

Left centre-back: Facundo Medina, 26 (Marseille, Argentina; True Value: £19m)

View 15 Images Facundo Medina in the World Cup final (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Lionel Scaloni gave left-footed centre-back Facundo Medina just 162 minutes at the World Cup, starting him against Cape Verde before bringing him off the bench in the World Cup final.

Even so, Medina completed 86.4% of his passes, including in the biggest match of the tournament, and won 63.6% of his duels.

Such a low tournament sample size is an obvious caveat, and Medina also only started 16 games in Ligue 1 last season. Despite that, he possesses a quality on the ball that could make him a solid option as a centre-back-left-back hybrid for a Premier League side.

Creativity is a rare strength for a centre-back, yet Medina ranks in the 97th percentile globally — a genuinely elite reading regardless of position. A regular for Marseille, he also sits in the top 5% for passing accuracy and is classified as a Complete 4 in Machine Football's category of player styles.

‌



Verdict: That passing profile is exactly why Arsenal stand out as a potential destination. Despite their miserly defensive record at home and in Europe, Mikel Arteta's side's defensive duels stats were not great. However, that reflects dominance rather than a weakness.

Arsenal simply keep the ball so effectively that opponents have fewer opportunities to engage them in defensive battles.

Arsenal already have a squad built around that identity. William Saliba and Cristhian Mosquera are both classified as Complete 4s – the same archetype as Medina — so his appeal is not that he introduces something unfamiliar, but that he provides a more polished, ready-made version of a profile Arteta already trusts.

View 15 Images Facundo Medina's solidity, technical ability and tactical flexibility could make him a good fit for Arsenal or Crystal Palace (Image: Machine Football)

‌



Given Arsenal already have two left-footed defenders who can play both wide and centrally in Riccardo Calafiori and Piero Hincapie, though, a club like Nottingham Forest could also suit Medina - where he would be expected to feature on the left of Oliver Glasner's back three in a role similar to the one Marc Guehi played at Crystal Palace.

Left-back: Ghislain Konan, 30 (Gil Vicente, Ivory Coast; True Value: £1.5m)

View 15 Images Ivory Coast's defender Ghislain Kona (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Ghislain Konan started three of four Ivory Coast matches on their run to the round of 16, averaging 7.7 progressive passes and 2.4 crosses per 90.

That's genuine attacking output from a left-back in a side that reached the knockout rounds. Konan was also a regular starter for Gil Vicente in Portugal's top flight last season, and no full-back in the division made more dribbles (1.72) or recoveries (5.68) per 90.

‌



Konan combines experience with attacking intent, and would suit a side who like to bypass central areas and create down the flanks.

Verdict: Which side could that be? Frank Lampard's Coventry City are a no-nonsense sort of side that completed the second-most crosses per 90 last season while ranking just fourth for possession, despite storming to the Championship title with 95 points.

Konan could provide experience and quality for a side who will be mainly focused on survival.

Right defensive midfielder: Lamine Camara, 22 (Monaco, Senegal; True Value: £40m)

View 15 Images Senegal's Lamine Camara against Iraq (Image: AP Photo/Stephanie Scarbrough)

‌



The highest-profile player on this list so far, Machine Football ranks Camara in the top 5% globally for his attacking contribution value, rare creative numbers for a holding midfielder.

The 22-year-old started for Senegal against France, Norway and Iraq at the World Cup, registering an assist in the latter, before appearing from the bench against Belgium.

Even as the Lions of Teranga struggled going forward, Camara averaged 3.4 interceptions per 90 across 288 minutes and registered a highly-impressive 0.32 expected assists per 90 from the base of midfield.

Camara was one of the stand-out midfielders in Ligue 1 last season with Monaco, proving his World Cup was no fluke. A combative and press-resistant player with plenty of quality on the ball, Camara is equally adept at sweeping up loose balls in midfield as he is putting opponents under pressure - making 7.68 recoveries per 90 and winning possession in the final third 1.02 times per 90.

‌



View 15 Images Lamine Camara is an all-rounder in midfield whose creativity has only grown - could be be a coup for Fulham or is he already set for a top club? (Image: Machine Football)

Verdict: The best fit for that skill set turns out to be Fulham. They ranked in just the 13th percentile for dribbling and 10th for offensive duels won last season, among the weakest ball-progression numbers in the Premier League.

Camara's passing range and composure address exactly that - while he would also add much-needed steel to a high-pressing, possession-focused team such as Liverpool.

Liverpool investment explained as Jeff Bezos talks revealed after FSG statement released READ MORE :

Andoni Iraola clarifies future of two Liverpool stars linked with exits READ MORE :

Left defensive midfielder: Gustavo Puerta, 22 (Racing Santander, Colombia; True Value: £8.3m)

View 15 Images Gustavo Puerta of Colombia vs Switzerland (Image: Curtis Wong/SPP/Shutterstock)

‌



A genuine value story, Puerta was playing in Spain's Segunda Division last season, yet at 22 already ranked in the top 5% for output at that level. His playing style combines control, progression and defensive awareness.

Colombia clearly trusted him with more than a bit-part role. Puerta started every match of their World Cup campaign and was never substituted, including the full 130 minutes of their penalty-shootout defeat.

Across 519 minutes, he completed 92.4% of his passes and averaged 2.4 interceptions per 90, showing remarkable composure for a 22-year-old.

At club level, he helped Racing Santander to a league title and automatic promotion last season as their midfield controller, making a team-high 1.2 interceptions and 57.3 passes per 90, while no other Racing outfielder made more recoveries than Puerta's 6.4 per 90.

‌



Verdict: On this evidence, where would he do most good? Michael Carrick's Manchester United side ranked in just the ninth percentile for offensive duels and 18th for dribbling last season and are a side more focused on getting the ball to their creator-in-chief, Bruno Fernandes.

Puerta's calmness in possession and ability to move the ball through the lines of midfield could help with that, at a fraction of the cost of a comparable player from a bigger league.

OPINION Six standout World Cup stars who Man Utd could sign next for Michael Carrick rebuild by Tom Victor

No. 10: Fares Chaibi, 23 (Eintracht Frankfurt, Algeria; True Value: £12.9m)

View 15 Images Fares Chaibi of Algeria (Image: Xinhua/Shutterstock)

‌



Machine Football classifies Chaibi as a 'Metronomic 8', although both club and country typically use him higher up the pitch in a No. 10 role or even on the wing.

Algeria's usage of the 23-year-old only strengthened that profile. He started all four of Algeria's matches, played over 100 minutes in all of them and was never substituted, completing 88.8% of his passes despite Algeria conceding eight goals.

In the Bundesliga, Chaibi racked up nine assists for Eintracht Frankfurt last season, creating 0.55 big chances per 90 and winning possession in the final third 0.60 times per 90.

Verdict: The clearest destination for that skill set is Crystal Palace. They produced one of the weakest attacking profiles of any Premier League side last season, ranking just third for offensive duels won. Chaibi's ability to win his individual battles and convert possession into chances directly addresses that particular shortcoming.

‌



Three things the Premier League must steal from World Cup 2026 and four things it must ditch READ MORE :

2034 World Cup could be delayed until following year as FIFA face Saudi Arabia dilemma READ MORE :

Right winger: Nestory Irankunda, 20 (Watford, Australia; True Value: £13.1m)

View 15 Images Australia's Nestory Irankunda celebrates scoring his team's first goal against Türkiye (Image: Getty Images)

Still playing Championship football despite a spell at Bayern Munich after leaving Australia, Irankunda already ranks in the top 5% for both dribbling and attacking output relative to his level.

His World Cup performances showed why he is one of the most intriguing young forwards in the Machine Football database. For Australia, Irankunda scored against Turkiye, assisted against Egypt and completed the full 90 against Paraguay.

Across 285 minutes of action he won 5.7 duels per 90 — a genuinely elite physical number for a 20-year-old winger. That profile is what allows Irankunda to also play as a centre-forward, where he can call upon his combative instincts to make a nuisance of himself and unleash havoc.

‌



Irankunda's ability to take players on was on full display for Watford last season, completing 2.44 dribbles and winning 2.13 fouls per 90 in the Championship.

Verdict: On the basis of that, Newcastle looks like the obvious destination. They ranked in the 30th percentile for dribbling last season, relying heavily on crosses rather than beating defenders one-on-one.

The right-footed Irankunda could address that effectively with plenty of room still to grow - complementing the Magpies' new left-footed youngster, Bazoumana Toure, on the opposite flank.

Irankunda has been linked with a move to Sporting CP so Premier League sides would have to act quickly. Everton have also been rumoured with interest.

‌



Left winger: Malik Tillman, 23 (Bayer Leverkusen, USA; True Value: £36.6m)

View 15 Images Malik Tillman celebrates after scoring a free kick against Bosnia (Image: AP Photo/Martin Meissner)

Tillman's World Cup performances were simply too strong to leave him out.

Tillman is probably the best-known player on this list alongside Camara, and he started every USA match through to the round of 16 - scoring against Bosnia-Herzegovina and Belgium and assisting against Paraguay.

Across 415 minutes at the tournament he averaged 0.43 goals, 0.22 assists and 7.6 duels won per 90 – a dangerous combination of output and physicality rarely found together at this level which reflects Tillman's time spent as a No. 9 in Bayern's youth ranks.

‌



Tillman scored six goals from just 18 starts for Leverkusen last season, timing his box-crashing runs to perfection, and also won 51.5% of his overall duels along with an eye-catching 63.4% of his aerial ones.

View 15 Images Malik Tillman is a versatile player who can contribute defensively as well as in attack, where his box-crashing runs cause problems for defences (Image: Machine Football)

That physicality would suggest he could thrive in the Premier League, and is backed up by Tillman's 0.97 interceptions and also 0.97 instances of possession won in the final third per 90.

Verdict: There is no perfect data match here, but Brighton come closest closest. They ranked in the 26th percentile for defensive duels and 22nd for interceptions last season, a system that presses hard without always winning the ball back.

‌



Tillman could help make that press more watertight as well as offering box threat from open play, suiting how Fabian Hurzeler wants his side to play whilst adding something Brighton don't have already with his physicality and potential usefulness at set pieces.

Striker: Julian Quinones, 29 (Al Qadsiah, Mexico; True Value: £16.2m)

View 15 Images Mexico's Julian Quinones (Image: AP Photo/Fernando Llano)

Few players anywhere matched Quinones for production this year. He ranks in the top 1% globally for both attacking positioning and finishing, scoring 33 goals in 31 Saudi Pro League matches.

How translatable that would be to the Premier League, in theory at least, remains to be seen. As yet, there aren't really any other examples of Premier League clubs signing high-volume Pro League strikers to compare Quinones to.

‌



But Quinones' performances up front for Mexico at the World Cup suggest he can be effective even against elite defenders. He started all five of Mexico's World Cup matches and scored against South Africa, Czechia, Ecuador and England.

His return of 0.82 goals per 90, backed by 2.86 shots per 90, is an elite scoring rate by any standard, and he has matched or overperformed his xG in each of his two seasons in Saudi Arabia.

Verdict: Which side needs a finisher more than anyone? Tottenham ranked in just the 25th percentile for shot volume and 31st for shot quality last season. They create enough chances, but Quinones looks like the sort of striker who finishes them.
