What Ábaco Actually Does

Ábaco operates in the unglamorous but vital niche of digital factoring. It buys a company’s accounts receivable at a discount, handing the business immediate liquidity instead of making it wait weeks or months for clients to pay.

The entire process runs online. A small retailer, distributor, or service provider can affiliate, submit an invoice, get an algorithmic credit decision, and receive funds in under 24 hours—sometimes in as little as eight minutes.

This speed is transformative for a neighborhood hardware store or a family-run food distributor that might otherwise halt operations while a large corporate client takes 60 or 90 days to settle a bill. By underwriting the receivable itself rather than the borrower’s balance sheet, Ábaco sidesteps the collateral trap that locks many small enterprises out of the banking system.

Why SME Lending Matters in the Region

Across El Salvador, Guatemala, and Costa Rica, small and medium enterprises employ the bulk of the workforce yet routinely struggle to access formal bank credit. Traditional lenders often demand real estate collateral or years of audited statements that young firms simply do not have.

Ábaco fills that gap by underwriting the receivable itself, using alternative data and artificial intelligence rather than brick-and-mortar guarantees. The company says it has already originated more than US$100 million in credit, charging a commission of roughly 3 to 4 percent per operation.

For context, the International Finance Corporation has long identified Central America’s SME financing gap as one of the widest in Latin America. When a small business cannot smooth its cash flow, it misses supplier discounts, turns down orders, or resorts to informal lenders whose rates can exceed 10 percent per month.

Ábaco’s model essentially turns a pile of unpaid paper invoices into a liquid asset class. For a foreign investor or impact fund watching the region, that represents a scalable way to back the real economy without taking on the concentrated risk of a single large corporate borrower.

Inside the US$53 Million Seed Round

The fresh US$53 million package blends equity and debt, a structure that lets the fintech strengthen its balance sheet while directly funding the invoices it purchases. The round drew backing from a mix of Latin American venture and impact investors, though a full list of participants was not disclosed in the initial announcement.

Before this raise, Ábaco had already assembled a notable cap table. A US$4 million pre-seed round brought in Caricaco Ventures, Cacao Capital, Innogen Capital Ventures, Invariantes Fund, Mercy Corps Ventures, and Bridge Latam, alongside regional business groups.

That earlier round was described as the largest by number of venture capital funds participating in Central American history. The presence of Mercy Corps Ventures, the impact-investing arm of the global humanitarian organization, signals that backers view SME financing as both a financial opportunity and a development tool.

For expat entrepreneurs or foreign investors unfamiliar with the local venture scene, the mix of homegrown funds such as Caricaco Ventures and Cacao Capital with international names like Invariantes Fund suggests a maturing ecosystem where Salvadoran startups can now attract serious institutional capital without relocating to Mexico City or Miami.

A Regional Platform Takes Shape

Ábaco intends to use the new capital to scale beyond El Salvador, with Guatemala and Costa Rica as its immediate targets. The company envisions a unified digital platform where SMEs across the isthmus can tap working capital on flexible terms, without the paperwork that bogs down conventional banking.

In a separate move, Pomona Impact Fund II announced a US$2 million mezzanine debt investment in Ábaco on March 28, 2025, signaling continued confidence from specialized impact investors who see SME financing as a lever for job creation and economic resilience in Central America.

Mezzanine debt sits between senior bank loans and pure equity, giving the lender a cushion if things go wrong while keeping the company’s ownership dilution in check. For a fintech that needs to fund thousands of small invoices, this layered capital structure makes practical sense.

Guatemala, with its large informal economy and deep cross-border trade ties to El Salvador, is a natural second market. Costa Rica offers a more regulated but higher-income testing ground where digital factoring could appeal to established SMEs that already use online banking but still face slow payment cycles from corporate and government clients.

What It Means for Expats and Investors

For foreigners living in or doing business with Central America, Ábaco’s rise signals that the region’s financial plumbing is modernizing. A digital factoring platform that works across borders could eventually let a Guatemala-based exporter discount a receivable from a Salvadoran buyer on the same platform, reducing the currency and timing friction that complicates regional trade.

From an investment perspective, the US$53 million seed round—unusually large for a Central American startup—suggests that venture and impact funds now view the isthmus as more than a niche market. Readers who follow Latin American fintech will recognize that deal sizes of this magnitude were, until recently, almost exclusively the domain of Brazilian or Mexican startups.

The round also highlights a broader trend: impact investors are increasingly willing to write meaningful checks for financial-inclusion plays that generate market-rate returns. For an expat with capital to deploy, Ábaco’s trajectory offers a case study in how digital infrastructure can unlock value in economies long dominated by cash and informal credit.

What Happens Next

Ábaco has not published a detailed timeline for its Guatemala and Costa Rica launches, but the company’s public statements suggest that building a multi-country regulatory and operational framework is the immediate priority. Each jurisdiction has its own financial supervisor, invoicing rules, and credit bureau infrastructure, so the expansion will be a phased, country-by-country effort.

The fintech will also need to prove that its algorithmic underwriting—trained largely on Salvadoran invoice data—travels well across borders. If it succeeds, Ábaco could become a template for other Latin American markets where SMEs face the same working-capital squeeze, from Honduras to the Dominican Republic.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is digital factoring?

It is a financing method where a company sells its unpaid invoices to a platform like Ábaco at a small discount in exchange for immediate cash, rather than waiting 30, 60, or 90 days for clients to pay. The platform then collects the full invoice amount from the client when it comes due, earning the difference as its fee.

Which countries does Ábaco serve?

Ábaco currently operates in El Salvador and is using its new funding to expand into Guatemala and Costa Rica, with a goal of building a regional SME financing platform that could eventually serve businesses across the Central American isthmus.

How fast can a business get funds from Ábaco?

The company says money can reach a client in less than 24 hours, and some businesses access a line of credit in as little as eight minutes after approval. The entire process—affiliation, invoice submission, algorithmic evaluation, and disbursement—happens online without physical paperwork.

World.title: The Batista Venezuela Oil Bet Grows With a PDVSA Stake
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Energy

Key Facts —The deal. Fluxus, controlled by Brazil’s Batista brothers, bought A&B Oil and Gas, giving it 49% of Petrolera Roraima, a joint venture with Venezuela’s PDVSA. —The asset. Roraima was once run by ConocoPhillips; in 2024 Venezuela granted it 25-year production rights. PDVSA holds the other 51%. —The wave. Reported by Bloomberg on 22 July 2026, it is the third such deal in a week, with more expected before a 28 July deadline. —The opening. The deals follow US sanctions relief: OFAC issued general licences in early 2026 allowing certain Venezuelan-oil activities. —The players. Joesley and Wesley Batista control meatpacker JBS and holding company J&F; their Venezuela ties date back over a decade.

Brazil’s billionaire Batista brothers are deepening a bet few Western companies will touch. The latest Batista Venezuela oil move gives their energy firm a stake in a PDVSA joint venture, as Washington eases the sanctions that long sealed the country off.

The Puerto La Cruz refinery in Anzoátegui, Venezuela. Brazil’s Batista brothers are expanding into the country’s oil sector. (Photo: Daniel Zambrano / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0)

Brazil’s Batista brothers built their fortune on meat. Now Joesley and Wesley Batista are pushing into one of the riskiest corners of the energy world: Venezuelan oil.

The move was reported by Bloomberg on 22 July 2026, and it fits a pattern the family has followed for years — moving into markets others avoid.

What the Batistas Just Bought

The vehicle is Fluxus Oil, Gas & Energy, a company the brothers control. It acquired A&B Oil and Gas, a firm that holds 49% of a Venezuelan production venture called Petrolera Roraima.

PDVSA, Venezuela’s state oil company, owns the other 51%. The field was once operated by the US major ConocoPhillips, before Venezuela seized foreign assets years ago.

In 2024, Venezuela’s petroleum ministry handed 25-year exploration and production rights over the project to A&B Investments, a firm led by Jorge Silva Cardona, a business associate of the Batistas. Buying A&B now folds that stake into the brothers’ empire.

Petrolera Roraima pumps heavy crude in eastern Venezuela — oil that needs blending and specialist handling, part of why so few firms have wanted to run it.

Fluxus has kept the financial terms largely under wraps, and neither it nor PDVSA has detailed how much was paid.

Why Now — the Sanctions Opening

The timing is not accidental. For years, US sanctions on PDVSA made investing in Venezuelan oil legally radioactive for most companies.

That has begun to shift. In early 2026, Washington’s Office of Foreign Assets Control issued a series of general licences authorising certain activities in Venezuela’s oil sector, partially reopening the door.

Bloomberg called the Fluxus deal the third to surface in a single week, with more expected before a 28 July regulatory deadline. A scramble for Venezuelan assets is under way.

US policy toward Venezuela has swung sharply between administrations, tightening and loosening with each change in Washington. That volatility is the central risk for anyone buying in now.

For Washington, the calculus is partly about oil supply and partly about leverage over Caracas. Loosening the rules encourages production; tightening them again is a ready-made pressure tool.

The Batistas’ Long Venezuela Story

The brothers are no strangers to Caracas. More than a decade ago, their meatpacking giant JBS signed a deal worth roughly US$2.1 billion to supply beef and chicken to Venezuela as the country reeled from shortages and hyperinflation.

Since then, the family — through the holding company J&F — has studied oil, mining, power and other infrastructure in the country.

Fluxus is the vehicle carrying that ambition into energy, and the Roraima stake is its most concrete oil bet yet. Where others see legal and political minefields, the Batistas have often seen bargains.

The brothers have faced legal scrutiny at home, too. Joesley Batista struck a plea deal in a sprawling Brazilian corruption case years ago, yet the family kept control of JBS and expanded it.

A High-Risk, High-Reward Wager

The logic is stark. Venezuela sits on the world’s largest proven oil reserves, and its fields can be bought cheaply precisely because sanctions and mismanagement scared others off.

If Washington keeps easing sanctions and output recovers, early movers stand to profit handsomely. If the licences are reversed — a genuine risk given US policy swings — those same investors could be trapped.

Venezuela’s own instability adds to the danger: crumbling infrastructure, an unpredictable government and, this month, earthquakes on the central coast.

Rivals are circling the same assets. Chevron has kept a foothold in Venezuela under its own US licence, and other traders and producers are now testing what the new rules allow.

What It Means for Brazil and the Region

For Brazil, it is a striking case of a homegrown conglomerate wading into a market its own government treats warily. Brasília has kept a careful distance from Caracas’s oil.

For the region, the deal signals that Venezuelan oil is back in play, drawing not just Chevron and other majors but opportunistic private money from across Latin America.

It also underlines how Latin American capital, and not only Western oil giants, is shaping who profits from Venezuela’s slow and uncertain reopening.

The Batistas have built their fortune by moving early and absorbing controversy; JBS has weathered corruption scandals and emerged larger each time. Whether Venezuela rewards that instinct, or finally tests it, is the open question.

For ordinary Venezuelans, foreign money could mean jobs and rebuilt fields after years of collapse — or another chapter in which the country’s oil enriches outsiders while little trickles down.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the Batista brothers buy in Venezuela?

Through their firm Fluxus Oil, Gas & Energy, they acquired A&B Oil and Gas, which holds a 49% stake in Petrolera Roraima, a joint venture with Venezuela’s state oil company PDVSA. PDVSA owns the other 51%.

Is it legal to invest in Venezuelan oil?

It has become less restricted. US sanctions long barred most dealings with PDVSA, but in early 2026 Washington’s OFAC issued general licences authorising certain Venezuelan oil activities, which is what has enabled a wave of new deals.

Who are the Batista brothers?

Joesley and Wesley Batista are Brazilian billionaires who control the world’s largest meatpacker, JBS, and the holding company J&F Investimentos. Their business interests in Venezuela date back more than a decade.

World.title: Medellín’s Casa de la Memoria Opens Public Digital Archive
World.content:
Colombia · Culture

Key Facts —Institution. The Museo Casa de la Memoria is Medellín’s municipal memory museum, created in 2006 and opened to the public in 2012. —New archive. The Laboratorio de Memorias digital archive launched with 1,473 records, including testimonies, photographs, and institutional files. —Collection period. Materials were gathered since 2003 from Medellín, Antioquia, and other regions of Colombia. —Access. Consultation is free and on-site at the museum to protect sensitive information and ensure preservation. —Mission. The space supports historical memory, symbolic reparation, dialogue, and the principle of non-repetition.

The Casa de la Memoria in Medellín has opened a new public digital archive, the Laboratorio de Memorias, bringing together more than 1,400 testimonies and documentary records that trace decades of Colombia’s internal armed conflict and the slow, careful work of peacebuilding.

A Living Archive, Built Over Two Decades

The archive draws from materials collected since 2003 by the museum and its partners, long before the museum’s physical doors even opened to the public.

It holds testimonies, photographs, institutional files, and other records documenting experiences from Medellín, the Antioquia department, and other regions of Colombia, creating a mosaic of voices from across the nation.

With 1,473 records at launch, the Laboratorio de Memorias is not a static collection gathering dust on a digital shelf.

Museum staff describe it as a growing documentary center designed for victims, researchers, activists, students, and any member of the public seeking to understand what happened during the country’s darkest chapters.

The collection continues to expand, ensuring that newly recovered stories and materials find a permanent home within this structured, searchable memory bank.

Why the Casa de la Memoria Matters Now

The museum itself was born from an initiative of Medellín’s Victim Assistance Program in 2006, a period when the city was grappling intensely with urban violence and the fallout from paramilitary and guerrilla conflicts.

It opened its doors to the public in 2012 as a permanent space for remembrance and reflection on the city’s and the country’s armed conflict and other forms of violence, quickly becoming a landmark for human rights education.

Its mission is to help people understand and overcome those violences, a goal that goes beyond simply displaying artifacts.

The museum frames its work around collective recognition, symbolic reparation, dialogue, and reconciliation, values that the new archive extends into a searchable, structured format accessible to a wider audience.

For a society still navigating a fragile peace process, this archive represents a concrete tool against forgetting, anchoring official and personal histories in one verified location.

How to Visit and Consult the Archive

The archive is accessible only on-site at the museum, located at Calle 51 #36-66 in Parque Bicentenario, a central and easily reachable area of Medellín.

The museum said this in-person requirement protects sensitive information and ensures the long-term preservation of fragile materials, a common practice for archives dealing with delicate historical records.

Admission is free, removing financial barriers for anyone who wishes to engage with Colombia’s complex past.

Regular visiting hours are Tuesday through Friday from 9:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., and Saturdays, Sundays, and holidays from 10:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.

Foreign visitors, expats, and researchers are welcome to consult the records during those times, making it a valuable resource for international scholars and curious travelers alike.

A Quiet Act of National Repair

Colombia’s armed conflict has lasted more than half a century, leaving deep wounds across urban and rural communities that no single peace agreement can instantly heal.

Memory initiatives like this one are widely seen as essential to the country’s ongoing peace process and to the promise of non-repetition, a principle that seeks to prevent history from repeating itself.

By organizing fragmented voices into a single, searchable archive, the Casa de la Memoria offers a sober space where personal grief becomes part of a shared historical record.

It is a quiet but powerful act of national repair, one testimony at a time, transforming individual pain into a collective call for a more peaceful future.

What This Means for Expats, Tourists, and Investors

For the international community living in or visiting Medellín, the archive offers a profound window into the context that shaped modern Colombia beyond the popular tourist narratives.

Expats and long-term visitors can use the Laboratorio de Memorias to better understand the social fabric of their adopted city, moving past surface-level impressions to grasp the resilience behind Medellín’s celebrated urban transformation.

Investors and business travelers often hear about Medellín’s innovation district and economic revival, but this archive provides the essential backstory of a society that has consciously chosen to confront its past rather than bury it.

Accessing these records, even for a brief visit, can deepen one’s appreciation for the stability and creativity that now define the city, qualities rooted in hard-won peacebuilding efforts.

The museum’s location in Parque Bicentenario also places it near other cultural landmarks, making it an easy and meaningful addition to any itinerary focused on understanding the real Medellín.

The Broader Landscape of Memory in Colombia

The Casa de la Memoria does not exist in isolation; it is part of a broader national movement to document human rights violations and honor victims through official and grassroots memory projects.

Colombia’s 2016 peace agreement with the FARC guerrilla group included provisions for truth-telling and historical clarification, fueling demand for accessible archives like this one.

Similar memory houses and museums exist in other conflict-affected cities, but Medellín’s stands out for its municipal origin and its deep integration with local victim assistance programs.

The Laboratorio de Memorias strengthens this network by offering a model of how cities can preserve sensitive histories responsibly while still inviting public engagement.

As Colombia continues to reckon with ongoing violence involving other armed groups, the archive’s role as a living repository becomes even more urgent, documenting not just a closed past but an evolving present.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Casa de la Memoria?

It is Medellín’s municipal memory museum, created in 2006 and opened in 2012, dedicated to remembrance, reflection, and overcoming Colombia’s armed conflict and other violences through exhibitions, education, and now a public digital archive.

Can I access the digital archive online?

No. The Laboratorio de Memorias archive must be consulted in person at the museum to protect sensitive information and ensure proper preservation of the records, a safeguard for both the victims’ stories and the physical materials.

Is there an entry fee for the museum?

No. Admission to the Casa de la Memoria and access to the archive are completely free for all visitors, ensuring that economic barriers do not prevent anyone from engaging with Colombia’s historical memory.

World.title: Colombia’s Grupo Cibest Sells Banistmo for $1.4 Billion
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Banking

Key Facts —The sale. Grupo Cibest, the holding company of Colombia’s Bancolombia, sold its Panama retail bank Banistmo for about US$1.4 billion, closing in mid-June 2026. —The buyer. Banistmo went to Banco La Hipotecaria, part of the Salvadoran group Inversiones Cuscatlán. —The twist. Despite exiting retail, Cibest is not leaving Panama; it is expanding a regional banking, investment and capital-markets hub there. —The scale. Its remaining Panama platform serves more than 33,800 clients and handled over US$107 billion in international transfers in 2025. —The parent. Grupo Cibest is the holding company created in 2024 to sit above Bancolombia, Colombia’s largest bank.

At first glance it looks like a retreat. Grupo Cibest, the parent of Colombia’s biggest bank, has just sold its Panama retail bank for US$1.4 billion. Look closer, though, and the group is not leaving Panama at all — it is doubling down on a richer slice of it.

Panama City’s financial district. Grupo Cibest sold its Panama retail bank but is expanding a regional banking and investment hub there. (Photo: Dronepicr / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0)

Grupo Cibest is the holding company that sits above Bancolombia, Colombia’s largest bank, together with its insurance and investment arms. It took the Cibest name in a 2024 reorganisation designed to look more like a diversified financial group than a single bank.

This month it completed a move that, on paper, looks like a step back: selling Banistmo, its retail bank in Panama, for about US$1.4 billion.

Yet the group is not walking away from Panama. It is quietly building something more profitable in its place.

The US$1.4 Billion Sale of Banistmo

Banistmo was Cibest’s everyday bank in Panama — branches, accounts, cards and loans for ordinary customers. That is the business it has now let go.

The buyer is Banco La Hipotecaria, part of Inversiones Cuscatlán, a Salvadoran financial group expanding across Central America. The deal, first announced in December, cleared its final Panama regulatory hurdle in mid-June 2026.

For the buyer, the prize is scale. Banistmo hands Cuscatlán a ready-made retail network and a quarter of a million customers in one of Central America’s wealthier banking markets; those personal-banking clients are due to migrate to the new owner in a handover both sides promise to manage without disruption.

Selling Banistmo dented the headline numbers. Cibest closed 2025 with net income of 3.8 trillion pesos (about US$960 million), down 39% on the year, largely because of the disposal.

What Grupo Cibest Keeps in Panama

The retreat is only partial. Cibest is holding on to — and expanding — a separate Panama operation built around banking, investment and capital markets rather than mass-market accounts.

That platform runs through Bancolombia Panamá, its local branch and Cibest Capital Panamá. It serves more than 33,800 clients, most of them companies and wealthier individuals.

The figures are large. The operation recorded more than US$107 billion in international transfers in 2025 and, by March 2026, managed assets of over US$9.5 billion.

Provisions for bad loans also fell 16% over the year, which Cibest points to as evidence that its remaining book is healthier and better suited to a fee-driven model.

It offers deposit products, including checking and savings accounts, fixed-term deposits, and investment products; credit alternatives solutions such as trade financing, working capital loans, mortgages, credit cards, personal, vehicle, payroll, and small business loans, and…

Why Sell Retail but Stay

The logic is about margins and focus. Retail banking — millions of small accounts, branches and cards — is costly to run and hungry for capital, especially for a foreign owner in a crowded market.

Wealth management, corporate banking and capital markets, by contrast, earn fatter fees on far less balance-sheet risk. For a group trying to lift returns, that trade looks attractive.

Cibest framed the sale to shareholders as a sharpening of strategy rather than a retreat, arguing that capital freed from Panama retail can earn more elsewhere in the group.

Panama also offers what Colombia cannot: a US dollar economy, light-touch financial rules and a role as a gateway between Latin America, the United States and beyond.

Panama as a Regional Hub

Panama has used the US dollar as legal tender for more than a century and hosts one of the region’s largest international banking centres. For a Colombian group, that makes it the natural place to serve clients who want hard-currency stability.

Cibest is betting that Panama can be its offshore platform for the whole region, not just a domestic market it happens to serve.

From there it can offer dollar accounts, cross-border payments and investment products to clients across Latin America who want to hold money outside their own volatile currencies.

That ambition helps explain why fee income is growing even as the balance sheet shrinks. Commissions rose 10% in 2025 and now make up about 18% of operating income.

What It Means for the Region

For Panama, the shuffle keeps a major Colombian group invested, even as it hands retail customers to a Salvadoran buyer — a sign of how fluid Central American banking ownership has become.

Salvadoran, Colombian and Brazilian banks have all been reshuffling their Central American holdings in recent years, buying and selling retail networks as they decide which markets are worth serving directly.

It fits a wider trend: as some foreign banks quit crowded retail markets, others carve out specialised niches — wealth, payments, capital markets — where expertise matters more than sheer scale.

For Bancolombia’s shareholders, the open question is whether the fee-led Panama strategy can replace the steady profits Banistmo once delivered.

For ordinary customers, little changes at first; Banistmo’s branches carry on under new owners. The bigger shift is upstream, in where Latin America’s banks now choose to place their bets.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Grupo Cibest sell in Panama?

It sold Banistmo, its Panama retail bank, to Banco La Hipotecaria, part of El Salvador’s Inversiones Cuscatlán, for about US$1.4 billion. The deal closed in mid-June 2026.

Is Grupo Cibest leaving Panama?

No. It is keeping and expanding a separate Panama operation focused on banking, investment and capital markets — through Bancolombia Panamá and Cibest Capital Panamá — which manages over US$9.5 billion in assets.

Who is Grupo Cibest?

Grupo Cibest is the holding company, created in 2024, that sits above Bancolombia, Colombia’s largest bank, along with its insurance and investment businesses.

World.title: Lázaro Ramos Named Ambassador of Brazil’s Afro Brasil Museum
World.content:
Brazil · Culture

Key Facts —Who is Lázaro Ramos? A celebrated Brazilian actor, director, writer, and presenter known as a public voice for Afro-Brazilian culture. —The institution. The Museu Afro Brasil Emanoel Araújo in São Paulo preserves and exhibits Afro-Brazilian and African-descended histories and arts. —The new role. Ramos was announced as an institutional ambassador in the museum’s Cultural Ambassadors Program in July 2026. —Collection size. The museum holds a major repository of over 6,000 objects, including sculptures, paintings, and contemporary art. —Mission. The ambassadorship aims to encourage visitation and broaden the museum’s dialogue with diverse audiences.

Lázaro Ramos, one of Brazil’s most respected actors and cultural figures, has been announced as the new institutional ambassador for the Museu Afro Brasil Emanoel Araújo in São Paulo.

A Warm Welcome for Lázaro Ramos

The announcement, reported in mid-July 2026, places Ramos at the heart of a vital cultural institution. He joins the museum’s Cultural Ambassadors Program to help expand its reach.

Ramos said the invitation carried deep personal meaning. It connected him directly to the references that shaped his own identity as a Black Brazilian artist.

Inside the Museu Afro Brasil

The Museu Afro Brasil Emanoel Araújo sits inside São Paulo’s sprawling Ibirapuera Park, the city’s most famous green space. It opened its doors in 2004 with a clear mission to preserve and celebrate Afro-Brazilian memory.

Its collection is a rich tapestry of more than 6,000 objects. Visitors encounter sculptures, engravings, ceramics, paintings, jewelry, photographs, and contemporary art spanning themes of religiosity, history, and Black contributions to Brazilian society.

A Mission Beyond Ceremony

As an ambassador, Ramos will take part in communication actions and promotional initiatives. The goal is to encourage more people to visit and to strengthen the museum’s dialogue with different audiences.

This role is not purely ceremonial. It actively reinforces cultural recognition and connects the museum’s historical mission to contemporary Brazil.

Preserving Memory and Belonging

The museum was created to challenge the erasure of African-descended histories in Brazil. It stands as a powerful space for valorizing Black presence in the nation’s cultural fabric.

Ramos highlighted the institution’s essential work in preserving Black memory. He emphasized how it strengthens a profound sense of belonging for millions of Brazilians.

A Legacy Rooted in Ibirapuera Park

For foreign visitors and expats, the museum’s location inside Ibirapuera Park makes it an accessible cultural stop in São Paulo‘s largest urban oasis. The park itself is a hub for art, with several major museums and architectural landmarks designed by Oscar Niemeyer.

The Museu Afro Brasil was founded by Emanoel Araújo, a renowned Bahian artist and curator who dedicated his life to showcasing the depth of Afro-Brazilian art. His vision turned the museum into a national reference point for understanding how African traditions have shaped modern Brazil.

What This Means for Expats and Investors

For expats living in Brazil, the appointment of a mainstream figure like Ramos signals a growing institutional focus on inclusive cultural programming. It may lead to more bilingual exhibitions and events that help non-Portuguese speakers engage with Brazil’s diverse heritage.

Investors watching Brazil’s creative economy should note that high-profile ambassadorships often precede expanded private-sector partnerships. The museum’s enhanced visibility could attract sponsorship from companies eager to associate with Brazil’s cultural and social progress.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Lázaro Ramos?

Lázaro Ramos is a renowned Brazilian actor, director, writer, and television presenter. He is widely recognized as a leading public voice for Afro-Brazilian culture and education, with a career spanning film, theater, and major TV productions.

What is the Museu Afro Brasil?

The Museu Afro Brasil Emanoel Araújo is a major museum in São Paulo’s Ibirapuera Park. Opened in 2004, it is dedicated to preserving and exhibiting the histories, arts, and memories of Afro-Brazilian and African-descended peoples through a vast collection of over 6,000 objects.

What will Lázaro Ramos do as ambassador?

Ramos will participate in communication and promotion initiatives to boost public visitation. He will also work to broaden the museum’s dialogue with new and diverse audiences across Brazil, using his public platform to strengthen cultural recognition.

World.title: US Miner Coeur Mining Bets Record $158M on Mexico Silver
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Mining

Key Facts —The spend. Coeur Mining is investing a record US$158 million in exploration in 2026, about double last year and its largest programme ever. —Mexico first. Two Mexican mines lead: US$27 million and 83 km of drilling at Palmarejo, US$24 million and 119 km at Las Chispas. —The prize. Drilling in Palmarejo’s Eastern District is hitting wide, high-grade silver and gold, with deposits still open in all directions. —The backdrop. Coeur reportedly gained Las Chispas by buying SilverCrest Metals for more than US$1.58 billion, completed in February 2025. —The company. Coeur is a US-based precious-metals producer listed in New York (NYSE: CDE).

Coeur Mining, a US precious-metals producer, is pouring record money into the ground in Mexico. Its 2026 exploration budget of US$158 million is the biggest in its history, and its Mexican silver and gold mines sit at the centre of the bet.

A 100-ounce silver bar. Coeur Mining is spending record sums drilling its Mexican silver and gold mines. (Photo: Ausecure / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0)

Coeur Mining is a US-based precious-metals producer, listed in New York, that digs silver and gold from a handful of mines across the Americas. Two of them are in Mexico.

This year the company is spending like rarely before. Its 2026 exploration budget of US$158 million is roughly twice last year’s level and the largest in Coeur’s history.

And Mexico, more than any other country, is where that money is going.

A Record US$158 Million Exploration Push

Exploration is the least glamorous part of mining, but it is where future production is born. Money spent drilling today decides how much metal a company can sell a decade from now.

Most of Coeur’s exploration dollars aim to prove up more metal at mines it already owns, rather than hunt for brand-new deposits. That is a lower-risk way to grow reserves when prices are high.

With silver and gold prices elevated, every extra ounce a driller confirms is worth more today than it was a year ago, which helps explain the sheer scale of the outlay.

The programme reaches beyond Mexico, into Coeur’s mines in the United States and Canada as well. But no single country commands as large a share of the budget as Mexico does.

Why Mexico Leads the Spending

Two of Coeur’s mines sit in Mexico, and both are getting heavy investment. Palmarejo, a gold-silver mine in the northern state of Chihuahua, is set for US$27 million and 83 kilometres of drilling.

Las Chispas, a silver-gold mine in the neighbouring state of Sonora, will receive US$24 million and 119 kilometres of drilling.

Together the two Mexican sites account for a large slice of the record budget, underlining how central the country has become to Coeur’s future.

Mexico is the world’s largest silver producer, and its northern states have drawn miners for centuries. Chihuahua and Sonora form part of a mineral belt worked since the colonial era, yet modern crews are still finding fresh veins in that old ground.

What the Drills Are Finding

The early results are encouraging. At Palmarejo’s Eastern District, holes at the San Miguel and La Unión targets have hit wide, high-grade intercepts of silver and gold.

Crucially, Coeur says the deposits remain “open in all directions” — mining shorthand for ore that keeps going beyond what has been drilled so far.

For a miner, that is the best kind of news. It suggests years of extra life may be added to assets that are already in production and generating cash.

Coeur plans to keep drilling through the year, and any confirmed extensions would feed into the reserve figures it reports to investors — the numbers that ultimately move its share price.

The US$1.58 Billion Bet Behind It

Coeur’s Mexican push is recent and expensive. It gained Las Chispas by taking over the Canadian miner SilverCrest Metals in an all-stock deal worth more than US$1.58 billion, completed in February 2025.

SilverCrest had spent years turning Las Chispas into one of the highest-grade silver mines in the world, so the ground was already known to be rich before Coeur swooped in.

That acquisition turned Coeur into one of the world’s larger silver producers, lifting combined output toward roughly 21 million ounces of silver in 2025.

Pouring exploration money into Las Chispas now is a way to justify that price tag — by finding more metal beneath the mine it has only just bought.

What It Means for Mexico and Investors

For Mexico, the spending is a vote of confidence in its mining sector at a time when the industry frets about permitting, security and a government wary of new open-pit projects.

Coeur’s Mexican mines are underground operations, which tend to draw less political heat than sprawling open pits. That may make its expansion plans easier to advance.

The bet is not risk-free, though. Mexican mining has grown politically sensitive, with tighter rules on concessions and water, and security remains a concern in parts of the north.

There is a wider context, too. Foreign miners have long been central to Mexican silver, and Coeur’s outlay adds to a wave of activity that includes local giant Fresnillo’s own recent dealmaking.

For investors, the record budget is a bet that high metal prices will hold long enough to reward aggressive drilling. If prices slip, the spending could look expensive; if they hold, Coeur may have bought itself years of cheap growth.

Its coming results will show whether the gamble is already paying off.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much is Coeur Mining spending on exploration in 2026?

About US$158 million, roughly double its 2025 budget and the largest exploration programme in the company’s history. Much of it targets its existing mines rather than new discoveries.

Where are Coeur Mining’s Mexican mines?

Coeur runs two mines in Mexico: Palmarejo, a gold-silver mine in Chihuahua, and Las Chispas, a silver-gold mine in Sonora. Together they are receiving more than US$50 million of the 2026 exploration budget.

How did Coeur acquire Las Chispas?

Coeur gained Las Chispas by acquiring Canada’s SilverCrest Metals in an all-stock deal worth over US$1.58 billion, completed in February 2025, which made Coeur a leading global silver producer.

World.title: H&M Argentina to Open First Store in Buenos Aires by 2027
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Retail

Key Facts —The arrival. H&M will open its first Argentine store in 2027, ending roughly a decade of on-and-off speculation. —The partner. It enters through Hola Moda, a Panama-based franchise operator that also runs labels such as Carolina Herrera and Michael Kors. —The location. The debut store is planned for the Alto Palermo shopping centre in Buenos Aires. —The map. Argentina becomes one of H&M’s last big Latin American markets; Paraguay opens first, late in 2026. —The politics. Milei’s government has hailed the move as proof its deregulation is drawing global brands back.

The arrival of H&M Argentina has been rumoured for a decade. Now it is official: the Swedish fast-fashion giant will open its first Argentine store in 2027, an early trophy for President Javier Milei’s drive to reopen the economy.

Inside the Alto Palermo shopping centre in Buenos Aires, where H&M plans its first Argentine store. (Photo: Fernando Martello / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0)
