World.title: Putin stepping up hybrid war on Latvia because he’s ‘losing in Ukraine’, PM Kulbergs says
World.content:
Latvia’s Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs has told Euronews that Russia and Belarus are intensifying their hybrid war against the Baltic state as Russia’s President Vladimir Putin looks to divert attention from losses on the battlefield in Ukraine.

 

Latvia has recently become thefocal point of what EU governments describe as Russia and Belarus' hybrid campaign against neighbouring states, with Belarus' President Aliaksandr Lukashenka using the state-sponsored exploitation of migrants to exert pressure on the EU's eastern border.

“We’re being tested,” Prime Minister Kulbergs told Euronews’ morning show,Europe Today. “At this moment, it is us. At any given moment it is our neighbours in Lithuania, Estonia, Finland or Poland.”

“This is a hybrid threat. This is a war threat. That's what Russia does,” he added.

Since 2021, Belarus’ President Aliaksandr Lukashenka has been luring in migrants from the Middle East and Africa and busing them to the border with Poland and Baltic states.

Many countries have fortified their border defences, including through building fences, in response.

On Wednesday, Latvia’s armed forces said they had fired a warning shot and used tear gas against migrants attempting to cross from Belarus.

Asked why Russia and Belarus seemed to be singling out his country, Kulbergs responded: “Because he's losing in Ukraine, simple. He needs to take attention somewhere else.”

He added that the asylum seekers attempting to cross were “men, 18 to 25, with a criminal past, all given visas from Belarus”.

“This is an organised threat towards us to find a weak link,” he explained, “and we all have to take all the measures to prevent that.”

Latvia recorded as many as 111 attempted illegal crossings from Belarus in a single day last week. That compared to just two attempts to cross into Lithuania, which shares a border four times as long with Belarus, on the same day.

The trend is reportedly prompting neighbouring Lithuania to mull introducing border controls with Latvia in order to prevent secondary migration, a prospect firmly rejected by both countries’ presidents. Secondary migration into Lithuania has spiked since Riga has been targeted with more migrant flows.

The increase also coincides with the start of the campaign ahead of Latvia's October parliamentary elections, suggesting that the move is a coordinated attempt to destabilise the region's democracy.

World.title: Countdown to the ballot: Zambia gears up for August elections
World.content:
This week on Spotlight on Africa, we're heading to Zambia, where general elections are set to take place on the 13th August. Voters will go to the polls to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs. Incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema has already picked up endorsements from within his own camp, the UPND Alliance, the coalition that's held power since 2021. So what's at stake, and who's in the running?

Advertising

This week on the podcast, we're heading to Zambia, which is gearing up for elections next month and is now in full campaign mode. Two of our RFI colleagues, Yang Mei and Igor Strauss, travelled to Zambia recently for in-depth reporting on four years of Hakainde Hichilema's rule, and his chances of re-election.

In power since August 2021, "HH", as he's most often called, is a businessman, farmer and politician, and the seventh president of Zambia.

General elections are due to be held in the country on 13 August 2026 to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs.

The year ahead for African democracy: who is going to the polls in 2026?

Hichilema has received endorsements from some members of the UPND Alliance, including from the leaders of the Party of National Unity and Progress and the Movement for Multi-Party Democracy.

According to an opinion poll conducted by a University of Zambia demographer, Hichilema is set to be re-elected, leading with 60 percent of the vote, while the combined opposition would take 35 percent.

Zambia's Hichilema sworn in, becoming rare opposition president in southern Africa

Our colleagues Yang Mei and Igor Strauss bring us some of the interviews they gathered on the ground, so join us as we hear from ordinary Zambians, as well as from leading journalist Joseph Mwenda, editor-in-chief at News Diggers, who has led multiple investigations into the current government's relations with China; and from Robert Mwale, an economist and Lead Public Finance and Economic Governance Researcher at the Centre for Trade Policy and Development (CTPD).

Among the issues at stake are a lack of freedom of expression, but also a legacy of economic growth, driven in no small part by China's heavy involvement in the economy.

Thanks to our reporters, Igor Strauss and Yang Mei, for their work and insight, and thank you for listening.

This is the last episode of the 2025–26 season. We'll be back in September with another one.

Spotlight on Africa is produced by RFI's English language service. This episode was mixed by Erwan Rome.

World.title: Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended
World.content:
On 16 July, Turkey marked a decade since the failed coup that shook the nation. Its defeat is widely viewed as the final curtain on military meddling in politics and as the moment when President Erdogan cemented his grip on power, yet the aftershocks for human rights and foreign relations still reverberate.

Advertising

On 16 July, Turkey marked a decade since the failed coup that shook the nation. Its defeat is widely viewed as the final curtain on military meddling in politics and as the moment when President Erdogan cemented his grip on power, yet the aftershocks for human rights and foreign relations still reverberate.

A decade ago, factions within the Turkish military, composed of rebellious officers and followers of the Islamic cleric Fethullah Gulen, launched a dramatic attempt to topple President Erdogan.

"I remember, as a soldier, those who started the coup," recalls Murat Aslan, an army officer at the time. "I had no idea that there were members of this organisation (Gulen followers); they were very secretive."

Erdogan tightens his grip

Now a security analyst at SETA, a pro-government think tank, Aslan describes the failed coup as a turning point that reshaped the course of Turkish democracy.

"The message was very clear. Turkish society collectively rejected it," said Aslan. "Thousands took to the streets; that's more than challenging, because you see tanks rolling and people trying to stop them, trying to capture the soldiers with their rifles. It takes more than courage." More than 250 people died resisting the coup.

In the aftermath, Erdogan imposed emergency rule and expanded his presidential authority through a sharply contested national referendum. "This military intervention actually consolidated the Erdogan-led government," Aslan added.

Turkey's military, relations with US to survive failed coup, ruling party vice-president

Hundreds of soldiers and officers faced prosecution as the government declared an end to the army's long history of political interference. Since 1960, the military had orchestrated three coups, the most recent in 1980.

A decade of purges and closures

In the wake of the failed takeover, tens of thousands were purged from state institutions, many never returning even after being cleared.

More than a thousand NGOs were shut down during two years of emergency rule. Milena Buyum, senior Turkey campaigner for Amnesty International, acknowledges the grave threat to democracy posed by the attempted coup: "The state has a responsibility to ensure the safety and security of its citizens and to investigate criminal acts like the ones carried out that night," said Buyum.

Turkey's Erdogan warms to Russia after West coup response

However, Buyum warns that many of the measures introduced under the state of emergency have since been written into ordinary law, permanently curtailing fundamental freedoms: "The right to freedom of expression, freedom of assembly and association: the impact on civil society was felt very sharply and starkly in the immediate aftermath of the coup, but that impact continues," said Buyum.

Ankara's alliances

The failed coup also drove a wedge into Turkey's long-standing alliance with the United States. "Ankara saw the hand of the United States behind the failed coup attempt," claims Ozgur Unluhisarcikli, who leads the Ankara office of the German Marshall Fund.

Even before the attempted coup, Erdogan's relations with President Barack Obama had been tense. Obama's belated support, offered only after the coup had failed, fuelled Ankara's suspicions of US complicity, particularly as Washington refused to extradite Fethullah Gulen, whom Erdogan blamed for orchestrating the plot. Gulen denied the accusation until his death in 2024.

Turks in France divided on failed coup

Unluhisarcikli observes that US-Turkish relations remained strained for years, while Erdogan gravitated towards Russian President Vladimir Putin, whose rapid show of support stood in sharp contrast to Washington's hesitation.

"Putin was among the first leaders, I believe even the first, to extend political support to the elected government in Ankara, and in those days I believe that support mattered greatly to President Erdogan," Unluhisarcikli said.

Rumours still persist in Turkey today that Moscow warned Erdogan on the day of the failed coup. Unluhisarcikli says it was only with the election of President Donald Trump, who shared Erdogan's animosity towards Obama and Joe Biden, that US-Turkish relations began to thaw, a shift highlighted at this month's NATO summit in Ankara. Yet the wave of mass arrests during the summit, enabled by post-coup emergency powers, served as a stark reminder that the shadow of the failed takeover still looms over Turkey.

World.title: EU imposes new round of sanctions against Russia
World.content:
The European Union has agreed upon a new sanctions package against Russia for its war in Ukraine, which includes a price cap on Russian oil.

Members of the European Union on Thursday agreed to impose a new round of sanctions against Russia over its war in Ukraine after weeks of negotiations.

The 21st round of the package was held up by lots of objections by member states to various proposed elements.

The agreement was reached after weeks of debates, with some members expressing concern that certain restrictions could cause greater harm to the EU economy than to the Russian economy.

The deadlock was overcome after Greece was granted an exemption allowing one of its shipping firms to carry on transporting Russian liquefied natural gas from the Arctic.

What does the 21st ⁠sanctions package include?

"Our 21st sanctions package targets the sectors with the highest impact: energy, financial services, crypto, and trade," European Council head Antonio Costa posted online.

Diplomats from the EU's 27 member states had been trying to reach a consensus over the price cap on Russian crude oil exports at $44 (€39) before the deadline.

As per the agreed deal, the current level will remain in place for the next 12 months.

Two EU diplomats said the deal also allows one-year ‌exemption for the transfer of Russian ‌liquefied ​natural gas (LNG) to third countries, with automatic renewal.

Putin's strategy behind Russia's largest missile attack To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The new package also targets Moscow's financial and crypto sector.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the package adds 32 ​Russian banks, crypto firms and oil trading ⁠platforms ​to the ​EU's transaction ban list.

The new set of EU sanctions also include entry bans and asset freezes on individuals and companies that can be linked to Russia's war against Ukraine.

Von der Leyen welcomed the agreement which will not let automatic adjustment of the international price cap on Russian oil.

She said it is to ensure "that the Russian war machine does not benefit from market shocks."

World.title: Europe wildfires prompt evacuations in France, Spain, Italy
World.content:
Fires are blazing across several European countries as the continent braces for another heat wave. In 2026, wildfires have already burnt more land in Europe than the annual average over the past two decades.

Thousands of people were urged to evacuate on Thursday as forest fires continued to blaze through parts of Europe.

The latest fires come as Europe prepares for another heat wave with temperatures of up to 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit) forecast in some areas.

So far in 2026, wildfires have burnt more land in Europe than the annual average over the past two decades.

Climate change is making extreme weather events such as heat waves and the forest fires that ensure more frequent and more severe.

France evacuates tourist hotspot

In France, authorities evacuated 7,000 people "as a precaution" on Thursday north of Cap Ferret, near the tourist hub of Arcachon Bay. This brings the total number of evacuees in the area to 12,000.

Fires had ravaged around 2,000 hectares (nearly 5,000 acres), authorities said on Wednesday.

Earlier, on Tuesday, two firefighters died while battling a fire that broke out near Bordeaux airport.

Fires have burnt thousands of acres of vegetation in northwest France Image: Manon Cruz/AP Photo/picture alliance

Spanish PM warns of climate change

Spanish authorities ordered the evacuation of several districts around Toledo, south of Madrid, on Wednesday.

Meanwhile, Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez visited a fire-ravaged area in Guadalajara, northeast of Madrid, where more than 30 villages were evacuated.

"Year after year we clearly see how climate change kills and destroys wealth in our communities," he said. "This isn't politics. It is science, it's about facts."

Authorities in Spain are battling blazes both north and south of Madrid Image: Ana Beltran/REUTERS

Italian officials blame 'malicious' arsonists

Around 6,000 firefighters, forest guards and civil protection officials have been deployed across Sicily after fires have raged for days.

Regional president Renato Schifani said about 50 fires were still burning despite the deployment of water-bombing aircraft.

And on mainland of Italy, in Calabria, more than 160 fires have been recorded.

Local officials in Calabria have accused "malicious individuals" of arson, pointing to rags doused in flammable liquid that were tied to the tails of stray cats to spread fires.

World.title: Germany news: FM Wadephul wraps up Africa tour in South Africa
World.content:
Skip next section South Africa should not be excluded from G20 Summit — Wadephul

07/23/2026 July 23, 2026 South Africa should not be excluded from G20 Summit — Wadephul

Wadephul spoke of a "crisis of multilateralism" during his remarks in Johannesburg Image: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance

Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, while visiting South Africa as part of his Africa tour, criticized US President Donald Trump's decision not to invite South Africa to the G20 Summit in Florida later this year.

"Excluding South Africa means sidelining an important African voice as well as a regional economic and political leader," Wadephul said during a visit to the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg.

This was in no one's interest, he added, "because, especially in times of growing global economic uncertainty, we need more cooperation, not less."

South Africa is a founding member of the G20, which gathers major global economies and serves as a key forum for multilateral engagement.

South Africa also hosted last year's G20 summit in Johannesburg, which the Trump administration boycotted after claims that South Africa was committing a genocide against the country's white farmers. South Africa has categorically denied the Trump administration's allegations.

Amid the rift, Trump announced that South Africa was disinvited to the G20 summit in December 2026, arguing "the country has demonstrated to the world they are not a country worthy of membership anywhere."

World.title: Mykhailo Drapatyi: Who is Ukraine's new commander-in-chief?
World.content:
Ukraine has a new army chief, with Mykhailo Drapatyi replacing Oleksandr Syrskyi as commander-in-chief. The change follows a cabinet reshuffle that ousted the popular defense minister, Mykhailo Fedorov.

On Tuesday (July 21), Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy appointed Mykhailo Drapatyi as the new commander-in-chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine. Zelenskyy wants him to develop a modern defense strategy and to continue the recently launched military reforms.

This comes after an unexpected cabinet reshuffle last week. Many ministers have retained their posts under new Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi, but not former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who had a major argument with former commander-in-chief Oleksandr Syrskyi about the strategic direction that Ukraine's war effort should take.



President Zelenskyy's military shakeup has been widely criticized Image: Ukrainian Presidential Press Service/Handout/REUTERS

The firing of the popular defense minister sparked outrage among parts of Ukraine's population. During mass protests, demonstrators not only demanded his return but also the dismissal of Syrskyi.

While the latter has now been removed from his post, Federov will not be returning. Zelenskyy has appointed Yevhen Khmara, who was previously head of Ukraine's Security Service (SBU), as the new defense minister.

'The army needs changes'

Mykhailo Drapatyi was the only general who publicly defended Fedorov after his dismissal. He wrote on Facebook that Fedorov's appointment to the defense ministry six months ago had been "a serious attempt to change conditions in the military system that were in place for years."

He added that the Defense Ministry had developed into a true partner for the army: "Cooperation between the troops and the Defense Ministry changed. There was a new willingness to listen to commanders, to take decisions more quickly and to support changes that came from the units themselves."

Drapatyj explained that many of the changes had had to be pushed through despite fierce resistance from the old system, and that there was a need to discuss problems in the army openly and honestly.

Zelenskyy fires armed forces chief Syrskyi To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Who is Mykhailo Drapatyi?

Mykhailo Drapatyi (born in 1982) is a highly decorated Ukrainian major general who has distinguished himself as a battle-hardened frontline commander since 2014. At the beginning of the Donbas War, the trained tank trooper became known for his resolve during what was then called an "anti-terror operation."

After Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, he coordinated — as deputy commander of the Ukrainian Joint Forces — the successful defense of the town of Kryvyi Rih as well as the liberation of strategically important areas in the south of the country.

Thanks to his reputation as a military crisis manager, who also stopped the Russian offensive near Kharkiv in 2024, he rose through the ranks of the general staff to become head of the ground forces of the Ukrainian army and eventually Commander of the Joint Forces.

Did Syrskyj want to eliminate a rival?

On June 1, 2025, Drapatyi handed in his resignation as army commander after a Russian missile strike targeting a training ground under his command killed at least 12 soldiers and injured more than 60 others.

On Facebook, he justified his decision, citing his "personal sense of accountability for this tragedy." This earned Drapatyi a reputation for not hanging on to a position at all costs and taking moral responsibility. President Zelenskyy, however, did not accept the resignation and later appointed Drapatyi Commander of the Joint Forces.

However, when Drapatyi was tasked with defending the Kharkiv region in autumn 2025, observers remarked that this was a deliberate move to restrict his influence. Some media outlets speculated that Commander-in-Chief Syrskyi wanted to sideline the popular general as a potential rival.

A crisis of the president's own making?

Observers point out that President Zelenskyy's personnel decisions seem to have been driven by growing public pressure.

Military experts are divided when it comes to assessing the change of power. Oleksandr Khara of the Ukrainian Center for Defense Strategies views the protests as an important democratic corrective in an era in which elections cannot take place.

"The president listened to the response from civil society and the military and drew his conclusions. Society has succeeded in steering events back onto a democratic course," he said.

Speaking to DW, Oleksiy Melnyk of the Kyiv-based Razumkov Center was more critical. While Zelenskyy had the right to make personnel decisions, he had nonetheless caused a major domestic political crisis that was completely unnecessary.

"This will definitely not turn out to his advantage. It is regrettable that the president has learned nothing from previous lessons, because exactly one year ago there was a similarly triggered home-grown crisis," he said.

This article was originally published in Ukrainian.

World.title: Peru: 10 killed in housefire in capital Lima
World.content:
The fire was reportedly started by extortionists. Investigators are trying "to determine the point of origin, the circumstances, and the causes of this fire."

At least 10 people have died after a fire broke out at ⁠a ⁠family home in a low-income neighborhood in ​Peru's capital, Lima, police said on ‌Wednesday.

According to relatives, five of the deceased were adults, and the other five were children.

Another two people were injured in the incident, the INDECI civil defense institute wrote in a social media post.

The fire ‌broke out ​early in the morning at ​a house located in Lima's ⁠La ​Victoria ​district.

The fire reportedly spread quickly due to flammable materials and parked vehicles outside of the house Image: Ernesto Benavides/AFP

Peru's president-elect Keiko Fujimori visited the ruins Wednesday, calling the deaths "a terrible massacre."

"What people are asking for is order and security, and that is the first thing we are going to do next week," she told the press.

Investigation is underway

Peruvian news outlet El Comercio reported that nine fire units responded to the scene to extinguish the flames, which, according to preliminary reports, spread rapidly due to the presence of flammable materials and parked electric vehicles.

Local media reports said the fire was started by extortionists Image: Ernesto Benavides/AFP

Authorities have launched an investigation "to determine the point of origin, the circumstances, and the causes of this fire," police chief Oscar Arriola told the media.

According to local media reports, extortionists who were threatening local businesses started the fire.

Colonel John Lujan, who is heading up the investigation, said "a possible deliberate act or a case of extortion" is among the possible causes that are being explored.

World.title: India: Modi orders fast-track courts for paper leaks amid protests
World.content:
07/23/2026 July 23, 2026 Protests 'dented' Modi's grip on India: Experts tell DW

As youth-led protests mount across India, experts told DW that they may have dented Prime Minister Narendra Modi's grip on India, steadily built over the last 12 years.

The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party has reached the peak of its political power in terms of parliamentary seats, political analyst and author Amit Julka told DW over a call. "It's ironic that it is at this point that the BJP government, or the broader NDA government, is facing this legitimacy crisis," he said.

The protests have changed societal discourse, Julka said. "There was this mythical, transcendental, sort of aura that Modi had built up for himself. There was this era of complete hegemony over public discourse ...a lot of consent towards Modi's Government and his style of functioning. And I think that has gotten dented," Julka said.

Indian writer and political analyst Ananya Vajpeyi said that the protests were "definitely embarrassing for the government."

"They are definitely on the back foot. I don't think they expected any of this," she told DW, adding that the scale of the protests were due to political miscalculation.

That said, it is not apparent if the threat will reach the ballots of India's next national elections in 2029. According to Julka, that depends on several other factors such as welfare schemes, community bias, local political dynamics and even how the "GenZ protest" shifts narratives at the grassroots level in India.

World.title: US hits Iran as Houthis claim strikes on Saudi tankers
World.content:
07/23/2026 July 23, 2026 Houthis 'snookered' into joining US-Iran conflict — Rubio

Rubio accused Iran of violating previous deals with the US, saying Tehran would "pay the price for it" Image: Brendan Smialowski/Pool AFP/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that he believed that Yemen's Houthi rebels had been tricked into joining the conflict with the United States by Tehran.

"The Houthis largely were smart and stayed out of all this throughout the conflict, but they now apparently have gotten themselves suckered into this, going after Saudi Arabia and their ships," Rubio told reporters on the sidelines of a summit of the ASEAN Southeast Asian bloc in Manila, the Philippines.

"I hope they will de-escalate, because I think the Houthis, frankly, got snookered into this thing by the Iranians," he said.

The militant group controls much of Yemen's most populous areas, including the capital, Sanaa, and is allied with Iran. It already began threatening merchant ships in the Red Sea in response to Israel's offensive in Gaza in 2023.

The Houthi rebel group is a longstanding ally of Iran Image: Khaled Abdullah/REUTERS

The top US official also accused Iran of going back on its commitments in peace talks.

"These people make deals ‌and then they break ‌it ​almost immediately or they decide, 'oh, let's change the deal'. ​That's not how deals work," he said.

"So now ⁠they're ​paying the ​price for it. And ​maybe they'll change ‌their mind here over the ​next ⁠few days as they continue to ⁠suffer ​great losses," Rubio added.

He said he believed Iran was not yet ready for a deal with Washington but said it might be soon, while also reiterating the US' position that Iran should be "denuclearized." Iran maintains its nuclear program is exclusively for civilian purposes.

Earlier this month, US President Donald Trump declared that a previous ceasefire deal with Iran was "over."

World.title: Iran war: Trump threatens bridges over Hormuz Strait attacks
World.content:
Skip next section Signs of ships avoiding second choke point off Yemen after Houthi warnings: tracker data

07/22/2026 July 22, 2026 Signs of ships avoiding second choke point off Yemen after Houthi warnings: tracker data

Houthi supporters rallied in Sanaa in support of the announcement of a maritime blockade earlier this week [FILE: July 20, 2026] Image: Mohammed Hamoud/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

Houthi threats to ships headed to or from Saudi Arabia's western shoreline could further impact commercial shipping, data trackers are warning.

The Houthis, who have de facto control over much of Yemen, have declared a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia and told ships to avoid the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the gateway to the Red Sea on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula from the Strait of Hormuz. It provides access to western Saudi coastal cities like Jeddah and Yanbu.

Data provider Kpler said shipping in both waterways was "under pressure," saying traffic in both straits had fallen sharply.

Ship broker Clarksons issued a similar warning, saying four vessels had registered new courses on Wednesday, avoiding the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and heading north through the Suez Canal towards the Mediterranean instead.

"The threat of Houthi hostile actions against Saudi Arabia ... has begun to have an overall effect on tanker activity," Clarksons wrote. "There are reports of several tankers, having ​loaded in Saudi Arabia's Yanbu port in the Red Sea, that have shifted course towards the Suez Canal rather than sail south towards the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, while ​others are holding their positions waiting for further instruction."

For ships headed to places like India, Pakistan, Indonesia or Australia, doing this would add well over 10,000 nautical miles (more than 20,000 kilometers) and weeks at sea to the typical travel distance.

"Anything that restricts shipping through the Red Sea would be problematic for the same reasons that the Strait of Hormuz is problematic," US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on the sidelines of a regional summit in the Philippines on Wednesday.

Pakistan's Foreign Ministry on Wednesday warned that the actions "threaten regional security, undermine freedom of navigation, challenge the rules-based maritime order and jeopardize uninterrupted flow of global commerce."

The Reuters news agency cited an advisory from the European Union's Aspides naval mission in the Red Sea as saying that ships with links to Israel, the United ​States or Saudi Arabia ‌were at a higher risk of being attacked by the Houthis and were advised to avoid voyages through the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden until the threat level decreases.

World.title: Mónica García: “Las lógicas partidistas no deben frenar una ley que busca evitar 140 muertes al día”
World.content:
La ministra de Sanidad se muestra convencida de que la nueva ley del tabaco será aprobada en el Congreso y espera mejorar el texto durante la tramitación parlamentaria

La ministra de Sanidad, Mónica García (Madrid, 52 años), presentó este martes la nueva ley del tabaco como una “gran victoria” para España y equiparó la iniciativa al reciente triunfo de la selección en el Mundial de fútbol. Hace 16 años, recordó, el primer éxito de España en este torneo también coincidió con la pionera ley del tabaco, que erradicó el humo de los espacios interiores de bares, restaurantes y centros de trabajo. Como entonces, sin embargo, el proyecto se ha topado con el rechazo de sectores como la hostelería, industria tabaquera y estanqueros, entre otros. Tras su paso por el Consejo de Ministros, el proyecto deberá ser aprobado por el Congreso de los Diputados, donde necesita del apoyo de formaciones como el PP o Junts, que ya han mostrado sus reticencias. Pese a ello, la ministra se muestra confiada en que la tramitación parlamentaria salga adelante, y que el debate mejore el texto en cuestiones como el empaquetado genérico, que evita que las cajetillas de cigarrillos actúen como un elemento publicitario más. La ministra atiende a EL PAÍS por teléfono.

Pregunta. ¿Por qué ha llegado el proyecto de ley al Consejo de Ministros ahora, justo antes de las vacaciones, y no antes?

Respuesta. Hemos tenido que alinear la ley con las directivas de la Comisión Europea y pasar por una serie de trámites que han alargado el proceso.

P. ¿Teme que el proyecto no pase el filtro del Congreso?

R. Sabemos que existen unos equilibrios parlamentarios que no siempre responden a las necesidades de los ciudadanos, sino a lógicas partidistas. Pero esta es una ley que nos pone otra vez en la vanguardia de la protección de la salud pública y esperamos que prime la responsabilidad y no frenen una norma que busca evitar 50.000 muertes al año, 140 al día. El tabaco en todas sus formas está detrás del 30% de los tumores y el 100% de los cardiólogos dicen que, si pudieran retirar un factor de riesgo evitable, este sería el tabaco.

P. ¿Ha tenido algún contacto con el PP o Junts?

R. No todavía. Lo que sí acabo de escuchar es al señor Alberto Núñez Feijóo diciendo que la ley es una cortina de humo y que va a dividir al país. No sé si se refiere a que dividirá a los que quieren tener cáncer y los que no. No sé exactamente a qué división se refiere. Sí sé que en 2010 escuchamos también augurios catastrofistas que no se han cumplido. Hoy tenemos un país con espacios cerrados sin humo, mucho más saludables. Y me alegra ver que bares y restaurantes siguen gozando de muy buena salud. También queremos que la tengan los trabajadores y usuarios de sus terrazas.

P. ¿Qué les ha llevado a dar el salto de prohibir fumar a los menores?

R. El tabaco en todas sus formas es un tóxico adictivo muy perjudicial para la salud y es nuestra obligación proteger a los menores, al igual que hacemos con el alcohol. Estamos viendo, además, que los dispositivos asociados al tabaco son una vía de entrada a la adicción para los menores y que causan daños como hemorragias pulmonares.

P. La ley prevé sanciones de 200 euros si un menor fuma. Serán los padres quienes hagan frente a la multa, que puede ser sustituida por trabajos a la comunidad. ¿Es esta una forma de implicar a todos contra el tabaquismo?

R. La ley, como las de este tipo, debe incluir un régimen sancionador, pero en términos de salud pública eso nos preocupa menos. El objetivo no es sancionar, es consensuar elementos que consideramos de sentido común y fundamentales. No buscamos perseguir ni recaudar, sino visibilizar, concienciar y dar respuesta a la evidencia científica.

P. Se ha criticado que España será una “excepción” europea al prohibir fumar en terrazas y que esto dañará el turismo y la imagen del país.

R. Más que motivo de crítica, debe ser algo de lo que estemos orgullosos. La Comisión Europea dijo en 2024 que había que extender los espacios sin humo, también a las terrazas. Ser de los primeros en aplicar una medida que protege la salud de la población y que con seguridad seguirán otros países debe satisfacernos. El tabaco también es la principal causa de muerte evitable en Europa y existe un consenso entre las sociedades científicas.

P. ¿Era tan importante equiparar los vapeadores al tabaco tradicional? Los críticos dicen que son menos dañinos...

R. Ese debate es engañoso. Si se pretende que estos dispositivos sean una forma de control de daños, deberían usarse bajo supervisión médica, como los parches de nicotina o las pastillas. La industria sabe que no es así y lo está usando como excusa para atraer a nuevos consumidores jóvenes con presentaciones más amables que crearán nuevos adictos. Lo que más nos ha preocupado de las encuestas es el aumento del consumo de estos dispositivos entre los jóvenes.

Mónica García, en la azotea del ministerio de Sanidad, en Madrid, este miércoles. Carlos Rosillo

P. ¿Cómo valora las reacciones de sectores como la hostelería y la industria? ¿Le sorprende que sean tan parecidas a las de 2010?

R. Me sorprende más que algunos sectores no tengan memoria, pero son minoritarios. Existe una amplia mayoría de la sociedad que apoya este tipo de medidas porque los beneficios logrados en 2010 siguen estando muy presentes. También nos hemos encontrado mucha gente que ha dejado el tabaco o quiere hacerlo y está de acuerdo en que se amplíen las zonas libres de humo porque esto les ayuda a dejar de fumar.

P. Usted decía que se ha retrasado la aprobación del proyecto de ley para alinearlo con las directrices europeas. Pero se les critica no haber esperado a que la Comisión Europea acabe de revisar las directivas sobre la materia.

R. No es cierto, estamos alineados con la Comisión. Hay una cosa en la que todavía no está definida la posición europea, por ejemplo, que es sobre los vapeadores desechables. Lo habíamos introducido en el texto, pero por ahora lo hemos retirado porque en Europa todavía no se ha consensuado. Dicho esto, la ley tiene un trámite parlamentario y hay cosas que, si se acuerdan en este tiempo en Europa, las podemos introducir.

P. ¿Tiene sentido criticar la ley con el argumento de que el tabaco aporta casi 4.000 millones al PIB y genera 60.000 empleos?

R. No existe la dicotomía salud a cambio de economía, es falsa. Si no hay salud, no hay economía. 50.000 vidas al año y el enorme sufrimiento que provocan las enfermedades causadas por el tabaco no tienen precio. Y más allá de los impuestos que puedas recaudar, los costes de la asistencia sanitaria de todas estas enfermedades los triplica. No tiene sentido plantearlo en estos términos. Otra cosa es que haya empresas que defiendan sus intereses económicos, pero nuestra función es proteger la salud de los ciudadanos. No se pueden contraponer los intereses económicos de unas empresas concretas a la vida y salud de toda una población.

P. ¿Por qué se ha quedado fuera de la ley el empaquetado genérico que haga indistinguibles las distintas marcas?

R. Había algunas carteras que no estaban de acuerdo con el empaquetado genérico. Decidimos posponer este punto para el trámite parlamentario. Sabemos que el empaquetado genérico funciona. Ya lo tienen otros países y hay evidencia científica de los beneficios que aporta que la propia cajetilla no sea un elemento de publicidad más.

P. Entonces, ¿el PSOE se opone y Sumar quiere convencerle en el Congreso?

R. Más que oponerse, hay algunas dudas. Esperamos resolverlas y convencer a todas las fuerzas parlamentarias de los beneficios de esta medida.

P. Otra cuestión clave es el precio del tabaco. Seguimos siendo uno de los países de Europa con el tabaco más barato...

R. Es cierto que la evidencia es muy clara y un incremento de precio ayuda a reducir la prevalencia del tabaquismo. Pero la competencia es de otra cartera [Hacienda]. En cualquier caso, es bueno que se abra el debate público, porque la evidencia científica demuestra que poner encima de la mesa estas cuestiones ayuda a que la sociedad reflexione sobre el daño del tabaco y ayuda a algunas personas a dar el paso para dejarlo.

Mónica García, ministra de Sanidad, en Madrid, este miércoles. Carlos Rosillo

P. ¿Cómo valora que el Reino Unido haya aprobado la “generación libre de humo”, en la que los nacidos a partir de 2009 no podrán fumar nunca tabaco convencional?

R. El objetivo de un futuro libre de la adicción al tabaco es compartido por todos. Nosotros pensamos que podemos llegar al mismo sitio por distinto camino, pero todos podemos aprender de los demás y adoptar medidas que tengan éxito en otros lugares. España llevaba sin tocar la Ley del Tabaco desde 2010 y era imprescindible ahora dar un impulso. Pero todos perseguimos el mismo fin: proteger a los menores de la adicción, ayudar a quienes quieren dejar de fumar y evitar que el humo de quienes aún fuman perjudique al resto de la población.

World.title: “Si no tenemos habilidades para tolerar la frustración o para empatizar vamos a tener muchas dificultades en la vida”
World.content:
La psicóloga y conferenciante Patricia Ramírez reflexiona con su hija Carmen Rodríguez sobre la importancia de aprender desde la escuela la gestión de las emociones. Es la primera charla de ‘Pensemos el mañana’, un proyecto de Fundación Unicaja para debatir sobre la educación que necesitamos

Patricia Ramírez @Patri_Psicóloga Psicóloga, escritora y conferenciante Cuenta con más de 27 años de trayectoria como profesional de la salud, es doctora en Psicología por la Universidad de Granada y dirige una clínica de consultas online Además de ejercer con sus pacientes, lo divulga: tiene más de un millón de seguidores en redes sociales y ha escrito trece libros. En 2024 publicó Cómo tener tiempo para todo (Grijalbo), sobre el impacto del ritmo de vida en el bienestar psicológico Carmen Rodríguez Representante y 'community manager' Tras estudiar Derecho, abandonar unas oposiciones después de dos años y trabajar en un obrador como repostera, decidió dar un giro a su carrera para incorporarse al proyecto de divulgación de su madre, la psicóloga Patricia Ramírez, de la que hoy es representante. Sus cambios laborales le han permitido comprender las inquietudes que comparten muchos jóvenes; la presión académica, las dudas y, en definitiva, la búsqueda de un camino propio

Hay quien regula las emociones con la comida, quien lo hace con horas de scroll infinito frente a un móvil y quien es capaz de gestionarlas de manera saludable. Ese aprendizaje es, para la psicóloga Patricia Ramírez, la esencia de la educación emocional. “Nos permite una mejor tolerancia a la frustración, responsabilizarnos de nuestra vida, tener mejores vínculos con otras personas y un mayor respeto hacia nosotros mismos”. Una herramienta para conectar con la vida, con otras personas y con uno mismo, dice.

“La gente que busca el perfeccionismo nunca está satisfecha con ella misma. Y esto afecta muchísimo a la autoestima”

Para poder desarrollar la educación emocional, la apuesta de Ramírez es que se introduzca desde los primeros años, en las aulas. “Materias como Matemáticas, Física o Geografía son fundamentales, pero, si no tenemos habilidades para tolerar la frustración o empatizar con otra persona, vamos a tener muchas dificultades en la vida”, asegura. Esa es su propuesta para la educación del futuro: “educar en valores desde que los niños son chiquitos: el respeto, el esfuerzo, la justicia, la bondad, el amor, la responsabilidad, la empatía. Los valores son los superpoderes de niños y adolescentes”, cuenta.

“A un adolescente exigente le diría que tiene que crear un espacio para poder comunicar lo que siente; lo bueno y lo malo, sus decisiones, sus dudas”

A Carmen Rodríguez le costó encontrar su vocación. “¿Tú has pensado alguna vez que yo perdía el tiempo?”, le pregunta a Patricia, que le contesta desde la doble perspectiva de madre y psicóloga: “Yo he pensado que estabas explorando diferentes caminos hasta que poco a poco has ido encontrando el tuyo. Y creo que ahí los padres no podemos influiros en qué decisiones tenéis que tomar, porque tú tienes que vivir tu vida, no la vida que un padre o una madre elige para ti”. Una charla que sirve de inspiración para afrontar retos e inquietudes.

Pensemos la educación del futuro ‘Pensemos el mañana’, un proyecto de Fundación Unicaja, busca fomentar el conocimiento, los valores de la educación, un aprendizaje sostenible y responsable y dar respuestas a los grandes desafíos de la educación del futuro. El proyecto pivota sobre seis ejes: 1 Aprendizaje y sentido vital 2 Bienestar y salud mental 3 Futuro y empleabilidad 4 Sostenibilidad y sentido colectivo 5 Tecnología y ética 6 Carácter y ciudadanía ¿Qué está ocurriendo en estos tiempos de cambios profundos y transversales? ¿Cuáles son los grandes retos para afrontar la transformación que viene? ¿Qué educación necesitamos? Diferentes personalidades de todos los ámbitos nos ayudarán a responder a estas y otras preguntas destinadas a impulsar cambios, dinamizar ideas y apoyar propuestas con impacto pedagógico y social. ‘Pensemos el mañana’ es un proyecto inspirador para las futuras generaciones llamadas a conquistar nuevas cotas del saber en un mundo complejo y cambiante.

World.title: Si decido comprar una vivienda anunciada por una agencia, ¿estoy obligado a pagar una comisión?
World.content:
Pregunta. ¿En qué supuestos existe obligación de pagar comisión por parte del comprador a la agencia inmobiliaria cuando quien contrata sus servicios es el vendedor? J. Ibáñez

Respuesta. En relación con la obligación de abonar los honorarios de la agencia inmobiliaria por parte del comprador, debe partirse del principio de libertad de pacto entre las partes. En las operaciones de compraventa inmobiliaria no existe una norma que imponga de forma general que la comisión de la agencia deba ser asumida necesariamente por el vendedor o por el comprador, ni de forma exclusiva por uno de ellos, por lo que la dependerá de los acuerdos alcanzados entre las partes.

La parte compradora estará obligada al pago de dichos honorarios cuando haya aceptado de forma clara y expresa asumir ese coste. En la práctica, es habitual que las agencias inmobiliarias incluyan esta cláusula en el parte de visitas, documento que se suele entregar al potencial comprador en la primera visita al inmueble y en el que, además de dejar constancia de que ha conocido la vivienda a través de la agencia, se puede incorporar una cláusula relativa al pago de los honorarios profesionales.

Si dicho parte de visitas contiene una cláusula clara sobre la obligación del comprador de abonar la comisión inmobiliaria, y esta ha sido firmada por la parte compradora, podrá entenderse que existe aceptación contractual suficiente para reclamar el pago de la comisión, siempre que la inmobiliaria haya intervenido efectivamente en la operación y la compraventa llegue finalmente a formalizarse.

Por lo tanto, en el caso que se expone habrá que revisar el documento firmado por el comprador, ya sea el parte de visitas, el documento de entrega de señal o el contrato de arras que habitualmente se suscribe antes de la compraventa. Si en cualquiera de dichos documentos consta expresamente la aceptación del pago de honorarios a favor de la inmobiliaria, sí podrá exigirse el abono de la comisión a la parte compradora. La ley únicamente establece la obligación de pago de los gastos de gestión inmobiliaria al propietario en los supuestos de arrendamiento de vivienda habitual, pero no en las operaciones de compraventa.

Si tiene dudas, sugerencias o simplemente quiere contarnos su caso, puede enviarnos un email a vivienda@elpais.es .

World.title: Highly contagious impetigo infection on the rise among children
World.content:
The highly contagious skin infection impetigo is on the rise on among Dutch children, with 2026 seeing more cases than in previous years.

For every 100,000 children, there have been a reported 350 to 400 children with the infection in the past three weeks compared to below 300 cases in previous years, according to research institute Nivel and based on data from GPs.

The infection, known as krentenbaard (currant beard) in Dutch, is mostly seen around the nose and mouth of young children, who develop red spots, bumps and blisters with a puss-like fluid that forms a crust when scratched.

The national public health institute RIVM advises parents to prevent their children from scratching the itchy and burning blisters and to have them routinely wash their hands with soap and water.

Impetigo, which is more common in the warm summer months, is caused by bacteria but can be treated with an antibiotic ointment. But because many people don’t seek medical help for its mild symptoms that often heal on their own, it’s difficult to assess how often it occurs.

According to Nivel, this year’s peaks coincide with the higher temperatures reported by the national weather institute KNMI.

World.title: Summery weather until Sunday, up to 29° in the southeast
World.content:
The Netherlands is in for a run of summery weather, with temperatures climbing towards the weekend before showers arrive on Sunday, weather service Weeronline said.

Thursday will bring clouds with the odd light shower, though most places will stay dry, and the clouds should break up in the afternoon to give some sunshine. Maximum temperatures will be between 18° and 24°.

Saturday will be the warmest day, staying dry for much of the time with sunny spells. A moderate west to northwesterly wind will keep the coast cooler, at 20° to 24°, while inland reaches 25° to 28° and the southeast up to 29°. There is a chance of a shower on the northern coast in the afternoon and evening.

Showers are expected more widely on Sunday, mainly in the afternoon, with temperatures back to between 20° and 24°. Next week brings a mix of showers and dry, sunny spells, with Monday between 19° and 24°.

World.title: Ali B cancels talk amid fears of media spectacle
World.content:
Rapper and convicted rapist Ali B has pulled out of a business event where he was supposed to be speaking on Thursday in Vinkeveen. The Missing Pieces entrepreneurial event has also been postponed until a later date.

“Due to the exceptionally large number of media applications for the Missing Pieces event, the evening is in danger of becoming a media spectacle. That is at odds with what this meeting is meant for,” reads a joint statement by the rapper and Missing Pieces on the latter’s website. “Therefore, we [Missing Pieces and Ali] have jointly decided to move the event.”

Ali B, or Ali Bouali, was booked, said the website, to speak about “why most entrepreneurs do not break through, despite their talent”.

But following Ali B’s three-year sentence for two rapes in May, including the 2014 rape of Dutch singer Ellen ten Damme, the resulting media interest made the event untenable, Missing Pieces said.

“The whole point was for the evening to be about entrepreneurship, without his personal situation being up for discussion,” reads the joint statement. “Due to the scale of the media attention, it is not feasible at this time.”

The activist group Dolle Mina had also announced a protest at The Harbour Club in Vinkeveen, where the event was scheduled to take place.

The 44-year-old rapper, who has denied all the charges, has appealed to the Supreme Court against the verdict – the highest form of appeal. Ali B has remained free for the years it’s taken his case to wend its way through the courts and will remain so while his appeal is ongoing.

Ticket holders will be able to attend the rescheduled event or get their money back.

World.title: Erasmus Bridge reopens after Rotterdam tram collision
World.content:
The Erasmus Bridge in Rotterdam reopened to all traffic on Wednesday evening after the two badly damaged trams which collided on it that morning were lifted clear of the tracks, broadcaster NOS reported. Trams are running over the bridge again.

Fifteen people were injured, one of them seriously, when a moving tram ran into the back of a stationary one waiting for the bridge to close, regional broadcaster Rijnmond reported.

The salvage operation took most of the day, with the trams having to be cut apart, RET director Linda Boot told the broadcaster.

Three investigations are now under way. Police are examining the crash, including with a drone team, transport company RET is carrying out its own inquiry, and the Dutch Safety Board has begun a preliminary investigation to decide whether to open a full one.

RET said initial checks showed the driver of the rear tram had not been under the influence of alcohol or drugs. He was among those taken to hospital. Boot said it was too early to speculate about the cause.

Rotterdam mayor Carola Schouten visited the scene and called it “a terrible accident”. No further information has been released about the condition of those hurt.

World.title: Sixteen councils still without a coalition, four months on
World.content:
Sixteen Dutch councils still have not formed a government coalition 126 days after the local elections on March 18 – the highest number ever recorded, according to local government news site Binnenlands Bestuur.

The summer recess will add another 30 days, meaning coalition talks in those councils will have run for more than 150 days. The average formation now stands at 87 days, up from 83 in 2022, and may rise to 90. By comparison, only four councils were still negotiating after the summer in 2022, and in 2018 just one was.

Binnenlands Bestuur points to three reasons. Coalition-building has become more formal, with councils now holding public debates on the election result and appointing scouts and informateurs, where the process was once settled by senior figures behind closed doors.

Councils have also become more fragmented, so a majority often requires four parties or more. And the shift towards right-wing and far-right parties has made it harder to assemble a stable majority, the site said, while vetting the background of candidates for alderman takes longer than it used to.

The outgoing executive stays in place until a new one is appointed, so no council is left without an administration. But caretaker administrations tend to avoid major or politically contested decisions, so new policy largely waits.

Leiden is the only large city still without a coalition, after talks collapsed last month over a lack of trust between PRO and D66. Of the 324 councils that have completed the process, 182 took longer than in 2022, while 115 were quicker – among them The Hague, which did not have a coalition until late September last time. The record is held by Vlieland, which needed 229 days in 2022.

World.title: Half a million Dutch households in energy poverty
World.content:
Around 503,000 Dutch households were living in energy poverty last year, or 6% of the total – unchanged from 2024, according to figures from statistics office CBS and research institute TNO published on Thursday.

The share had dropped to under 4% in 2023 while government compensation for high energy bills was in place, then jumped back once the support ended. It remains below the 2019 level of nearly 10%.

Researchers looked for the first time at how far people fall short, and found households on low incomes with high energy bills were on average €624 a year short of escaping energy poverty, up from €577 in 2024. Lifting them all out would have cost around €256 million.

Average monthly energy costs rose from €167 to €181 across all households, and from €177 to €188 for those in energy poverty, who now spend 11.5% of their income on energy – more than twice the national average.

The number of low-income households facing high energy bills rose from 385,000 to 410,000, while the number living in poorly insulated homes continued to fall.

Energy poverty is most common in the big cities, north-east Groningen and south Limburg. The deepest shortfalls are in homes with very poor energy efficiency (€1,295 a year) and among owner-occupiers (€967).

World.title: Ivory and a rhino skull among 5,800 items handed to RVO
World.content:
Some 5,800 prohibited objects including elephant ivory have been anonymously handed in to the Netherlands Enterprise Agency (RVO) over the past year, a more than fivefold increase on the previous year.

“Never before has so much been handed in,” says The Hague-based RVO, including “moving boxes with a thousand [pieces of] ivory jewellery, a rhino skull with a gunshot wound, crocodile leather bags, musical instruments and an elephant’s leg.”

The objects also included taxidermy animals such as a long-eared owl, peregrine falcon and turtles. Pictures on broadcaster NOS show ivory binoculars and crocodile leather bags.

The sale and trade of elephant ivory are strictly regulated under European CITES laws (Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species), with permits required for the possession and trade of protected plants or animals.

Most of the items, which can be handed in at a drop-off bin in The Hague or even by post, are destroyed to prevent them from (re)entering the illegal trade. The RVO says it uses a small number of the items for research and education.

World.title: Thuisbezorgd hides costs and fakes discounts: consumer group
World.content:
The food delivery platform Thuisbezorgd.nl hides compulsory charges and advertises fake discounts, the Dutch consumer association Consumentenbond said on Tuesday, calling on the company to stop and to compensate affected customers.

Mandatory costs should be clearly shown before a customer starts ordering, the association said, but Thuisbezorgd’s app and website do not reveal compulsory “service” charges – for items such as bags, plastic packaging and sauce – until part-way through or at the end of an order, adding an average of €2 to €4 to the bill.

The association also said the company broke rules on special offers. Under Authority for Consumers and Markets (ACM) rules, a struck-through sale price must be the lowest the seller charged in the previous 30 days. In one case, the association found Indian snacks that had previously cost €3.75 being offered “on sale” from €7.50 to €6.

“We have been in talks with Thuisbezorgd since March, but the platform is still confronting customers with hidden costs and fake discounts,” said Consumentenbond director Sandra Molenaar, noting the company has more than six million users in the Netherlands.

Because the practice has probably been going on for years, the association estimates the hidden costs run into the hundreds of millions of euros in total. A Thuisbezorgd spokesperson said the company did not recognise the association’s accusations.

The Consumentenbond said it had also found hidden costs at Uber Eats, which made changes in June, though no fake discounts. The findings are part of a wider campaign against hidden charges and misleading offers that also named Bol and Amazon last week.

The association can press companies to change but cannot impose penalties; that is a matter for the ACM, which has fined firms including Leen Bakker, G-Star and Jysk in the past.

World.title: President to swear in new judge to Poland’s disputed constitutional court
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! President Karol Nawrocki has agreed to swear in a new judge to the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), ending weeks of doubt as to whether the opposition-aligned president would accept the judge appointed by the government’s parliamentary majority. Although Sławomir Patyra will now be accepted onto the court, four other judges appointed by parliament earlier this year continue to be excluded after Nawrocki refused to receive their oaths and the TK’s chief justice, also aligned with the opposition, blocked them from taking office. W najbliższy wtorek 28 lipca Prezydent Karol Nawrocki działając na postawie art. 4 ust. 1 ustawy o statusie sędziów Trybunału Konstytucyjnego, przyjmie ślubowanie od prof. Sławomira Patyry i tego samego dnia wręczy powołania czterem nowym sędziom Sądu Najwyższego. W przyszłym… — Zbigniew Bogucki🇵🇱 (@BoguckiZbigniew) July 22, 2026 Under Polish law, when a vacancy emerges among the 15 positions on the TK – for example when a judge’s nine-year term expires – the lower house of parliament, the Sejm, chooses who should fill it. However, to take office, the judge must swear an oath before the president. In April, after the Sejm had chosen six candidates to fill vacancies on the court, Nawrocki took the unprecedented step of inviting only two of them to be sworn in. He argued there were doubts over the legality of how all six had been chosen, but decided to accept two to ensure the TK had the necessary quorum to function. Those two have been able to take up their seats on the court, but the other four remain in limbo. Although they arranged their own private swearing-in ceremony without the presence of Nawrocki, the TK’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, has refused to accept them. In May, the European Court of Human Rights ordered that the quartet be allowed to take up their positions. But the TK – where judges appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government retain a majority – issued its own ruling endorsing Nawrocki’s right not to swear in the new judges. On 11 June, the Sejm then chose another judge, Patyra, to fill a newly opened vacancy on the court. In his case, the legal doubts Nawrocki had expressed regarding the previous appointments, which in some instances were made more than a year after the vacancies had arisen, did not seem to apply. Yet for weeks the president refused to confirm whether he would swear him in. That prompted Patyra to write to Nawrocki in early July and then again this week, asking the president to indicate a date on which he could take his oath. Patyra himself has also made clear on which side of the dispute he stands. In an interview with news website Onet in May, he accused Nawrocki and Święczkowski of “blatantly unlawful actions” in deciding which TK judges can and cannot take office and suggested that the police should intervene. Sędzia TK prof. Patyra po raz kolejny zaapelował do Prezydenta o wyznaczenie mu terminu na złożenie przysięgi. Ignorowanie sędziego TK przez Prezydenta jest kolejnym przykładem psucia państwa. To pokazuje, jak bardzo siły anty-demokratyczne boją się odbudowy niezależnego TK.… — Dariusz Mazur (@_Dariusz_Mazur) July 21, 2026 Finally, on Wednesday this week, Nawrocki’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, announced that Nawrocki had invited Patyra to the presidential palace on Tuesday next week to take his oath. Speaking to Polsat News, Bogucki said that, in the case of Patyra, initially “there were some doubts, but the president dispelled them”, without specifying what they were. In the end, they concluded that “we had a fundamentally clean situation here” and Patyra was chosen “in accordance with all procedures”, unlike the six new judges chosen by the Sejm in March to fill longstanding vacancies. “It was not President Nawrocki or the current opposition who destroyed and are destroying the tribunal; it is the government that is doing it,” he added. The European Court of Human Rights has ordered Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) to accept four judges whom opposition-aligned President Nawrocki refused to swear in. The decision was welcomed by the government but rejected by the TK itself https://t.co/9NxInPdYk9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 6, 2026 The TK has been at the heart of the rule-of-law crisis that has developed in Poland over the last decade. In 2015, former PiS-aligned President Andrzej Duda refused to swear in three judges legally chosen by the Sejm. Shortly afterwards, PiS won parliamentary elections and nominated three replacements for those judges, who were sworn in by Duda. Those three judges and their successors have been deemed illegitimate in a succession of rulings by Polish and European courts. Due to their continued presence on the court, the current government, which replaced PiS in 2023, rejects the TK’s legitimacy and refuses to recognise its rulings. Under both Święczkowski, a former member of the PiS government, and his predecessor Julia Przyłębska, a close personal associate of PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński, the TK has been widely seen as issuing rulings aligned with the political interests of PiS. While Poland already hosts various allied forces, the presence of German troops is particularly symbolic given the two countries’ difficult history. “United, we will prevail,” wrote the General Staff of the Polish Armed Forces (SGWP), announcing the deployment. “This is what allied cooperation looks like in practice, which translates into greater military readiness and strengthens NATO’s defensive potential.” Polscy i niemieccy żołnierze razem wzmacniają granicę z Rosją. Takie rzeczy możliwe tylko za Tuska ☺️ pic.twitter.com/oNBME2gBsv — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 22, 2026 Last December, the Polish and German defence ministries revealed that a “mid-double-digit number” of German troops would be deployed from mid-2026 until the end of 2027 to support implementation of Poland’s East Shield operation, which seeks to bolster defences along the borders with Belarus and Russia. They said that the German personnel would mainly engage in engineering work, such as digging trenches, laying barbed wire and constructing anti-tank barriers. Today, Poland’s SGWP confirmed that “several dozen” German troops, including “highly specialised engineering forces” along with their equipment, had since June been temporarily deployed to “support the Polish armed forces in expanding defence infrastructure on NATO’s northeastern flank”. It emphasised that the East Shield project is “purely defensive in nature” and comes in “response to threats stemming from, among others, Russian aggression against Ukraine”. While the armed forces did not reveal the location of the deployment, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk indicated in a social media post that it was on the Russian border. Poland has a 210-km frontier with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. German public broadcaster Deutsche Welle reports that the activities of the German sappers are focused in particular on improving defences around the so-called Suwałki Gap, a strategically important stretch of land around the Polish-Lithuanian border between Belarus and Kaliningrad. “Together, we are ensuring Europe’s security,” said Lieutenant General Alexander Sollfrank, the Bundeswehr’s operational commander, announcing the deployment today. “Through our engagement in Poland, we are strengthening NATO’s defence capabilities and underscoring the alliance’s unwavering commitment to ensuring peace through unity and credible deterrence.” Poland and Germany have signed a bilateral security agreement that will see the two neighbours and NATO allies increase cooperation in areas such as military mobility, logistics infrastructure, maritime security in the Baltic Sea, and cybersecurity https://t.co/6BPX2WxvxH — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 17, 2026 SGWP, which shared footage of Polish and German forces installing anti-tank barriers, said the work aims to “hinder and delay an aggressor’s actions in the event of a threat”, thereby “increasing the time for a response from the Polish armed forces and the entire [NATO] alliance”. It also seeks to “create conditions for the efficient reception, deployment and use of NATO forces on Polish territory”. SGWP welcomed “the involvement of the German contingent as a practical expression of allied solidarity and the result of consistently developing military cooperation between Poland and Germany”. It also noted that the cooperation would help the two sides improve their ability to operate jointly, including “developing the competencies necessary for conducting a joint defence operation”. However, it emphasised that the current deployment is focused on training and engineering, with no combat component, and that the German troops are unarmed. SGWP also emphasised that the East Shield operation remains entirely a Polish national programme. The leaders of eight countries on the EU's eastern flank have met in the first summit of its kind to discuss closer security cooperation. The agreement is a sign that the two countries now stand “shoulder to shoulder, as equals”, declared German defence minister Boris Pistorius. Poland is also currently seeking a new permanent US military base on its territory, after President Donald Trump recently pledged to boost American troop numbers. Poland’s climate and environment ministry has inaugurated the first of 11 planned “community forests” around large cities, with the aim of giving residents a place for recreation and contact with nature while also helping to fulfil the government’s pledge to reduce logging. Plans for the forests were announced in 2024, and the first has now been established around Wrocław, Poland’s third-largest city. Ten other major urban centres, including Warsaw, Kraków, Poznań and Łódź, are set to follow. Dotrzymujemy słowa. Powołaliśmy pierwsze lasy społeczne w Polsce, to lasy ochronne wokół Wrocławia. Kolejne miasta przed nami. @MKiS_GOV_PL pic.twitter.com/RxhsMZShj9 — Paulina Hennig-Kloska (@hennigkloska) July 21, 2026 “This is a historic moment and the beginning of a new approach to forest protection – with residents in mind first and foremost,” said climate and environment minister Paulina Hennig-Kloska at an inauguration ceremony outside Wrocław on Sunday. “Community forests are places where residents can relax, play sports and simply spend time close to nature,” she added. “At the same time, they are crucial to our security and quality of life: they retain water, regulate the climate, purify the air and protect the soil.” An area covering 13,000 hectares (32,124 acres) has been designated as a community forest around Wrocław. Forest management there will now be aimed at “maximising the forest’s social functions”, says the ministry, while timber harvesting is also restricted. The area will be divided into three zones, including “natural forests”, where nature will be left to take its course, and “near-natural forests” with minimal intervention. However, the largest zone, amounting to over 8,000 hectares, will be “social forests”, which the state forestry agency says “will be managed in a way that ensures the comfort of those who use the forest and its benefits related to wellbeing, physical exercise and recreation”. Hennig-Kloska noted that, in the latter area, educational trails as well as hiking and cycling paths would be established. However, given that such facilities already exist in many forests, it remains unclear how the new community forests will differ. The ministry is now conducting consultations and analysis on establishing community forests around ten other designated urban centres: Bielsko-Biała, Tricity (Gdańsk-Gdynia-Sopot), Katowice, Kielce, Kraków, Łódź, Poznań, Szczecin, Toruń-Bydgoszcz and Warsaw. On Sunday, Hennig-Kloska said that the “next in line” to have their community forests established are Kielce and Bielsko-Biała, reported the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Shortly after coming to power in December 2023, the current government announced that it would halt planned logging in some forests. The former Law and Justice (PiS) administration had faced criticism for overseeing an increase in logging, especially in Białowieża Forest. The current government also launched plans to create Poland’s first new national parks in over two decades. However, PiS-aligned President Karol Nawrocki last year vetoed that move, arguing that it would “block the economic development of the region” and threaten Poland’s security. Poland has joined a European Union project developing a secure satellite internet service that would provide an alternative to networks such as Elon Musk’s Starlink. Warsaw has committed €656 million (2.8 billion zloty) to the IRIS² programme, with the money coming from Poland’s EU post-pandemic recovery funds. In return for joining the project, Poland will gain access to the secure satellite communications network for government institutions, the armed forces and emergency services, while the growing Polish space industry will be eligible to compete for contracts linked to the development of the constellation Today Poland🇵🇱joins the EU🇪🇺space programme #IRIS² w/additional €656 mln. 🇵🇱 is on a remarkable space journey to build a strong space economy & secure connectivity for the defence of Poland, the Eastern Flank & 🇪🇺. IRIS² brings greater unity & strength for the entire Europe. pic.twitter.com/TwS59vpXtm — Andrius Kubilius (@KubiliusA) July 21, 2026 “This is a big day for Poland, the eastern flank and the entire European Union,” declared the EU’s defence and space commissioner, Andrius Kubilius, at a signing ceremony in Warsaw on Tuesday. “By investing in space, Poland is investing in its security, its economy and its future.” Speaking alongside him, Poland’s interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, said that IRIS² would help “ensure our security and strategic independence” while “demonstrating that Poland aims to be a leader in the European space industry and remain at the centre of EU security efforts”. “No single country is able to build such a [satellite] constellation so efficiently, which is why we are joining this major project – to be part of it and one of its managers,” he added. The IRIS² programme aims to deploy a constellation of nearly 300 satellites in low and medium Earth orbit, providing encrypted, interference-resistant communications for governments, defence agencies, emergency services and selected commercial users across the EU. First announced in 2022, the project is part of the EU’s efforts to reduce dependence on non-European satellite operators amid growing concerns over cybersecurity, hybrid threats and the resilience of critical infrastructure following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. “It is super important for Europe to have a sovereign capacity, and Starlink will never do that,” said Eva Berneke, CEO of Eutelsat, one of the companies involved in the project, quoted by Politico Europe. The project is expected to cost €10.6 billion, including €6.5 billion in public funding and around €4 billion from private investors. IRIS² is expected to become operational in 2030. 🇪🇺 The IRIS program is Europe's replacement for Starlink. The constellation will consist of over 300 satellites to serve Europe alone. Security and sovereignty! Like Galileo, it could surpass its US counterpart. Fewer satellites, smarter coverage. Eventually more could be added pic.twitter.com/Uswmuotw7F — Mariska den Eelden 🇪🇺🇳🇱 (@eeldenden) February 22, 2025 As part of its contribution to IRIS², Poland will finance six large satellites in medium Earth orbit (MEO) and six smaller satellites in low Earth orbit (LEO). It will also build a ground gateway station in Warsaw to connect the satellites with GovNet, the country’s secure government fibre-optic communications network. Earlier this year, the Polish government approved the use of money from its share of the EU’s post-pandemic reconstruction fund to cover its contribution to IRIS². Sięgamy gwiazd!! Polska przystępuje do europejskiego programu budowy bezpiecznej łączności satelitarnej 🛰️📡! W ten sposób zaspokoimy wszystkie potrzeby łączności służb i administracji państwowej. IRIS² zapewni nam bezpieczeństwo i niezależność. Dziękuję @KubiliusA za współpracę pic.twitter.com/c8u2QH0Wyn — Marcin Kierwiński (@MKierwinski) July 21, 2026 Once the system is up and running, Poland’s police, border guards and other emergency services would be able to use the network during natural disasters, power outages and other emergencies when terrestrial communications infrastructure is unavailable. The system would also make it possible to provide temporary connectivity for civilians through emergency hotspots, says Poland’s interior ministry. Polish companies will now also be able to compete for contracts covering satellite manufacturing, telecommunications equipment, software and ground infrastructure, expanding the country’s role in Europe’s space industry. “It is estimated that each zloty invested in the project will generate a five-zloty return through new jobs, innovation and the development of domestic technologies,” the ministry said in a statement. World.title: Archaeologists uncover synagogue in Warsaw Jewish cemetery destroyed by Germans in WWII
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Archaeological work at a Jewish cemetery in Warsaw has uncovered the foundations of and many objects from a former synagogue and funeral home that was destroyed by the Nazi-German occupiers in 1943. The finds were made at the cemetery on Okopowa Street, which, at around 33.5 hectares in size and with some 250,000 people buried there, is the second largest in Poland, after the Łódź Jewish cemetery, and one of the biggest anywhere in the world. Following the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising of 1943, the Germans liquidated the ghetto, sending most of its remaining inhabitants to the gas chambers and destroying the buildings that remained there, including the synagogue and burial houses. In June this year, archaeological work began at the site of the former synagogue, commissioned by Warsaw’s Jewish community, which owns and manages the cemetery. The two-storey building, designed by architect Adolf Schimmelpfennig, a Pole of Dutch Lutheran descent, was constructed in 1877 and existed until 15 May 1943, when it was destroyed with explosives. The archaeological work aims to “uncover, document and preserve the remains of this historic complex, maintaining the memory of this place and passing it on to future generations”, says the office of the conservator of monuments for Masovia, the province in which Warsaw is located and which is supervising the work. Archaeologists have so far discovered numerous items that offer “silent testament to the daily life of the community that was connected to this site for decades”, says the conservator. They include ceramic floor and wall tiles, glass bottles and tiles from stoves used at the funeral home. “Every discovered brick, fragment of flooring or piece of furniture helps reconstruct the history of one of the most important buildings in historic Warsaw,” adds the conservator. Among the finds is an item that relates to a well-known and tragic story from the war, a door plaque from the office of the then-director of the cemetery, Abram Pozner. Pozner brought members of his extended family to the funeral home at the start of the war, where they were initially able to remain in relative safety, away from the horrors of the ghetto that the occupiers forced Jews to live in. As life became ever more brutal and dangerous for Jews, Pozner created an underground hideout within the cemetery. The Germans eventually found the bunker and killed most of those hiding there. However, two of them managed to survive imprisonment in German labour camps, one of whom, Avraham Carmi, remains alive today and lives in Israel. The current archaeological work is expected to be completed by the end of July, after which the foundations will be re-covered with earth. Warsaw’s Jewish community then hopes to restore the previous building, adapted to current conditions and needs, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. “The goal is to determine whether the funeral home could be rebuilt on these remains, or whether it would make more sense to display them as a monument within a newly constructed building, and also whether erecting a building on this site is even realistic,” cemetery director Witold Wrzosiński told the newspaper. Archaeologist Szymon Lenarczyk, who has led the work at the site, says he has proposed that the structure of a future building should feature an underground room where discovered artefacts can be displayed. Before World War Two, Warsaw was home to around 350,000 Jews, a third of its population and more than any city in the world other than New York. However, the vast majority were killed in the Holocaust, meaning that only a small Jewish community remains today.
