World.title: Live: Quaynor booed by Crows fans despite pleas in crunch Pies clash
World.content:
Quaynor was booed by sections of the Adelaide Oval crowd from his very first touch tonight. To me, it seemed like those boos were getting louder as the quarter progressed.

Quaynor has become a target of Adelaide fans since he was on the receiving end of a homophobic slur from Crows star Izak Rankine. Rankine was suspended and missed Adelaide's ill-fated finals campaign.

The booing also occurred in the qualifying final between these teams last year, prompting Adelaide to release a statement denouncing the abuse as players from both teams also criticised it.

Meanwhile the first openly gay AFL footballer, Leigh Ryswyk, also urged fans to show respect during tonight's match.

Quaynor, for what it's worth, had a team-high 10 disposals in the quarter. The booers are going to wind up with a mighty sore throat at this rate, which certainly is a damn shame.

World.title: Taiwanese woman sentenced for attempted murder of Australian exchange student
World.content:
A Taiwanese woman has been sentenced to 11 years in prison for the attempted murder of Brisbane exchange student Alex Shorey, Taiwan state media has reported.

The woman, identified as Yang Jinping, befriended the then-23-year-old Australian while he was studying a Chinese literature program in Taiwan in early 2023, with the two beginning an on-again, off-again relationship.

Prosecutors alleged Yang began to poison Mr Shorey with the rat poison superwarfarin after he expressed a desire to cut his time in Taiwan short.

She continued to mix the rat poison into food and drink for Mr Shorey, including while he was in hospital.

Mr Shorey was treated in a Taipei hospital before being medically repatriated. (Supplied: Shorey Family)

Mr Shorey was admitted to hospital multiple times in 2023 before being medically evacuated to Australia.

During the case, Mr Shorey's mother told the court she had found an empty bottle of rat poison in her son's rental apartment in Taiwan.

Yang was charged with Mr Shorey's attempted murder in late 2024.

Taiwanese media has reported Jinping was convicted of attempted murder in the Taipei District Court yesterday.

She has been sentenced to 11 years and two months in prison, local media reported.

University of Queensland student Mr Shorey had been in Taipei on an exchange at Tamkang University. (ABC News: Mitch Woolnough)

Mr Shorey's family crowd-sourced more than $200,000 to have him medically evacuated back to Australia.

His father, Stephen Shorey, previously told the ABC his son had recovered from the poisoning.

He said at the time their family was grateful to everyone who helped bring Alex home in 2023, as the retrieval "saved his life".

"We were blessed," he said.

World.title: One of WA's longest bridges to be built after Indigenous dispute resolved
World.content:
One of Western Australia's longest bridges will be built to fix a road to nowhere in Perth's east — resolving a four-year-long deadlock over fears the bridge would destroy an ancient rock shelter and billabong.

The state government began work on the Great Eastern Highway Bypass Interchanges project in 2021 to create a "free-flowing gateway" into Perth's Hills.

Building the Lloyd Street Bridge across the Helena River from Midland to Hazelmere was just one part of the almost $400 million project.

Four-lane roads on either side of the river were built, but construction came to a halt in 2022 when traditional owners raised concerns about an ancient rock shelter and billabong in its path.

The half-built road is severed by the Helena River, where cultural sites of significance are located. (Supplied: Nearmap)

"We're not against development but we are against destruction of our traditional sites and the river is our cultural heritage site," the group's spokesman Greg Ugle said at the time.

" My connection is here, it was a playground for us, for Noongar kids. "

Since then, the surrounding suburbs have surged with traffic, and the unfinished cul-de-sacs became dumping grounds for rubbish and a racetrack for hoons.

The Lloyd St extension has become a dumping ground for rubbish and is littered with tyre marks. (Supplied: Nearmap)

New bridge settled

The government has announced it has struck an agreement with traditional owners on a new design, with construction pegged to begin by the end of the year.

Transport Minister Rita Saffioti said it would avoid the culturally significant sites with support piers positioned away from the sensitive areas.

The ancient rock shelter near Helena River. (ABC News: Grace Burmas)

"The state could have referred [the traditional owner's application] to the Federal Government for formal determination and continued to build the previous design, against the wishes of the Traditional Owners and other community representatives," she said.

"Instead, our government, Main Roads, and the City of Swan listened, worked with the Traditional Owners to get a better understanding of their concerns and set out to work towards a design the whole community could be proud of."

Ms Saffioti said the four-lane bridge will be 180 metres long — one of the longest multi-span bridges in the state.

The Lloyd Street roundabout is covered with tyre marks from drivers doing burnouts. (ABC News: Nicolas Perpitch)

A state government spokesperson has confirmed the Lloyd Street Bridge is part of a package of works including upgrades to the Great Eastern Highway Bypass and Abernethy Road intersection, with a total current budget of $180 million.

World.title: Bystanders hailed as 'heroes' after stopping attempted murder on CCTV
World.content:
WARNING: This story contains vision and details that may distress some readers.

A man who "doggedly" tried to kill a woman outside a Perth apartment complex in a horrific attack captured on CCTV has been sentenced to 16 years in prison.

Mihael Vrhovsek, 29, was convicted of attempted murder for the attack in Rivervale in 2024.

The Supreme Court jury was shown a graphic video of Vrhovsek confronting the woman, which the ABC has published excerpts of.

Loading...

The 29-year-old grabbed the woman by the throat, lifted her off her feet and carried her, before dropping her limp body to the ground.

A man then intervenes, confronting Vrhovsek, which allowed the woman who was walking her dogs an opportunity to drag the victim away.

She was able to walk on her own, but Vrhovsek — having broken free of the man who had confronted him — ran after her and again began to choke her.

The man who had intervened returned, punching and kicking Vrhovsek in a bid to get him to let go, before the woman walking her dogs was again able to drag the victim away.

Mihael Vrhovsek was seen on CCTV before the attack. (Supplied: Supreme Court of Western Australia)

The court also released the victim's Triple Zero phone call earlier, where she could be heard screaming and repeatedly shouting "get away from me" during the attack.

The call lasted for more than eight minutes, and when asked by the operator if the Vrhovsek had weapons, the victim replied: "Does he need to have weapons to be f***ing threatening?"

While the operator was asking her questions, she said: "He's here … send the goddamn police right now!"

'Abusive, menacing and sinister'

In court today, Justice Alain Musikanth said Vrhovsek had used extreme violence, including continuing to strangle the woman once she had lost consciousness.

"Your actions involved deliberate and controlled choices … you were doggedly determined to kill her," he said.

A man intervened to stop the attack. (Supplied: Supreme Court of Western Australia)

Justice Musikanth praised the courage of the bystanders who were "instrumental" in saving the woman's life, describing them as "heroes".

In the days leading up to the attack, Vrhovsek called or texted her more than 230 times using multiple mobile phones, many of which Justice Musikanth said were "abusive, menacing, and sinister".

"I accept she was so affected by the avalanche of abusive communications from you she reported your action to police, saying she was scared you were going to kill her," he said.

CCTV video shows man's 'inexcusable' attack on woman The WA Supreme Court releases disturbing CCTV footage of a man attacking a woman on a Perth street, after a trial in which he was found guilty of her attempted murder.

The defence said Vrhovsek had a "troubled upbringing", and struggled against his "demons", which "included self-medication".

They said his conduct was serious but aberrant, arguing he is not likely to reoffend, and that he had expressed "visceral" remorse when the CCTV footage of the incident was shown to the court.

But Justice Musikanth said he was unable to find Vrhovsek had any true empathy, or remorse for his victim.

He will become eligible for parole in 2038.

World.title: Court hears complainant's evidence challenged in police officer's rape trial
World.content:
The defence team of a former NSW Police officer, accused of raping a teenage girl almost 28 years ago, has told the court the complainant was relying on phone calls made years later to refresh her memory.

David Robert Blackbourne was serving as a police officer when he allegedly raped the 17-year-old in a town near the NSW-Victoria border in October 1998.

He has been charged with two counts of assault with an act of indecency, two counts of sexual intercourse without consent, and one count of holder of public office misconduct.

Mr Blackbourne was arrested in 2023 and has pleaded not guilty to all charges.

His trial began this week at Sydney's Downing Centre District Court, and today his defence team continued to cross-examine the complainant.

The court has heard that on the morning of October 17, 1998, the girl went to a police station where Mr Blackbourne gave her a police hat to be worn at a year 12 muck-up day.

Defence barrister Matthew Johnston SC asked the complainant whether she walked 4.5 kilometres from her home to the police station on the morning of the alleged rape.

"You gave evidence you were picking up a hat; what were the arrangements?" said Mr Johnston.

"I cannot recall the arrangements," the complainant said.

She later went on to say that despite not remembering the arrangements or the exact date, she would not have walked to the police station if it was not pre-arranged.

The complainant told the court earlier this week that in October 1998, she attended a police station, where David Blackbourne gave her a police hat. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

Earlier this week the complainant told the court that shortly after she arrived at the station, Mr Blackbourne took her behind the front counter and sexually assaulted her.

She said he then took her to another room and sexually assaulted her again.

Today Mr Johnston asked the woman whether she said anything when her pants were allegedly pulled down by Mr Blackbourne.

"No," she replied.

"Did you say anything when he pulled his pants down?" Mr Johnston asked.

"No," she said.

Mr Johnston later suggested she was not kissed without consent.

"It definitely happened," she replied.

"I want to suggest to you that the man you believed to be Dave did not have sexual intercourse with you," Mr Johnston said.

"It definitely happened," she said.

Covertly recorded call

Mr Blackbourne's defence team questioned the reliability of the complainant's evidence and whether it was influenced by phone calls made years after the alleged rape.

During a cross-examination of the complainant yesterday, Mr Johnston asked whether the woman was relying on phone calls with her former boss in 2020 to piece together what happened.

She agreed that she was.

David Blackbourne's defence team has questioned the reliability of the complainant's evidence and whether it was influenced by phone calls. (ABC News: Adriane Reardon)

"Do you think you adopted these memories … because you want them to be true?" Mr Johnston said.

"That is not correct at all," she said.

Earlier this week, the complainant told the court that months before the alleged rape, Mr Blackbourne showed her a picture of his young daughter at the police station.

In 2021, during a phone call between the complainant and Mr Blackbourne that was covertly recorded by police as part of an investigation, he told the woman he had two daughters.

During cross-examination, the defence suggested Mr Blackbourne never showed her a picture of his child.

"I disagree," the woman said.

"Can I suggest you made it up after he provided you with information during the phone call?" Mr Johnston said.

"That is incorrect," the woman said.

The trial, presided over by Judge Huw Baker SC, is expected to wrap up on Friday.

World.title: Argument over dog leads to shooting murder and 22 years' jail
World.content:
A man found guilty of a shooting murder that was sparked by an argument over a dog has been jailed for 22 years.

Luke Willcockson will spend at least 16 and a half years behind bars, after a jury found him guilty of fatally shooting Paul Davy through the screen door of a Kendall home on November 22, 2023.

Mr Davy's sister said hearing the sentence being handed down was "bittersweet", but it had restored her faith in "the system".

"No amount of time is going to get back my brother," Dona Davy said.

"I'm elated that it's a lot more than we had envisioned and it's wonderful to see the trial process and the outcome.

"He was my guardian, he was my teacher, my big brother in every sense of the word, the biggest clown anyone would meet, the funniest person, so smart on so many levels and cheeky."

CCTV played to the court showed Luke Willcockson (left) leaving the property shortly after the shooting. (Supplied: The Supreme Court of NSW)

Willcockson, 40, pleaded guilty to two counts of intending to pervert the course of justice and guilty to manslaughter, but not guilty of murder.

He was convicted of murdering Mr Davy by a jury in February.

During the trial, Willcockson said he was unaware his gun was loaded, before "accidentally" firing a single shot into Mr Davy's chest at close range.

He remained expressionless while receiving his sentence.

'A box of ashes'

Mr Davy's mother, Sue Magowan, told the court describing the loss of her son was like "trying to describe the colours a blind person is missing out on".

Paul Davy's niece, Lana Davy-Brandon, mother Sue Magowan and sister Dona Davy welcomed the sentence outside Port Macquarie Court. (ABC News: Marina Trajkovich)

"All we've got left is a box of ashes," she said.

Ms Magowan said she was "pleased" with the sentence.

Disputes over a dog

Court facts show on the day of Mr Davy's murder, Willcockson and friends took a dog from a property in Coolongolook.

It was taken to a home on Batar Creek Road, where Mr Davy arrived a short time later.

An argument erupted at the front door when Mr Davy tried to retrieve the dog.

Paul Davy came to the property to retrieve the dog taken from his friend and former girlfriend's house. (Supplied: The Supreme Court of New South Wales)

CCTV footage played to the court showed him saying it was "a child's dog mate, it's not his".

Willcockson then took a rifle from his bag and approached the door, where Mr Davy was heard to say "you won't do it, you won't shoot me".

Moments later, he was shot in the chest.

Paul Davy's family said his death had significantly affected their mental health and the sentence was "bittersweet." (Supplied: Dona Davy)

In delivering Willcockson's sentence, Acting Justice Ian Harrison said Mr Davy's death was "senseless, unprovoked and tragic" as well as "spontaneous and unplanned."

"Yet another example of total and unqualified stupidity that regularly sees expression in criminal cases in this court," he said.

"The consequences are no less tragic for that."

During sentencing, he noted Willcockson's letter of remorse accepting responsibility for Mr Davy's death, his drug dependency, challenging upbringing and current medical conditions, as well as victim impact statements from Mr Davy's family.

Willcockson will be eligible for parole in November 2040.

World.title: Sovereign citizen question to gun owners shut down by senior officer
World.content:
One of Tasmania's most senior cops sought the contrition of a subordinate after they asked suspected sovereign citizens to prove they were "fit and proper" gun owners.

Documents released through the state's right to information (RTI) system show police asked some Tasmanians to confirm or deny in writing if they aligned with sovereign citizen ideology.

Police then visited some of the Tasmanian firearm licence holders and a "small number" of licences were "temporarily suspended".

The head of Tasmania's police association says, "you don't want to be giving them the heads-up [that] you're attending their address". (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

This prompted an internal review, and Assistant Commissioner Doug Oosterloo to point out an increased risk to officers if they visit the property of a suspected sovereign citizen who believes police may be coming to take their guns.

Tasmania Police Assistant Commissioner Doug Oosterloo questioned the strategy. (Supplied: Tasmania Police)

The assistant commissioner's intervention was welcomed by the police association and the Australian Lawyers' Alliance, who warned of potential "authoritarian" overreach if groups of people with shared ideologies are targeted.

At least four letters sent to suspected sovereign citizens

'I do not consent': How pseudolaw supports 'sovcit' ideas "Sovereign citizens" believe Australian laws do not apply to them. That's where pseudolaw comes in.

Sovereign citizen ideology contains a broad swathe of beliefs, but in a 2023 briefing the Australian Federal Police said they traditionally "dissociate from society and refuse to engage with societal requirements like paying tax".

The briefing said "the movement itself is generally claimed to be non-violent", but that some members "can be hostile" and should not be considered non-dangerous.

The RTI documents released contain three letters sent in November last year to existing firearms licence holders and one to a firearms licence applicant from a Firearms Services (FAS) team member.

Assistant Commissioner Oosterloo said the letters may create a dangerous situation for any officers visiting suspected sovereign citizens' properties. (Supplied: Tasmania Police)

The four letters were contained within 16 pages of otherwise entirely redacted documents.

The letters said the team was "required to take into account the ability of a licence holder to exercise reasonable and responsible control over a firearm".

"Information available to this office suggests you may align with sovereign citizen ideology", the letters said, and requested a written response to that suggestion.

Once received, the letter said, further consideration would be given to the application for, or retention of, a firearms licence.

In a statement, Tasmania Police confirmed some firearms licence holders were visited, and "a small number of firearms licences were temporarily suspended … where there were credible safety concerns."

"Under the Firearms Act 1996, anyone who holds a firearms licence must be able to satisfy Tasmania Police that they are a 'fit and proper' person, can safely and responsibly control a firearm, and do not pose a risk to themselves or others," they said.

" No licences have been cancelled solely because a person was suspected of holding sovereign citizen views. "

Oosterloo intervened, police changed approach

A few months later, Assistant Commissioner Oosterloo sought a briefing from Firearms Services on "what has occurred … relative to the 'sovereign citizen' letters".

In an email published in the RTI documents, he asked, among others, the following questions:

On what basis were [individuals] identified as 'sovereign citizens'?

What is the specific legislative authority for suspending a firearms licence on the basis of the person being considered a 'sovereign citizen'? and

Did FAS consult or seek advice on issues relating to 'sovereign citizens' before taking action?

In the email, Assistant Commissioner Oosterloo also pointed out the letters may create a dangerous situation for any officers visiting suspected sovereign citizens' properties.

"Police attendance at the address may be perceived to be an action to take their firearms and therefore increases risk to police officers," he said.

He went on to ask for a detailed reflection about what mistakes had been made, what lessons had been learned, and what action was being taken or was needed.

"I would appreciate some honest reflection/contrition if it is conceded there were errors made," he wrote.

Since his intervention, letters have not been sent to suspected sovereign citizens and police have introduced mandatory training "to help officers identify relevant behaviours".

"Each case is now assessed individually, with input from police officers and intelligence analysts, and any action is taken after considering operational risks," police said in a statement.

Changes to process welcomed by officers, lawyers alliance

Police Association President Shane Tilley said it was appropriate the FAS letters program had been shut down, and welcomed the mandatory training.

"When you … write to people with these ideologies you really are setting yourself up to fail, in my view," he said.

" You don't want to be giving them the heads-up [that] you're attending their address or something similar. "

He said police risk assessments had improved in recent years in the wake of the killing of Victorian police officers by suspected sovereign citizen Dezi Freeman and the murder of Tasmanian Police Constable Keith Smith.

Australian Lawyers' Alliance spokesman Greg Barns SC said some sovereign citizens had come to the attention of police in the past, but that did not mean all sovereign citizens were going to use firearms illegally.

"It's got an authoritarian element to it and … I think it's a dangerous practice because it sets a precedent," he said.

Mr Barns said, for example, it would be problematic if police began writing letters to members of protest groups for environmental causes.

World.title: Setka to be sacked: Threats, abuse behind push to remove former CFMEU boss
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaBuilding Bad Setka to be sacked: Threats, abuse behind push to remove former CFMEU boss Nick McKenzie July 23, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

John Setka is set to be expelled from the union he led for 12 years and a powerful Victorian organiser has been summarily removed from the CFMEU in a dramatic effort by the union’s new administrator to reassert control of the rogue Victorian branch. The move to formally tear up Setka’s CFMEU membership for repeatedly threatening and intimidating administrator Michael Crosby and his staff comes after the disgraced former union chief was photographed dining at an upmarket steak and oyster restaurant with a building company boss notorious for ripping off union members and subcontractors. Lunch companions Frank Nadinic (left), John Setka (centre) and John Perkovic (right). Nathan Perri Also at the Esca Grill Seafood and Steak restaurant lunch with company boss Frank Nadinic— who the CFMEU once labelled “cruel Frank” for rorting workers — was Setka’s former union lieutenant John Perkovic. Perkovic is under active federal police investigation for taking up to $3 million in suspected bribes from other building company bosses also accused of exploiting workers.



Five industry and union insiders said the sight of Setka rubbing shoulders with Nadinic - an exploitative building firm boss whose building firm Setka attacked publicly in 2015 for conduct that denied dozens of union members their entitlements — was illustrative of the demise of the CFMEU under Setka’s reign into a union that privileged company and gangland bosses above ordinary workers. This masthead could not confirm allegations from those sources that Setka and Perkovic were assisting Nadinic in handling a building industry dispute, as all three men were not able to be contacted. John Setka outside his lunch venue. The Age In his LinkedIn profile, Nadinic describes himself as an “experienced senior consultant with a demonstrated history of working in the construction and development industry” and a “strong consulting professional with a First class honours focused in Life from School of hard knocks”. Perkovic was sacked from the union last October after this masthead revealed he had received undisclosed benefits worth up to $3 million from company bosses he oversaw as a union official.



Over the last two years, this masthead’s Building Bad series has revealed how multiple companies with track records of mistreating workers or offering them insecure gigs in labour hire roles were given preferential treatment by the CFMEU. Editor's pick Exclusive

Building Bad Top Victorian CFMEU official sacked over alleged mistreatment of union organiser It has also revealed how Setka and Perkovic’s underworld ally, union fixer Mick Gatto, has been paid millions of dollars by companies that have gone bust owing workers or paid the underworld veteran to keep the union from enforcing hard union-won pay and conditions EBAs. On Wednesday evening, Crosby wrote to Setka saying he intended to initiate formal proceedings to rip up Setka’s CFMEU membership “for a period of 5 years” for allegedly engaging in “misconduct” by threatening, abusing and denigrating administration staff by calling them dogs in expletive-ridden tirades on email and in other forums. As recently as Sunday, Setka threatened Crosby with violence in an interview he gave to this masthead.



“If he wants to come after me, he better f---ing watch himself,” Setka said on Sunday. “Because if I run into him in the street, it’s not going to be good for him ... He’s not a f---ing koala bear. He’s not, f---ing, a protected species.” Editor's pick Updated

Victorian Parliament ‘I don’t just ditch my mates’: New minister defends CFMEU links Police have also moved to obtain a personal intervention order for Crosby against Setka following the remarks. Setka, who did not return calls on Thursday, has until August 7 to make his case to Crosby as to why he should not be expelled as a member of the CFMEU. His expulsion would complete an extraordinary fall from power of a man who once wielded significant influence over the Victorian Labor Party and who continues to have allies in select union and political circles, including Allan government minister Luba Grigorovitch.



The move against Setka by Crosby comes after the administrator declared on Monday the culture in the union’s previously all-powerful Victorian arm remained broken and warned that the pariah branch would stay in administration indefinitely while its sacked former bosses still exert control. In the interview, Crosby also called on government and the wider industry to do far more to combat the construction industry organised crime and corruption that Victoria Police has separately warned it is powerless to tackle. Loading On Thursday, Crosby also moved to sap the ongoing influence of ex-CFMEU vice president Joe Myles, who this masthead revealed on Monday was still influencing the activities of union officials on Labor’s Big Build. Crosby removed union organiser Adam Olsen from the CFMEU amid concerns Olsen, who is a close friend of Myles, was still acting on Myles’ orders. Olsen and Myles could not be contacted for comment.



Myles was previously the top CFMEU official on the Big Build and has been accused - including in a report tabled in the Queensland royal commission into the union - of placing bikie gang members as union delegates on state government rail and road projects. World.title: Unused spaces transformed, 50,000 homes built: City’s wishlist for Olympic legacy
World.content:
NationalQueenslandBrisbane 2032 Olympics Unused spaces transformed, 50,000 homes built: City’s wishlist for Olympic legacy William Davis July 23, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Underused land including the space under the rail line at South Brisbane would be transformed with skate parks, climbing walls, public art and pickleball courts, under a Brisbane City Council vision for the Olympics legacy unveiled on Thursday. Up to 50,000 additional homes around Games venues would also be delivered, as would river taxi services, a web of shaded pathways across the city, 24-hour precincts, improved ferries, a Metro expansion and upgraded parks. The council document titled “Brisbane Beyond the Games” outlined how the city could secure the best long-term gain from hosting the world’s biggest sports event. An artist impression of a new basketball court published by Brisbane City Council, which says it will upgrade parks across the city before the 2032 Brisbane Olympic Games. Brisbane City Council It listed more than a dozen significant infrastructure and transport projects the council hoped to deliver before athletes would arrive.



“It’s actually not about the opening ceremony,” Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner told several hundred industry leaders during a lunch at The Star on Thursday. Related Article Road to Brisbane 2032 Olympic pool renders show grand plans, but details yet to be finalised “It’s about what people think … 10 years after the games. “This community will all come together, and we will look back, and we will make a decision on that date whether this has been a good thing for Brisbane.” Dr Tony Matthews, an urban planner at Griffith University, said the Olympic committee had to focus first and foremost on delivering the basics.



“I don’t want to be all down on the Olympics, but there’s an enormous task ahead of us, and I don’t think we’ve taken the advantage that we could have from the time we had,” he said. “I’m just a little wary of trying to get so much done in a relatively narrow time window at this stage. We can promise a lot and aspire to a lot, but delivering a lot is a different situation.” A digital render of water taxis operating on the Brisbane River, which could become a reality if pontoons are opened to private operators ahead of the 2032 Brisbane Olympic Games. Brisbane City Council Queensland University of Technology urban planner Dr Mark Limb said the document was light on detail, but the single most important thing Brisbane City Council could focus on to benefit residents in the long term was expansion of rail and metro services. A proposal called the “Low Line” – a twist on New York’s High Line, which runs along the top of an abandoned railway bridge – was included in the document.



Artist impressions showed a revitalised space underneath South Brisbane’s raised rail line, with a skate park, playground, rock climbing wall, outdoor gym equipment, basketball court, and street murals. Brisbane City Council said the proposal, which came from Aria Property Group and Urbis, could also feature pickleball courts, dog parks and public gardens. An artist impression of the “low line” shows a skate park, playground, rock climbing wall, outdoor gym equipment, basketball court and extensive street murals. Brisbane City Council “We will use the games as a catalyst to transform leftover land around major infrastructure into vibrant urban sports parks and community spaces,” the document said. The ferry network would also be upgraded, according to the document, and pontoons across the river could be opened to private operators to allow introduction of water taxis.



Limb questioned how functional this would be in a city with a narrow, winding river. “I think if there was a true market for a water taxi, you’d probably have them already … it’s not really a useful mass transit option.” Dr Tony Matthews agreed the best legacy the Olympics could leave for Brisbane would be expanded public transit. Courtney Kruk The document said infrastructure investment in areas such as Fortitude Valley, Kurilpa, Milton, Newstead and Woolloongabba could lead to about 50,000 new homes being built in those areas. Limb added that private investment tended to lag well behind zoning changes, and extensive development may take longer than six years.



A web of shaded pathways, known as the Green and Gold Grid, is also planned across the city. Related Article Exclusive

Public Transport Victoria Bridge shade secured, but Metro expansion hits Games hurdle New connections between the CBD and Suncorp Stadium were planned before the start of the 2027 Rugby World Cup, while shade cloths for the Victoria Bridge could be installed within weeks. Multiple other routes are planned. “This will lead to a lasting legacy of walkability, urban greening, thriving precincts and healthier, more connected communities,” the document says. Schrinner told the lunch his absolute priority was expansion of the Metro into the suburbs. He has previously said this could not be done without funding from the federal government.



“I think if you’re looking for real long-lasting impact, it’s aspects related to mass transit that’s going to help us,” Limb said. Matthews added one of the best legacies Brisbane City Council could achieve through the games would be expansion of green spaces. An artist impression of Brisbane Stadium being built at Victoria Park. Cox Architecture “I would say placemaking and urban greenery … should be the key guiding principles of the legacy,” he said. “We have a relatively low volume of green space available … and we’re going to be sacrificing a fair bit of it for the stadium.



“There’s just endless amounts of well-founded research out there showing that the higher volume of urban green space you have in a city … the better all sorts of things for the residents.” Related Article Road to Brisbane 2032 Evicted pool tenants told to negotiate compensation themselves The document also references plans to capitalise on Brisbane’s “dawn economy”, as well as the possibility of 24-hour precincts, a Global Food Hall, and Pride House for LGBTIQ+ athletes and fans. The Labor opposition on Brisbane City Council highlighted the fact proposed new housing did not include affordability mandates. “[Schrinner] reheated old announcements to pretend he’s achieving something new exactly six years out,” leader Jared Cassidy said.



“Basic services and infrastructure are falling to the wayside … more missed bins, shocking roads, crippling congestion and a homelessness crisis are what this Lord Mayor will be remembered for. “Brisbane needs a champion for 2032. Adrian Schrinner is not it.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Ed Husic has taken on the role of Labor’s conscience. Will it last?
World.content:
Anthony Albanese let his guard down last week when asked about former minister Ed Husic’s suggestion that Labor was going soft on big artificial intelligence firms. The government’s AI regulation was “something that Ed wouldn’t be familiar with because this has been a cabinet process”, the prime minister retorted. The jab brought into public view a tense relationship that broke down when Husic was pushed out of the cabinet last year in a factional cull. Labor MP Ed Husic addresses reporters outside the party’s national conference in Adelaide. Dominic Lorrimer Far from sulking on the sidelines, Husic has turned into the chief irritant within Labor’s caucus and, as this week’s national conference has highlighted, the lead advocate on nearly all the issues of importance to the Labor base: AUKUS, gas tax, Gaza, Indigenous reconciliation after the Voice.





The western Sydney MP, who was the first Muslim to enter cabinet, has morphed from a lower-profile minister to a backbencher who generates more media attention, often by criticising the direction of the cabinet in which he served. These criticisms sound louder given the strict discipline of Albanese’s caucus, who show no appetite for rocking the boat while the party remains so dominant. While several of his colleagues sat inside the official conference room on Thursday, sponsoring motions and giving speeches to the floor, Husic spoke at a press conference on a range of topics and was one of very few MPs scheduled to address the “fringe” section of the national forum. As its name suggests, it’s where the edgier issues are raised. Husic sat on a panel hosted by the left-leaning Australia Institute to argue for a gas tax – an issue that Treasurer Jim Chalmers and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese earlier in the day downplayed. “We’ve got to move quicker on these things,” Husic told the room of fewer than 100 people on the sidelines. “It shouldn’t take 10 bloody years to get these major reforms done.” Asked how he would act if he were the treasurer, Husic quipped: “That’s what I need, to upset the treasurer again.”



It was one of several jokes – about lack of debate on the floor of conference, and his own tendency to push limits and speak out of turn – that demonstrated his fresh appetite for candour. Related Article ALP Israel accused of ‘extraordinary’ intervention in Labor politics “I’ll just leave that there, don’t need to say anything further, don’t say it Husic,” he joked, as an aside, at one point. Then later: “In the best of Yes, Minister – it is a very brave government that would ignore the views of the public on this.” When he was being serious, Husic gave something of a rallying cry to members in the audience – urging them to exert maximum pressure on his own colleagues. “That is the type of activism that is required out of the rank and file of the party, where you’re saying to your MPs and your senators: our expectation’s a better deal,” he said. He said cutting funds to vulnerable people in programs like the National Disability Insurance Scheme would not fly with the public if they thought companies were getting off scot-free. “We should seize the moment, and have the steel and spine to do so,” he said.



Ministers often vent in private about Husic, and MPs loyal to Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles, the Victorian Right faction leader whom Husic blamed for dumping him from cabinet, emphasise it was Husic’s own allies in NSW who ultimately removed him. Husic, according to his critics, was too slow to execute the government’s industrial policies as minister and did not live up to the job. They grumble about what they perceive to be his attention-seeking, maximalist style, which fails to grapple with policy trade-offs. But there is no doubt about the effectiveness with which Husic has championed Labor’s progressive instincts. At a national conference that has come to exemplify Albanese’s yearning for control, Husic has added colour – and a sense of jeopardy. How he handles Friday’s sensitive debate over Israel and Gaza – as his colleagues seek a moment of unity – will test his position as the party’s new conscience. World.title: How to choose the ideal colour palette for your home
World.content:
PropertyLivingInterior design How to choose the ideal colour palette for your home Dan F Stapleton July 23, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

You might expect an interior-design tastemaker like Greg Natale to have decorated his own home in shades of fashionable white and cream. But Natale is a fan of colours that grab you. “In my own apartment, a maroon theme runs strong,” he reveals. Interior designer Greg Natale is a fan of colours that grab you. Anson Smart Maroon reminds Natale and his partner of a cherished trip to Paris, where they saw the colour everywhere. “Having maroon walls and carpet transports us back to a city we love,” he says. Natale happily admits his maroon-led colour scheme is not on trend, acknowledging that, in 2026, many homes that hit the market or are featured in magazines are cream-coloured copies.



While many home owners default to white, experts say those who plan to stay in their homes long-term should embrace hues that speak specifically to them, and can do so successfully by following simple rules. But those who are looking to sell may prefer to take a different approach. Related Article Interior design Quiet luxury and boho chic: Are our homes becoming boring? Home owners who want their interiors to reflect their personality often engage Natale, known as something of an interior-design chameleon, adapting to clients’ preferences. For one recent residential project in the United States, he employed a mix of patterns, animal prints and deep colours such as olive green and burgundy. “Another house, for a client in Sydney who loved colourful Murano glass, became a jewelled box, with each room taking on its own character, defined by colour,” he says.



He believes no colour is off-limits in a home. “When applied thoughtfully and in the right context, any hue has the potential to bring depth, character and brilliance to a space,” he says. That’s not to say he operates without guiding principles. He often works with one-colour palettes, for example, combining multiple shades to create visual texture. Natale employs principles such as one-colour palettes. Anson Smart “By working with different shades and intensities of the same hue, you can create a nuanced interior that feels considered,” he says. Fellow interior designer Thomas Hamel agrees. “Rather than introducing lots of competing colours, it’s often more effective to establish a foundation and layer in subtle tonal variations, creating depth and longevity,” he says.



He says nature-inspired tones evoke a sense of comfort and calm. “Warm whites, gentle greys, stone, sand, sage greens and muted blues all have an enduring quality and tend to create spaces that people genuinely enjoy spending time in.” Nature-inspired tones can create a sense of calm. Anson Smart However, he says there’s no “wrong” choice when choosing a palette to live in long-term. “Colour is deeply personal,” he says. “For some clients, richer tones such as deep olive, oxblood, aubergine and navy can create wonderfully intimate and sophisticated spaces when used thoughtfully.”



The key to success, he says, is to select colours that reflect the style of the home – ornate or minimalist, for example – and its residents’ personalities. Related Article Interior design Real estate agents love this look. But it won’t make a house a home He cautions home owners against following the crowd when it comes to colour, as trends can date quickly. It’s also important to consider how natural and artificial light will affect a colour scheme throughout the day, he says. “Testing colours in situ and viewing them at different times of day is always worthwhile.”



While Hamel and Natale encourage clients to choose colours based on personal preference, BresicWhitney agent David Smith-Cameron takes a different position when advising those looking to sell. “White is always the safest bet,” he says, adding homes painted in other colours can be “a bit overwhelming” to many buyers. “It’s something we often find with deceased estates that haven’t been touched for decades. Most buyers will walk into a colourful property and immediately feel like they need to make a change, which isn’t always what you want when selling.” BresicWhitney is selling a semi in Sydney’s upmarket Woollahra that was previously for sale in early 2021, when it had striking brown cornices and beige walls in the living room, combined with busy styling. The same home now has off-white walls and minimal styling, making the living room look calmer.



Smith-Cameron describes painting a property white as an “easy win” that can deliver a strong return on investment when selling. “I’m renovating a house in Paddington at the moment, and I’ve just spent 30 grand painting it for that exact reason,” he says. Related Article Residential property The room you shouldn’t bother renovating before you sell your house But choose your whites carefully. “There are 100 different shades of white, and they’re all very different. A warm white can have a yellowy undertone, whereas a cool white might have a blue undertone.” He suggests home owners choose a white that corresponds with other colours and materials in the home. “People who have cool-coloured features throughout, such as darker floors or blue or grey stone, should paint with a cool white, and those with warmer-coloured features should choose a warm white.” For those determined to buck the all-white trend, Smith-Cameron offers some guidance: “A home with personality is a great thing, but an interior that is too loud can put people off.”

World.title: Setka to be sacked: Threats, abuse behind push to remove former CFMEU boss
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaBuilding Bad Setka to be sacked: Threats, abuse behind push to remove former CFMEU boss Nick McKenzie July 23, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

John Setka is set to be expelled from the union he led for 12 years and a powerful Victorian organiser has been summarily removed from the CFMEU in a dramatic effort by the union’s new administrator to reassert control of the rogue Victorian branch. The move to formally tear up Setka’s CFMEU membership for repeatedly threatening and intimidating administrator Michael Crosby and his staff comes after the disgraced former union chief was photographed dining at an upmarket steak and oyster restaurant with a building company boss notorious for ripping off union members and subcontractors. Lunch companions Frank Nadinic (left), John Setka (centre) and John Perkovic (right). Nathan Perri Also at the Esca Grill Seafood and Steak restaurant lunch with company boss Frank Nadinic— who the CFMEU once labelled “cruel Frank” for rorting workers — was Setka’s former union lieutenant John Perkovic. Perkovic is under active federal police investigation for taking up to $3 million in suspected bribes from other building company bosses also accused of exploiting workers.



Five industry and union insiders said the sight of Setka rubbing shoulders with Nadinic - an exploitative building firm boss whose building firm Setka attacked publicly in 2015 for conduct that denied dozens of union members their entitlements — was illustrative of the demise of the CFMEU under Setka’s reign into a union that privileged company and gangland bosses above ordinary workers. This masthead could not confirm allegations from those sources that Setka and Perkovic were assisting Nadinic in handling a building industry dispute, as all three men were not able to be contacted. John Setka outside his lunch venue. The Age In his LinkedIn profile, Nadinic describes himself as an “experienced senior consultant with a demonstrated history of working in the construction and development industry” and a “strong consulting professional with a First class honours focused in Life from School of hard knocks”. Perkovic was sacked from the union last October after this masthead revealed he had received undisclosed benefits worth up to $3 million from company bosses he oversaw as a union official.



Over the last two years, this masthead’s Building Bad series has revealed how multiple companies with track records of mistreating workers or offering them insecure gigs in labour hire roles were given preferential treatment by the CFMEU. Editor's pick Exclusive

Building Bad Top Victorian CFMEU official sacked over alleged mistreatment of union organiser It has also revealed how Setka and Perkovic’s underworld ally, union fixer Mick Gatto, has been paid millions of dollars by companies that have gone bust owing workers or paid the underworld veteran to keep the union from enforcing hard union-won pay and conditions EBAs. On Wednesday evening, Crosby wrote to Setka saying he intended to initiate formal proceedings to rip up Setka’s CFMEU membership “for a period of 5 years” for allegedly engaging in “misconduct” by threatening, abusing and denigrating administration staff by calling them dogs in expletive-ridden tirades on email and in other forums. As recently as Sunday, Setka threatened Crosby with violence in an interview he gave to this masthead.



“If he wants to come after me, he better f---ing watch himself,” Setka said on Sunday. “Because if I run into him in the street, it’s not going to be good for him ... He’s not a f---ing koala bear. He’s not, f---ing, a protected species.” Editor's pick Updated

Victorian Parliament ‘I don’t just ditch my mates’: New minister defends CFMEU links Police have also moved to obtain a personal intervention order for Crosby against Setka following the remarks. Setka, who did not return calls on Thursday, has until August 7 to make his case to Crosby as to why he should not be expelled as a member of the CFMEU. His expulsion would complete an extraordinary fall from power of a man who once wielded significant influence over the Victorian Labor Party and who continues to have allies in select union and political circles, including Allan government minister Luba Grigorovitch.



The move against Setka by Crosby comes after the administrator declared on Monday the culture in the union’s previously all-powerful Victorian arm remained broken and warned that the pariah branch would stay in administration indefinitely while its sacked former bosses still exert control. In the interview, Crosby also called on government and the wider industry to do far more to combat the construction industry organised crime and corruption that Victoria Police has separately warned it is powerless to tackle. Loading On Thursday, Crosby also moved to sap the ongoing influence of ex-CFMEU vice president Joe Myles, who this masthead revealed on Monday was still influencing the activities of union officials on Labor’s Big Build. Crosby removed union organiser Adam Olsen from the CFMEU amid concerns Olsen, who is a close friend of Myles, was still acting on Myles’ orders. Olsen and Myles could not be contacted for comment.



Myles was previously the top CFMEU official on the Big Build and has been accused - including in a report tabled in the Queensland royal commission into the union - of placing bikie gang members as union delegates on state government rail and road projects. World.title: Memo Hanson, for many it’s not easy to leave
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Memo Hanson, for many it’s not easy to leave July 23, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Badiucao To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Speaking about family violence, Pauline Hanson says ″⁣women can lose their cool as well″⁣ (″⁣Anger at Hanson’s ‘two-way street’ call″⁣, 23/7). Yes, of course, we can all lose our cool, and yes women can be violent – to children, to other women and to men. But there would be very few men who live in fear of their women partners, very few men who spend their day wondering what their partner will be like when he comes home – whether this will be a time when he is violent or threatening or abusive, when he doesn’t like what she cooks or how she behaves. Yet that is the reality for far too many women. Women who work hard at keeping their family together, who forgive their partner for the violence, women who know that if they try to leave that is when he will become extremely dangerous. It is not easy just to leave. Tell it to the many women who either were killed or subjected to further violence, abuse and stalking after they left. Family violence and its causes should never be used to achieve cheap political headlines.

Marg D’Arcy, Rye No details is the default position

In her domestic violence can be a ″⁣two-way street″⁣ comments on a Brisbane radio station, Pauline Hanson again displayed a total lack of knowledge, understanding and empathy. However, just as telling and typical, was after describing DV as a ″⁣scourge″⁣, she said, ″⁣I’m not going to go into detail.″⁣ This is Hanson’s default position. Why? Because she is unable to give any detail. It’s an inconvenience, it’s too difficult. She has somehow made a 30-year career by avoiding detail, by trumpeting stereotypes and bigotry so outrageous that they deflect genuine attention and scrutiny.

It would be interesting to see how a ″⁣would-be″⁣ prime minister, would go into ″⁣detail″⁣ around federal portfolios such as: health, education, defence, home and foreign affairs, treasury and finance, industry, innovation and science.

Craig Jory, Glenroy, NSW Little surprise in comments

We can condemn Pauline Hanson’s comment that domestic violence is a ″⁣two-way street″⁣, but we should not be surprised. In 2019, she said that while one woman was dying each week at the hands of her partner, 21 men were committing suicide, blaming the family law system for ″⁣killing dads″⁣. Men were being forced to pay too much child support, she said, suggesting this was a factor in men’s suicides. Violent men are emboldened by these baseless and irresponsible claims by Hanson that women are as much to blame as men. They can also be a factor in dissuading women from leaving a violent relationship.

Neil Hudson, East Melbourne



Feeding the manosphere with grievance

Pauline Hanson’s recent public pronouncement about domestic violence serves only to highlight her adroitness at perpetuating commonly held tropes about a complex subject. The negative effect of this is that her ill-informed and dangerous commentary becomes fodder for the manosphere of misogynist grievance.

What Hanson and others don’t understand – as promulgated by survivor Orly Lavee (Comment, 22/7) – is that “The mechanics of abuse are not symmetrical” and underpinned by the common denominator of coercive control. That is, whatever manifestation of abuse the woman is being subjected to, but often times multiple types of abuses at once.

Moreover, when police become involved at the pointy end of a DV incident it is acutely apparent of how readily a victim can be misidentified as a perpetrator (ie due to her heightened emotional distress and seeming ‘incoherence’) and concomitantly, how police can unwittingly collude with the actual perpetrator (due to a fundamental lack of understanding of the mechanics of coercive control).

Jelena Rosic, Mornington Danger can follow women out the door

Pauline Hanson seems to suggest women can just avoid domestic violence by simply leaving the relationship. The trouble is that women are often actually in more danger when they leave, the abuser can just become angrier, and track them down.

Terry Kelly, Coburg THE FORUM Lens on Big Build

Professor David Hayward provides a further lens on the jaw-dropping allegations surrounding the Big Build and rightly calls for an inquiry into what has become a blight on our state (“Independent inquiry into the Big Build is urgently needed”, 23/7). In another time, if a politician had faced the accusations that have been levelled against the premier, they would have stood aside and allowed a due process to take its course. In refusing to take this step, the Victorian government, the union movement and the public service will continue to be viewed with deep suspicion by the electorate until we know the full story.

As Professor Hayward highlights, the privatisation agenda comes under further scrutiny. The government, as the custodian of taxpayer dollars, bears the responsibility of ensuring that money is used judiciously for the benefit of its citizens whilst the public service acts as the guardian ensuring procurement and contracting processes are undertaken with integrity and transparency. With so many unanswered accusations it is difficult to have trust in either institution. Premier, it is time to act to clear the stench surrounding the Big Build.

Anne Lyon, Camberwell Read the room

Jacinta Allan should read the room: rural voters will dump her government into a very large pothole come November unless they see multiple teams in high-vis dealing ASAP with the dangerous state of country roads. And, a Big Build Royal royal commission will help save the city vote.

Greg Malcher, Hepburn



Compelling reasons

While I agree strongly that public school teachers and the system in which they work needs to be better valued and funded, I consider that teachers need to come to an agreement with the government soon. There are two reasons for this. First, the ongoing disruption to the lives of students’ parents will ultimately result in a loss of their support. Second, and more importantly, based on current polling the teachers could soon be dealing with a Liberal-National Coalition or One Nation-led government. Based on the Coalition’s attitude to public servants such as teachers and nurses in the past and One Nation’s stated attitude towards all workers, good luck getting what they want from them.

Kevin Bailey, Croydon Tackling the grifters

All political parties, when out of power, use grievance and criticism of those in power to gain ascendancy. As Shaun Carney observes (Comment, 23/7), both the Coalition and One Nation’s proposals to address these grievances rely on a combination of returning to the very economic paradigms that have caused our current imbalances and a grab bag of irrelevant culture war distractions. This worked for Donald Trump, but his time in office is an unravelling disaster. We are seeing rhetoric coming from Anthony Albanese and the new UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham that acknowledges the validity of some of the grievance zeitgeist.

An awareness is developing that the way to beat the populist grifters is to enact policies that address the underlying economic grievances they rely on. Yet we don’t have an overarching economic framework to supplant the post-war Keynesian welfare state system and the neoliberal globalist system that replaced it. We desperately need one.

Graeme Henchel, Yarra Glen Importance of home

What a good reminder about the importance of housing v the current government’s focus on other concerns. Your correspondent (Letters, 23/7) beautifully states the basic benefits of why housing is so important, useful, supportive and necessary – stability, a place for family to establish themselves, security – and that for most people, it is a commitment to remain long term in their home, not use it as a short-term investment. I hope someone in the government is paying attention.

Joyce Butcher, Williamstown Points of difference

Your correspondent is spot on about Labor and the Coalition not seeing how Pauline Hanson, like Donald Trump, is too different from regular politicians to be defeated by the usual rules (Letters, 23/7). However, let’s hope that Australians are too different from Americans to allow that to happen.

Henry Herzog, St Kilda East Disturbing views

The issue of immigration (key planks in the policies of Donald Trump and in Brexit) continues to raise its ugly head with it being a key plank in One Nation’s rise in popularity.

This xenophobic, discriminating and economically stupid policy is disturbing enough being espoused by One Nation, but add Hanson’s views on domestic violence and the views of Senator Malcolm Roberts, makes it even more disturbing when one looks at the numbers of people willing to vote for them.

Phil Mackenzie, Eaglemont



Zero understanding

Even if you don’t interpret Pauline Hanson’s “two-way street” comment as victim blaming, at the very least it demonstrates zero understanding of the complex limitations, both psychological and financial, for a woman needing to leave an environment of domestic violence.

Claire Merry, Wantirna Not the same basket

Your correspondent (Letters, 22/7) hits the nail on the head in relation to migration and Australia. They mention the Afghan cameleers who came to Australia and, not only ″⁣dug dams, put up the telephone poles and helped build the inland roads″⁣ also opened trade in the interior.

We also have many other cultures to thank for greatest impacts on ″⁣settlement outcomes″⁣: Chinese during the gold rushes, Greek, Italians and others from Europe at the end of WWII building the Snowy Mountains scheme, all the people from Asian countries. And yet for some reason people like Pauline Hanson, Barnaby Joyce want to both stop these people providing their knowledge about how their way of life can improve ours. By all means screen them to ensure we accept the truly genuine people but, do not put all immigrants in the same basket.

Rosemary Berrell, Ashburton Erasing history

From the sidelines of the federal Labor Party national conference comes the Australian Manufacturing Workers’ Union demanding the removal of the Union Jack from the Australian flag along with the removal of “offensive colonial statues” (“Flying the flag for fight that nobody else in the party, especially PM, wants to have”, 23/7). Like it or not, these artefacts tell important parts of our history.

While they are busy prising loose statues, perhaps the union could liberate us from the Westminster system of government and the rule of law as we know it. It brings to mind the way Stalin removed faces and persons from photographs in the 1930s so he, too, could control the narrative of history.

John Whelen, Box Hill Sth Energy crisis

Australia must urgently expand its electricity supply.

Oddly, an obstacle is terminology: certain terms — “renewables”, for instance — seem to cause angst. More precise language may help. There is inexhaustible clean “electron energy”, ie, solar, wind, hydro, which generate power by moving electrons. And “combustion energy” produced by burning finite fossil fuels, with resultant carbon emissions and pollutants.

Take solar as an illustration of energy potential.

Elon Musk calculated that a 160 kilometre by 160 kilometre solar array could power the United States.

Split across the outbacks of Queensland, NSW and South Australia, each state would need an area of just 93 kilometres by 93 kilometres, under 1.1 per cent of their land, to match US supply, which is 15 times our current electricity generation. Using clear unemotive terms like “electron energy” may help defuse the culture wars, allowing urgent action to secure our energy future.

Carlo Ursida, Kensington Like, what she said

In total concurrence with your correspondent (Letters, 23/7). It’s not just young people’s overuse of the word “like” that offends, but interviewees of all ages tend towards overuse of ″⁣like″⁣.

Often the sentences start with “Like” and the word is interspersed after every third word thereafter, like.

Like, it’s so annoying.

Sue Parrington, Port Melbourne



Address gambling

When my father returned from overseas service in WWII in 1945, he would bet on two flies climbing up the wall. We didn’t have television or a TAB, so he became a starting price bookmaker and not a very good one. My brother and I sold newspapers in the 1940s and ’50s so we could put food on the table as our father continued down the path of gambling destruction. I spent my early years as a blue-collar worker, supporting Labor principles and for the last 50 years have been involved in finance.

I am now 90, and was impressed with the late Peta Murphy’s work on gambling advertising, but the watering down of Murphy’s propositions by this government disappoints me greatly. It seems to me that gambling advertising is on the increase in all mediums.

Gambling has never interested me personally and I hope the Labor conference sees fit to extend the advertising bans in sport to totality even if it means a loss of donations.

Kenneth Clarke, Wangaratta Photo: Matt Golding AND ANOTHER THING Trump

In Donald Trump’s logic it’s fine for Saudi Arabia to have nuclear power, but not Iran? As usual, does he have any idea of what he’s doing?

Tim Durbridge, Brunswick Along with AusAlert, will we learn how to duck and cover in preparation for Donald Trump’s next level of warfare?

Bryan Lewis, St Helena



Furthermore

The PM has turned down the heat on climate debate at the ALP national conference. But it’s a sure bet that he’ll be feeling it this predicted El Niño summer.

Jenny Smithers, Ashburton For more than 10 years our car registration plates have said Victoria, ″⁣The Education State″⁣. Maybe it is time for a change. I suggest ″⁣Victoria – The Big Build State″⁣.

Tony Wheeler, Doncaster East Victoria can’t give teachers a 28per cent pay rise. Victoria is broke.

David Hughes, South Melbourne Your correspondent (Letters, 23/7) suggests teachers of English have a class competition to see if any student can make a sentence without the word “like” in it. As a teacher of English, I like that idea.

Deborah Morrison, Malvern East The criminal waste of money on the Big Build has added to Victoria’s dire financial standing. Apparently, it will be investigated, subject to electoral convenience.

Bill Burns, Bendigo



It is immaterial whether one is pro-Israel or pro-Palestine: Hamas is a listed terrorist organisation and as such Labor is morally and ethically obliged to call for it to be disarmed.

Louise Kloot, Doncaster Bubble bubble toil and trouble Neil Mitchell, you’ve really stirred the cauldron, although not in the way you wanted (Comment, 19/7).

Jane Ross, San Remo Finally

There are more letters about a dog than Donald Trump,which is a bonus. And a dog has even made it to the front page of Green Guide. But, doggone it, it’s enough already.

Myra Fisher, Brighton East

World.title: Unused spaces transformed, 50,000 homes built: City’s wishlist for Olympic legacy
World.content:
NationalQueenslandBrisbane 2032 Olympics Unused spaces transformed, 50,000 homes built: City’s wishlist for Olympic legacy William Davis July 23, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Underused land including the space under the rail line at South Brisbane would be transformed with skate parks, climbing walls, public art and pickleball courts, under a Brisbane City Council vision for the Olympics legacy unveiled on Thursday. Up to 50,000 additional homes around Games venues would also be delivered, as would river taxi services, a web of shaded pathways across the city, 24-hour precincts, improved ferries, a Metro expansion and upgraded parks. The council document titled “Brisbane Beyond the Games” outlined how the city could secure the best long-term gain from hosting the world’s biggest sports event. An artist impression of a new basketball court published by Brisbane City Council, which says it will upgrade parks across the city before the 2032 Brisbane Olympic Games. Brisbane City Council It listed more than a dozen significant infrastructure and transport projects the council hoped to deliver before athletes would arrive.



“It’s actually not about the opening ceremony,” Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner told several hundred industry leaders during a lunch at The Star on Thursday. Related Article Road to Brisbane 2032 Olympic pool renders show grand plans, but details yet to be finalised “It’s about what people think … 10 years after the games. “This community will all come together, and we will look back, and we will make a decision on that date whether this has been a good thing for Brisbane.” Dr Tony Matthews, an urban planner at Griffith University, said the Olympic committee had to focus first and foremost on delivering the basics.



“I don’t want to be all down on the Olympics, but there’s an enormous task ahead of us, and I don’t think we’ve taken the advantage that we could have from the time we had,” he said. “I’m just a little wary of trying to get so much done in a relatively narrow time window at this stage. We can promise a lot and aspire to a lot, but delivering a lot is a different situation.” A digital render of water taxis operating on the Brisbane River, which could become a reality if pontoons are opened to private operators ahead of the 2032 Brisbane Olympic Games. Brisbane City Council Queensland University of Technology urban planner Dr Mark Limb said the document was light on detail, but the single most important thing Brisbane City Council could focus on to benefit residents in the long term was expansion of rail and metro services. A proposal called the “Low Line” – a twist on New York’s High Line, which runs along the top of an abandoned railway bridge – was included in the document.



Artist impressions showed a revitalised space underneath South Brisbane’s raised rail line, with a skate park, playground, rock climbing wall, outdoor gym equipment, basketball court, and street murals. Brisbane City Council said the proposal, which came from Aria Property Group and Urbis, could also feature pickleball courts, dog parks and public gardens. An artist impression of the “low line” shows a skate park, playground, rock climbing wall, outdoor gym equipment, basketball court and extensive street murals. Brisbane City Council “We will use the games as a catalyst to transform leftover land around major infrastructure into vibrant urban sports parks and community spaces,” the document said. The ferry network would also be upgraded, according to the document, and pontoons across the river could be opened to private operators to allow introduction of water taxis.



Limb questioned how functional this would be in a city with a narrow, winding river. “I think if there was a true market for a water taxi, you’d probably have them already … it’s not really a useful mass transit option.” Dr Tony Matthews agreed the best legacy the Olympics could leave for Brisbane would be expanded public transit. Courtney Kruk The document said infrastructure investment in areas such as Fortitude Valley, Kurilpa, Milton, Newstead and Woolloongabba could lead to about 50,000 new homes being built in those areas. Limb added that private investment tended to lag well behind zoning changes, and extensive development may take longer than six years.



A web of shaded pathways, known as the Green and Gold Grid, is also planned across the city. Related Article Exclusive

Public Transport Victoria Bridge shade secured, but Metro expansion hits Games hurdle New connections between the CBD and Suncorp Stadium were planned before the start of the 2027 Rugby World Cup, while shade cloths for the Victoria Bridge could be installed within weeks. Multiple other routes are planned. “This will lead to a lasting legacy of walkability, urban greening, thriving precincts and healthier, more connected communities,” the document says. Schrinner told the lunch his absolute priority was expansion of the Metro into the suburbs. He has previously said this could not be done without funding from the federal government.



“I think if you’re looking for real long-lasting impact, it’s aspects related to mass transit that’s going to help us,” Limb said. Matthews added one of the best legacies Brisbane City Council could achieve through the games would be expansion of green spaces. An artist impression of Brisbane Stadium being built at Victoria Park. Cox Architecture “I would say placemaking and urban greenery … should be the key guiding principles of the legacy,” he said. “We have a relatively low volume of green space available … and we’re going to be sacrificing a fair bit of it for the stadium.



“There’s just endless amounts of well-founded research out there showing that the higher volume of urban green space you have in a city … the better all sorts of things for the residents.” Related Article Road to Brisbane 2032 Evicted pool tenants told to negotiate compensation themselves The document also references plans to capitalise on Brisbane’s “dawn economy”, as well as the possibility of 24-hour precincts, a Global Food Hall, and Pride House for LGBTIQ+ athletes and fans. The Labor opposition on Brisbane City Council highlighted the fact proposed new housing did not include affordability mandates. “[Schrinner] reheated old announcements to pretend he’s achieving something new exactly six years out,” leader Jared Cassidy said.



“Basic services and infrastructure are falling to the wayside … more missed bins, shocking roads, crippling congestion and a homelessness crisis are what this Lord Mayor will be remembered for. “Brisbane needs a champion for 2032. Adrian Schrinner is not it.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Want to volunteer at the 2032 Brisbane Games? Lord mayor announces ‘passport’ plan
World.content:

A system to reward Brisbane residents who already contribute to the community and want to volunteer at the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games has been announced by the lord mayor.

Under the “volunteer passport” system, existing volunteers will build up “credits” that are recognised when the highly competitive application process opens.

Artist impressions of the proposed Brisbane Stadium, to be built at Victoria Park for the 2032 Olympic Games. COX Architecture

At the 2024 Paris Games, about 300,000 people applied for just 45,000 places.

“Effectively, people who are already volunteering out there are developing stamps in their passport – or volunteering credits – which set them up to be a volunteer in 2032, because we want the absolute best,” Adrian Schrinner told a crowd of industry leaders on Thursday.
